Between the North Sea and Nissum Fjord lies a stretch of land the wind has never quite let go of. The dunes wander. Sand settles along the field boundaries. Behind the line of dunes the ground sinks into low, wet stretches where the water does not run but seeps.

A place like that was called a kær — a marsh.

And one of them was called Silkjær.

Later the name was carried by fishermen, beach bailiffs, lifeboatmen, skippers and families who left the place but took it with them.

The family’s history holds two shipwrecks, a religious revival, a prison sentence, secret voyages during the Occupation — and three sisters who, within six years, each gave a son the name Niels Silkjær.

This is the story of the place, and of the people who made it a family name.

The same first names return in every generation — there are eight Nielses and three Ane Johannes in what follows. If the threads become hard to hold, they are set out in the key to the names at the back, together with the family tree.

Where the sources fall short, the text says so. The small circle? opens the caveat for what stands just before it: what is documented, what is inferred, and what is still a guess. All sources are gathered in the list of sources.

The chronicle’s main line

The chronicle sees the family from one particular place in the tree: the author’s. The six links below are the backbone of the work — it is from the last of them that the questions have been asked backwards, and that is why these very people, their brothers and sisters and their children, fill the chapters.

The story does not always run straight. It follows first the smallholding and the beginning of the name, then several of Niels Thomsen’s ten children — the fishing skipper in Esbjerg, the gravedigger on Djursland — but each time it returns to the line here. And notice the quiet paradox: this very line lost the name along the way, when Ane Johanne married a Madsen and Laura a Mikkelsen — and this is exactly where it came back.

Part I

The place before the name

Chapters 1—4 · 1700s—1869
1
Chapter 1 · The place before the family

The marsh

Silkjær was a place long before it became a family name. The name appears as a locality in its own right in Husby parish in Danmarks Stednavne, the national register of place names — a field, a marsh, a property. How old it is, we do not know. But it was the name of the place and not of the family when the first of them we can follow were born out on Sønder Klit in the 1700s.

Today the place lies at Øhusevej 1B in Vester Husby — cadastral no. 13b, divided off from the farm at Øe. The sources call it two things: the parish registers write Økjær, the censuses Øe. These are not two addresses. Øe was the cadastral district, the larger designation; Økjær was the parish’s name for this part of it — the marsh and the houses around it. A family could therefore live on 13b and still have Økjær written in the parish register.The censuses of 1890, 1901 and 1911 record the household directly on matr. 13b, and the land register follows the title from the deed of 1854/55 to the sale out of the family in 1924. That Økjær covered several households can be seen with Thomas Jensen’s brother Esper: his children are born at “Øe”, the newspapers call him Ø., and at his death in 1883 the parish register records him as a smallholder “at Økjær” — the same household, three designations. The property that bears the name Økjær today lies on cadastral no. 15 and is a different property from the family’s. The line of owners is set out in Appendix A. [S60, S61, S65, S66]

Silkjær
The name, split in two
Sil-
Not finally interpreted. A likely candidate is silje — in Old Norse silja — an old name for the willow. The dictionaries also know sil as still or slowly flowing water.
-kjær
Certain. Damp, low, boggy ground. Exactly the kind of meadow that lies squeezed between dune and fjord.

The strongest local parallel points to “the willow marsh”: the farm Silbjerg in the same parish — it lies closer to Husby Sø, some way west of Silkjær — was explained as early as 1900 from silja, an older name for the willow — the slope “has in old times been overgrown with willow”. Whether the two names really share a first element can only be settled if an older form of Silkjær is found. “The marsh by the still water” is another possible reading. Both are interpretations, not facts.The first element has not been established by place-name scholarship. The willow reading rests on P. Storgaard Pedersen’s explanation of Silbjerg (1900) and the dictionaries’ silje/silja; the alternative on the ODS entry sil. The oldest source form found — “Silkjær” in the deed of 1854/55 — looks like the modern one and does not settle the first element; an even older form such as Siljekær could. [S4, S22—S24, S59, S63] All caveats →

One thing, on the other hand, is certain: the name has grown out of the ground — whether the first element is willow or still water, both readings belong to the same wet meadow.

The papers let us watch the property come into view. At Øe lay the farm on cadastral no. 13, which Thomas Miltersen had until then owned and lived on. In 1847 he handed the farm over to his son Jens Thomsen. In 1851 the son had a piece of the land parcelled off: parcel no. 2, cadastral no. 13b, out towards the low marsh. That same summer he sold the parcel to Niels Jensen Poulsgaard, who had himself been born at Øe and had just been widowed. [S40, S61, S62, S63]

“Öby” on the survey sheet.
Image 1c · Survey sheets 1:20,000, sheets Ø15 and Ø16, surveyed 1872 · free map material · credit historiskekort.dk

Niels Jensen kept it only a few years. By a deed signed on 18 December 1854 and registered on 4 April 1855 he sold it on to a young smallholder and fisherman, Thomas Jensen of Husby. What changed hands the deed describes in a single phrase: “a detached house, situated in Silkjær” (»et fritliggende Huus, der er beliggende i Silkjær«). The deeds suggest that the house may have been built during his short ownership — the deed of 1851 mentions no buildings, while that of 1854 expressly refers to a house — but they cannot prove it. The seller stayed on in the house as a retired man in the new householder’s keeping. [S60, S63]

The three words are the name’s oldest dated attestation — and its most down to earth. Here Silkjær does not follow anyone’s name: it describes the place where the house stood, and the buyer is simply called Thomas Jensen. So he did not buy a house that was later named after the family. He bought a house, perhaps quite new, in a place that was already called Silkjær. The family came to the place first; the name came to the family afterwards.

»beliggende i Silkjær« — “situated in Silkjær” — three words in the deed signed on 18 December 1854 and registered on 4 April 1855: the oldest dated source form of the name. Here Silkjær is used to describe a location: the house lay in the locality that bore the name.
Image 36 · [S63] · Rigsarkivet · Ulfborg-Hind Herredsfoged · Arkivalieronline

This is how place names could become personal names in the district. They told where a person belonged. And because a small parish held far too many people called Niels, Jens and Thomas, the place also became a way of telling people apart.

A man could be Niels, son of Thomas.
He could be Niels Thomsen.
He could be Niels from Silkjær.
In the end he could be Niels Silkjær.
Read more about the landscape and the sources

Danmarks Stednavne records Silkjær as a locality in its own right in Husby parish, Ulfborg Hundred. The oldest dated record found is the deed of 1854/55 [S63]. The second element kær is common throughout the West Jutland lowland and consistently denotes wet, low-lying ground.

The first element has a close parallel in the farm name Silbjerg in the same parish — Storgaard Pedersen places the farm south-east of the rectory, and the local archive describes it as lying closer to Husby Sø, some way west of Silkjær. Silbjerg and Silkjær are two different farms and must not be confused. [S114] P. Storgaard Pedersen wrote in 1900 that Silbjerg “probably took its name from the slope having in old times been overgrown with willow, whose older name was Silja” — and selje/silje, in Norse form silja, is given in the dictionaries as an older name for kinds of willow, known also in Danish and Jutlandic usage. If the two names share a first element, Silkjær is the marsh with siljer: the willow marsh. Trap Danmark also knows another Silbjerg in Staby parish, written “Silbiers Bol” in 1688 — the two farms must be kept apart in the sources. The oldest spelling found — “Silkjær” in the deed of 1854/55 — looks like the modern one and does not settle the question; what would settle it is an even older form such as Siljekær or Siliekier, and no such form has been found.

Sources: Danmarks Stednavne, “Silkjær — Husby s., Ulfborg h.” [S4] · Ulfborg-Vemb Lokalhistoriske Arkiv, H318, Wos i æ hawbjerre [S3] · ODS, the entries sil and Selje- [S22—S24] · P. Storgaard Pedersen, Ulfborg Herred, 1900 [S59] · Ulfborg-Vemb Lokalhistoriske Arkiv, correspondence 2026 [S114].

2
Chapter 2 · The 1800s

The sea-hills

It is tempting to read this landscape as holiday country. It was not.

For centuries drifting sand had eaten its way across the fields. The soil was poor, the wind blew from the west all year round, and in winter the storms could take roofs, boats and crops in a single night. And there lay the sea, a few kilometres from the church, without a single harbour.

Fishing was done from the open beach. The boats were dragged down over the sand, launched through the surf and hauled up again on the way home. You went out when the weather allowed, and you read the weather yourself. The families lived from both at once: a smallholding on land and nets in the sea.

The dunes and the open beach at Husby Klit.
Image 1c · Survey sheets 1:20,000, sheets AA16 and Ø16, surveyed 1872 · free map material · credit historiskekort.dk

In the dunes behind the beach — what the district called havbjergene, the sea-hills — the farms lay low and sheltered, their fields turned away from the wind. This was where the family belonged.

“A dune farm like the ones the family lived in. The wreck timber in front of the house is not decoration — it was part of the economy.”
Photo: Jørgen Hanssen · Ulfborg-Vemb Lokalhistoriske Arkiv, B1575 · arkiv.dk
“The hearth in Strandgården. Porch with cobbled floor, a wash copper and smoked meat hung up in the chimney — this was what everyday life looked like indoors.”
Photographer unknown · Ulfborg-Vemb Lokalhistoriske Arkiv, B2329 · arkiv.dk
“Map sheet Ø16 HUSBY, surveyed in 1872 — six years before Thomas Jensen drowned. Notice the names: Nørrekjær, Sønderkjær, Grimkjær, Amtskjær. The whole district is named after its wet ground.”

3
Chapter 3 · 1710—1863

The family on the dunes

Thomas Jensen was born on 12 December 1825 in Husby and became a smallholder and fisherman at Økjær — and the parish’s beach bailiff. His name says what people then needed to know: he was Jens’ son.

And behind him the line goes on. His father was Jens Olesen Klit, born 1785. His father in turn was Ole Jensen Klit, born 1753 on Sønder Klit. The byname says it all: before the family was Silkjær, it was Klit — dune — named after the same landscape, only another part of it. The sand before the marsh.

The family’s root lies a good century and a half before the Silkjær name, out on Sønder Klit, and the pattern is older than the name: here you always took the place with you when you had to say who you were.

Four generations can be followed on the dunes, back to Ib Jensen Klit, born on Husby Klit on 8 September 1710. He and Jens Nielsen Klit, born around 1720, held copyhold farms on Sønder Klit — two neighbours on the same line of dunes, each with his farm held in tenure under the lord of the manor.The generations before 1814 rest on the family file’s own readings of the Husby parish register, where the oldest entries are summary and the names unstable. The sequence hangs together, but the individual links have not been checked in the original. [S40] All caveats →

Their children married each other. Ole Jensen Klit, born on 7 November 1753, and Kirsten Ibsdatter, born on 14 March 1754, came into the world four months apart on the same dune — and became husband and wife. That is what a dune district looked like from the inside: you married the neighbouring farm, because there were no other farms.

Jens Olesen and Maren grew old together and died four days apart: she on 3 March 1861, he on the 7th. Thomas was one of their many children — among his brothers and sisters were his brother Esper and his sister Anne Marie, who both come to matter later in this story (chapter 5). [S40, S69]

One word in the line deserves to be read slowly. Ole Jensen Klit was a strandfoged — a beach bailiff. It was not an office you applied for; it was one you were appointed to. The beach bailiff was the authorities’ man on his stretch of coast: he had to keep watch over wrecks, salvage and record what the sea threw up — timber, rope, barrels, and the drowned — and answer for it to the wreck commissioner. On a coast without a harbour this was the post where the parish’s relationship with the sea turned into paperwork.

Sixty-two years after his death his grandson drowned in the same water — with the same office on his shoulders. Thomas Jensen too was a beach bailiff, says the newspaper that reported his death.

The wives did not come from far away either. Only one did: Maren Thomasdatter was born in Stadil, north-east of the fjord, where her father Thomas Nielsen Langager appears in the census of 1801 as “smallholder with land and enrolled seaman” — entered in the naval rolls and so liable to be called up for the fleet. In the year the list was made, the English fleet lay in the roads off Copenhagen. From that house came the girl who married into Husby Klit.

The woman Thomas Jensen married deserves more room than the sources usually give her.

Generation 1 · The Klit family

Generation 1 · married 20.11.1853
Anne Marie Jansdatter
1827 — 1863 · the Tarpgaard family, Vedersø
Open person card →

When she stood as a bride in Vedersø Church on 20 November 1853, she was not marrying up. The marriage entry records the groom as “bachelor and fisherman Thomas Jensen of Husby Klit” — he had no roof of his own but lived with his brother Ole Jensen out on the dunes. The witnesses were the two fathers: Jan Andersen Tarpgaard and Jens Olesen. A fisherman from the dunes owned less land and more risk than the home she came from; what she thought of the exchange we do not know, for no one wrote it down. But she made it, and moved from the fields of Tarpgaard to the line of dunes by the sea. [S68]

There the young couple stayed for a year or so. Then Thomas bought the house in the marsh — the deed was signed in December 1854 (chapter 1) — and they moved the few kilometres inland. Seen across the family’s long history, the shift from sand to marsh looks like a drift over generations; in the life actually lived it was a single year in a young marriage. And with a house of their own came a new title: the fisherman from the dunes appears in the following year’s papers as smallholder and fisherman.

On 9 July 1855, three months after the deed was registered, she gave birth to their son Niels: the young couple gained a home and a son in the same spring.

The census of 1 February that year shows the house as it stood while she was carrying the child. Thomas, thirty, “smallholder and fisherman; lives mostly by fishing”. Anne Marie, twenty-eight. And two who stayed on after the sale: the seller Niels Jensen, fifty-three, now “retired man, kept by the householder” — and his unmarried stepdaughter, Sidsel Cathrine, thirty-five, who made her living by spinning. The young couple did not move into an empty house: four adults and a child on the way, out in the marsh. [S60] And when the boy was carried to baptism in July, both worlds turned out: among the godparents stood “Niels Poulsgaard” — by all appearances the retired man himself, the man who had sold them the house — and Johanne Cathrine, married to Thomas’ brother Esper, who had also moved in from the dunes to Øe. “The girl Ane Marie Jensdatter” and “bachelor Ole Jensen” may be Thomas’ sister and brother of the same names. [S65, S69]

She had barely nine years there. On 15 August 1863 she died, only 35 years old, leaving small children — six weeks before her birthday.

Anne Marie is the first of several places in this story where a woman carries the family on and then almost disappears from the papers. That is a bias of the sources, not of life.

Without the daughter from Tarpgaard there would have been no Niels — and none of the chapters that follow.

4
Chapter 4 · 1863—1869

When death
came to the house

At Økjær the summer of 1863 took two from the same house.

“Husby Church and churchyard. The lowest courses of the nave are the old granite ashlars; the tower with its spire is whitewashed. Here Anne Marie Jansdatter was buried on 23 August 1863 — the day her daughter Kirstine died — and four days later the child herself; in 1869 her daughter Karen Marie, and on 17 November 1878 Thomas Jensen.”
Photo: ClausNe · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Anne Marie Jansdatter, Thomas Jensen’s wife, died on 15 August 1863, thirty-five years old. The register of deaths writes 36 — she would have turned it six weeks later — and enters her as the parish knew her: “Wife of smallholder Thomas Jensen at Øekjær. Born at Tarpgaard in Vedersø. Father Jan Andersen.” She was buried on 23 August. [S38, S92]

The same day their little daughter Kirstine died — in the register Kjerstine Thomsen, two and three-quarter years old, “daughter of the above-mentioned smallholder at Øekjær Thomas Jensen and his late wife Anne Marie Jansen, born at Øekjær”. The pastor entered them as no. 4 and no. 5 and bound them together with one word: ovennævnte, above-mentioned. The child was buried on the 27th. [S38]

Thomas Jensen stood in the churchyard by his wife’s grave. That same day his daughter died. Four days later he walked out there again.

Six years later, on 6 July 1869, another daughter died, Karen Marie — in the register Karen Marie Thomsen, “daughter of smallholder at Økjær Thomas Jensen and his late wife Ane Marie Jansdatter. Born at the same place.” She was seven years old and was buried on 11 July. [S38]

Anne Marie

Seven years. Six summers later.

The register of deaths has a column for the cause of death. In 1863 it is empty — for Anne Marie, for Kirstine and for several others in the parish. The silence is not the household’s; it is the year’s. In 1869, by contrast, the column is in use, and one word recurs: halssyge, throat sickness. The pastor wrote it beside a two-year-old, a four-and-a-half-year-old, two adults of thirty and the neighbours’ child whose entry stands just before Karen Marie’s. Beside her own name there is nothing.Halssyge was the nineteenth-century word for a throat infection with a danger of choking. It most often covered diphtheria, but was also used for croup and for scarlet fever affecting the throat; the pastor wrote down what could be seen, not a medical diagnosis. The chapter therefore gives the source’s word and puts no disease on any of the three dead. The neighbours’ child’s entry says something about what was going round the parish — not what Karen Marie died of. [S38] All caveats →

Three children were left: Niels, who was eight when his mother died, Maren, six, and Marie, four. [S40]

Thomas Jensen was left a widower with the surviving children. So he remained for fifteen years.

Then came the fifteenth summer, and after it a day in November.

Part II

The wreck and the beginning of the name

Chapters 5—8 · 1878—1916
5
Chapter 5

9 November
1878

Thomas Jensen was lost at sea. He was buried in Husby on 17 November. He was 52 years old.

The parish register’s wording, verbatim: “drowned when capsizing with a sea-boat” (druknet ved kæntring med havskib). A havskib was the flat-bottomed West Jutland beach boat, launched straight from the open beach — there was no harbour. The accident happened on a Saturday. Before the week was out, the whole event was in print in at least two newspapers: a letter written from the west coast that same day was printed in Dannevirke in Haderslev on 13 November and in Korsør Avis on 14 November 1878. The account was written on the day of the accident, and Thomas Jensen is named in it.The newspapers’ date, place and names agree with the parish register; both papers list “beach bailiff Thomas Jensen Silkjær” among the dead. The newspapers, written on the day of the accident, reported that none of the bodies had drifted ashore; the parish register’s collective note at the burials eight days later singles out only one body that did not come ashore — and it was not his. [S2, S25, S42, S43, S67] All caveats →

What we know is enough: a fisherman from Økjær sailed out one November day and did not come home.

Six men · one boat
the outer sandbarthe inner barStage lifeboat stationAnders KnudsenEsper Jensen Ø.two rockets11 am

The boat had gone out in the morning to take in the nets, which as usual had been set the evening before. The weather had turned hard and the sea was running high, but they got safely over the outer sandbar. When the boat reached the inner bar, a violent breaker came down on it and overturned it. It was eleven o’clock in the morning. [S67]

It was seen from land. The accident happened close to the Stage lifeboat station, and both the lifeboat and the rocket apparatus were brought to the spot at once — but the sea was in such violent uproar that the lifeboat could not go out. Two rockets were fired. The man they were chiefly meant for, farmer and beach bailiff Anders Knudsen, swam about for a long time on an oar after the others had drowned. He never reached for the line; either he was too exhausted, or he did not see it. In the end he sank.

There were six men on board. One reached land: the steersman, the so-called “formand”, smallholder Esper Jensen Ø., who saved himself on an oar. The other five drowned, and the newspapers name them all:

Smallholder Peder Jensen Kløve
Smallholder Iver Kristian Olesen Kløve
Farmer and beach bailiff Anders Knudsen Ø.
Smallholder Laurids Mikkelsen
Beach bailiff Thomas Jensen Silkjær
All five of Husby · four fathers of families, the fifth a widower

Thomas Jensen was the fifth. By then he had been a widower for fifteen years.

And the boat was not just a fishing crew. Esper Jensen Ø., the man who reached land on the oar, was Thomas’ younger brother — another son of Jens Olesen Klit, who had moved in from the dunes to Øe. And Anders Knudsen Ø., the beach bailiff who swam so long and never reached for the line, was by all appearances their brother-in-law: their sister Anne Marie was married to Anders Knudsen Øe. Two brothers and a brother-in-law in the same boat. [S69]

Two words in that list move the chronicle. One is strandfoged, beach bailiff. Thomas Jensen was not just a fisherman; he held the parish’s office of taking care of wrecks and stranded goods along the coast. Two beach bailiffs drowned that day, in the same boat. The other is Silkjær. The newspapers write it after his own name — and it was not their invention: two years earlier he had appeared as “Thomas Jensen Silkjær” in a registered deed when he bought land in Vedersø. The death notice shows that the name was in use in the district too. [S64]

So the father was called Silkjær while he was alive — at least in the usage the district passed on to the newspapers. It is his son Niels who makes the name a family name on paper, but he is not the first to bear it.

The current was so strong that none of the bodies drifted ashore. They drifted south, like the boat. The letter-writer feared that the bereaved “would perhaps not even have the comfort of finding their loved ones and laying them to their last rest”. But the letter was written on the day of the accident. The parish register takes stock eight days later, at the burial on 17 November, in a single collective note on the five drowned — and it singles out just one of them: “Iver Chr. Olesen Kløve’s body did not come ashore.” The other four, then, came ashore in the days between. Thomas Jensen was given his grave in Husby churchyard. [S67]

He was not alone at sea that morning. Another fishing crew came ashore a little to the north without mishap; a third boat was swamped by a breaker so close to land that the whole crew got in, three of them only just. And an accident of this size had not happened in Husby since 5 September 1851, when a fishing crew from Husby Klitte was lost in the same way.

The aftermath

The survivor walked home. Esper Jensen was badly shaken when he came ashore, but after resting a little while at the Stage lifeboat station, changing into dry clothes and taking some refreshment, he walked to his home, which lay a good way from the station. The letter-writer calls it a trait typical of the West Jutland fisherman’s toughness.

And then the newspaper draws up the account of those left behind. The last three named — Anders Knudsen, Laurids Mikkelsen and Thomas Jensen Silkjær — were reasonably well off, with grown-up children; only Anders Knudsen’s one child was 11. It was worst for the two smallholding families from Kløve: Peder Jensen left seven children not yet confirmed, the youngest not three months old, and Iver Kristian Olesen four children, the eldest not yet eight. Both families were extremely poor. Only by the fathers’ “untiring diligence and ability” had they earned their daily bread without becoming a burden to anyone, and now they would have to turn to poor relief unless a collection were started.

That sentence about “grown-up children” is a piece of information about our own family, written by a stranger: Thomas Jensen’s eldest was Niels, 23 years old. Five days after the accident he stood as a bridegroom.

The brother who survived had been there all along: when Thomas’ first-born was baptised in 1855, Esper’s first wife Johanne Cathrine stood among the godparents (chapter 3). [S65, S69]

The sea did not let him go. On the night between 15 and 16 June 1883 he left land again, six men in Jørgen Sørensen’s boat. They were last seen on Saturday afternoon, four or five Danish miles from land — thirty to forty kilometres — by the fishermen on another boat from Vedersø Klit, who were themselves making for shore because a south-easterly gale was breaking. No one saw what happened. It was not an accident the lifeboat service could reach; it was a boat that did not come home. Later the hull was seen drifting, capsized, far up the coast at Hanstholm. [S66]

On 17 July — exactly a month later — his body drifted ashore on the beach at Fjaltring, and on 22 July he was buried in Husby churchyard. He was 54. Niels Silkjær was then in his fifth year of service at the lifeboat station in Vedersø (chapter 7). His uncle did not drown in front of the station, as his father had. He vanished. [S58, S66]

The parish register records him as “Jesper Jensen (Klit)”, smallholder “at Økjær”, born on Husby Klit. The newspapers had called him Ø. after the place where he lived; the parish register remembered the place he came from. He too carried his places as names.

The fishing ground “Stage” at Vedersø is the same locality that gave its name to Stagegaarden — whose man, Anthon Stage, stood thirty-seven years later as number twelve in the lifeboat crew.

Which station

The newspaper calls it “the Stage lifeboat station”, and that is not the station’s official name. The lifeboat service’s own book of 1927 knows only one station here: Vedersø, founded in 1852. Its first superintendent was beach bailiff Chr. M. Stage, and from 1864 to 1908 it was Morten Th. Stage. The district named the station after the men who ran it — and after the fishing ground of the same name.

That means the lifeboat that could not go out on 9 November, and the rockets fired in vain, came from Vedersø. The same book records a new boatman at the station on 1 January 1879. His name is Niels Silkjær. [S58]

His son Niels was 23 — old enough to know the sea, young enough to have his whole life ahead of him with that knowledge. Five days later he stood as a bridegroom.
Read the whole article in transcription — “A fishing crew drowns”
Dannevirke, Haderslev · 13 November 1878 · translated from the paper’s own text

A fishing crew drowns. A terrible accident occurred on Saturday the 9th of Novbr. — so it is written to “Nattd.” — on the sea off Husby, when a fishing crew consisting of 6 men was drowned, all save the steersman, the so-called “formand”, who saved himself ashore on an oar.

In the morning the boat had gone out to take in the nets, which as usual had been set the evening before, and came safely over the outer bar, although the weather had turned hard and the sea was running high; but when it came to the inner bar a violent breaker came down and overturned the boat.

From land the accident was seen, and help was given at once, which was the more easily done as the accident happened close to the Stage lifeboat station, and both the lifeboat and the rocket apparatus were immediately brought to the scene of the accident, but the sea had risen into such violent uproar — it was, namely, heavy squally weather — that the lifeboat could not go out, and although 2 rockets were fired, no rescue was possible, since he for whom the rockets were chiefly meant, farmer Anders Knudsen, who swam about for a long time on an oar after the others had drowned, had either become so exhausted that he could not grasp the line thrown to him by the rocket apparatus, or did not see it; he made no attempt to grasp the line, and at last he sank.

The dead were: smallholder Peder Jensen Kløve, smallholder Iver Kristian Olesen Kløve, farmer and beach bailiff Anders Knudsen Ø., smallholder Laurids Mikkelsen and beach bailiff Thomas Jensen Silkjær, all 5 of Husby, as the rescued man, smallholder Esper Jensen Ø., also lives in Husby.

Of these the first four named were fathers of families and the fifth a widower; but the three last named were in reasonably good circumstances with grown-up children, save Anders Knudsen, whose only child is but 11 years old; Peder Jensen Kløve, on the other hand, has 7 unconfirmed children, the youngest not 3 months old, and Iver Kristian Olesen leaves four children, the eldest not yet 8 years old; both these families were extremely poor, so that it was only by the untiring diligence and ability of the now drowned fathers that the families had their daily bread without becoming a burden to anyone; but it goes without saying that there is now such great need in these two families that, unless private charity steps in very soon, they will be forced to turn to public poor relief; but it is to be hoped that an association will be formed to work for a collection to be set going to relieve the distress of those left behind, and it is further to be hoped that the appeal of such an association will not sound in vain; for if there is need anywhere, it is here.

As the current was so strong at the time the accident happened, none of the bodies of the dead drifted ashore, but drifted south, just as the boat did, and those left behind will now perhaps not even have the comfort of finding their loved ones and laying them to their last rest.

At about the same time as the accident happened, another fishing crew came ashore a little to the north without any mishap, whereas a third boat was swamped by a breaker; but most fortunately it was right by the land, and although the crew went into the sea, and 3 men were only with the greatest difficulty saved from drowning, they nevertheless all came ashore alive, though naturally very much exhausted.

A trait characteristic of the West Jutland fisherman’s toughness and endurance is that the “formand” of the fishing crew that drowned, Esper Jensen Ø., who as mentioned saved himself on an oar, although he was badly shaken when he came ashore, nevertheless, after resting a little while at the Stage lifeboat station, changing into dry clothes and taking some refreshment, walked to his home, which lies a good distance from the said lifeboat station.

Although the sea often demands its sacrifices, an accident such as this has nevertheless not occurred in Husby since 5 September 1851, when a fishing crew from Husby Klitte was lost in the same way as the one mentioned above; but of those lost on that occasion only two men were from Husby.

The transcription follows Dannevirke, which has the fullest text. Korsør Avis prints the same letter two days later with small differences — the paper the letter was addressed to is abbreviated there “Rtd.”, and the year 1851 is unclear. A few letters are worn in the print and have been read from the context. The parish register’s collective note at the burials differs from the letter on one point: there the crew was at sea “after their hooks”, not after nets. [S42, S43, S67]

6
Chapter 6 · 1855—1928

Niels Thomsen
becomes Silkjær

Niels Thomsen was born on 9 July 1855 in Husby and baptised on 22 July. Like his father he became a smallholder and fisherman at Økjær. But before anything else happened in his life, this happened:

Nine days in November 1878
91011121314151617
9 NOVEMBER
His father is lost at sea.
14 NOVEMBER
Niels marries Ane Johanne Kristensen.
17 NOVEMBER
His father is buried in Husby.

He married five days after his father’s death and three days before his funeral. It sounds like a scandal, and it was not.

The marriage entry itself settles it. In the column for witnesses there are two names: N. Nielsen Skytte and Thommas Jensen — the groom’s father. The witnesses’ declaration was made when the banns were published, and under the ordinance of 1824 the pastor had to read the banns from the pulpit on three Sundays in a row; for a wedding on 14 November that means from the middle of October. So the father had signed while he was alive: the wedding was being prepared before he drowned, and was neither arranged nor hurried by his death. It was the custom of the house: when Thomas himself stood as a bridegroom in 1853, the witnesses were the two fathers — his own and the bride’s (chapter 3). And the last column of the entry says “In the church” — not a quiet wedding in a home, but a public one. Five days after the sea took the father, the son stood at the altar, and the father’s name stood on the paper. [S28]

The bride was born in 1843 — twelve years older than her husband. In a home whose breadwinner had just drowned, a smallholding and a fishery had to be kept going at the same time. Whether the age difference or the practical circumstances had any bearing on their marriage, the sources do not say.

1878 was also the year another register closed around him. The levying roll for Husby — district 28 — had known him since 1873, when he was entered at eighteen: Niels Thomsen, son of smallholder Thomas Jensen, born in Husby on 9 July 1855, 62¾ inches tall — about 164 centimetres. In 1878 the draft board added its note: 29½ inches round the chest, found exempt from military service — and the entry was struck through diagonally, as was done when a man was deleted from the roll. The army had no use for the slim fisherman from Økjær. The sea made other demands: from January 1879 he stood by the lifeboat at Vedersø, and there he stayed for thirty-seven years. [S112]

The marriage was short. Ane Johanne Kristensen was born on 25 September 1843 in Rindom parish. She gave birth to their daughter Ane Marie on 2 March 1880 — and died at Økjær on 13 September the same year, a little over six months after the birth, 36 years old. She was buried in Husby churchyard on 19 September.

In under two years Niels had lost his father and his wife and been left a widower with a baby. A little over a year later, on 10 November 1881, he married in Husby Ane Jensen, born on 29 April 1858 at Landtingmark in Ejsing near Vinderup and baptised on 2 May. The Husby parish book points to her parents: a Jens Claus and a Stine — and so to the explanation of whom the son of 1886 was named after.The parish book lists “MF Jens Claus, MM Stine” as Ane Marie’s maternal grandfather and grandmother. Ane Marie’s own mother, Ane Johanne Kristensen, died when she was six months old, and the entry calls the mother simply “wife Ane” — that is, the stepmother Ane Jensen. Jens Claus and Stine are therefore very probably her parents. The identification has not been checked in the original; the Ejsing parish register, births 1858, has not been read. [S27] All caveats →

There may be one more trace of her father. On 15 April 1846 the parish council met at Husby rectory, and among the business was an application to have the schoolboy Jens Claus Mattzen released from school. The request had been sent in too late — it should have been made straight after the autumn examination — so the boy was tested in arithmetic, passed with a satisfactory result, and the release was granted. The local history that recounts the meeting adds that the foreign-looking spelling of the surname is probably because Jens Claus had been born and baptised in Angeln in South Schleswig. A boy who left school in 1846 was born around 1831. If the schoolboy is Ane Jensen’s father — name, parish and age fit — the family’s thread towards the duchies gains both a place and a figure.The local history does not itself connect the schoolboy with Ane Jensen; the identification rests on the name, the parish and the age — a release from school in 1846 fits the family file’s year of birth, c. 1831. In that case the family later moved inland: Ane was born at Landtingmark in Ejsing in 1858 and came back to Husby at her marriage. See caveat 07. [S169] All caveats →

Here too it is worth pausing for a moment. Ane Jensen stepped into a home with a baby after a dead wife, bore a large family of children herself — and ended her days, as we shall see, somewhere quite different from where she began.

Where they lived · censuses and deeds

The census of 1880 places Niels Thomsen and his first wife, Ane Johanne Kristensen, at Øe — but the census gives no cadastral number. The censuses of 1890, 1901 and 1911 then record Niels and his second wife, Ane Jensen, on cadastral no. 13b: the cadastral number Silkjær stands on.

The deeds tie the ends together: the father, Thomas Jensen, bought the house on 13b in 1854/55, and in January 1879 — two months after the wreck — Niels acquired title to the place by allotment in his estate. So Niels did not move to a strange farm; he took over his father’s house in the marsh, and the name followed — first with the children, then with himself. The history of the property from the parcelling-off in 1851 is told in chapter 1; the documentation — and the line of owners up to the sale out of the family in 1924 — is in Appendix A. [S60, S61, S63]

His two sisters went the other way. Maren, born 1857, married Jens Mikkelsen of Tim in 1883 and had eight children there; one of the sons was named Thomas Jensen Mikkelsen — which points back to her drowned father, but Silkjær did not come with it. Marie, born 1859, married Christen Jensen Poulsgaard in Husby Church in 1888 and stayed in the parish all her life; she died at Højtoft in 1925 and lies in Husby churchyard. By the time Silkjær became the family’s name, both sisters had long since married into other names. The name did not pass to the whole family of brothers and sisters — it stayed with the one who had taken over the house. [S40]

The transformation of the name, as the papers show it

The middle step of the staircase can be dated. In the census of 1890 the household stands on matr. 13b with the parents recorded as Niels Thomsen and Ane Jensen — and with all five children recorded as Silkjær: Ane Marie Nielsen Silkjær, Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, Ane Johanne Nielsen Silkjær, Jens Klaus Nielsen Silkjær and Esper Nielsen Silkjær. The father Thomas had already appeared as Thomas Jensen Silkjær in a deed of 1876, and the newspapers used the name in 1878 — but in Niels’ own household it came in from below. [S60, S64]

So the name entered the papers from below, through the children, while the parents still stood under the patronymic. And it applied to the whole family of children: Ane Marie too, the daughter of the first wife, was given the farm name. Silkjær clung to the household and the place, not to one particular mother’s children. The last step came with a document: on 21 November 1905 Niels received a certificate permitting him to bear the name Niels Silkjær — the farm name had become a legal family name. The parish register carried the certificate all the way back to the starting point: in the margin by his baptismal entry of 1855 the name Silkjær was added, “according to certificate”.The date 21 November 1905 follows the parish register’s annotation at the baptism; the land register’s reference to the certificate is read as 27 November 1907. The discrepancy has not been resolved. [S64] All caveats → [S64, S65]

The parish book remembers the same

The Husby parish book from around 1950 points the same way. In the entry on Ole Lauridsen, his wife Ane Marie has her grandparents listed, and it says: “FF Thomas Silkjær, FM Ane Marie”. That is Thomas Jensen and Anne Marie Jansdatter — the man who drowned in 1878, and his wife. In the parish’s own book he too carries the name.

A parish book from 1950 is a backward-looking source: it names ancestors as the family and the parish remembered them, seventy years on, and the parish register’s contemporary entries call him Thomas Jensen. But the memory has a foundation: Thomas Jensen owned the house in Silkjær from 1855 and was recorded as Thomas Jensen Silkjær in the deed of 1876. The parish book does not remember a wrong name — it remembers the man who first carried it.Source: Vort Sogns Historie, Husby parish, p. 334, the entry Ole Lauridsen — Ulfborg-Vemb Lokalhistoriske Arkiv, the PDF HUSBY-SOGN. No earlier attestation of Silkjær together with a personal name than the deed of 1876 has been found in the sources examined. [S27, S64] All caveats →

It is a small thing on paper and a large thing in reality. A patronymic dies every generation; it says only who your father was. A place name can be inherited. With Silkjær the family had, for the first time, a name that could be handed on.

He died on 17 June 1928 in Esbjerg and was buried in Gormsgade Cemetery, which the sources then called Esbjerg New Cemetery — not in the parish where the name was born. But before that move lie thirty-seven years on another stretch of coast, at the station that had watched his father drown.

7
Chapter 7 · 1879—1916

The boatman
at Vedersø

After a long series of disastrous strandings the state founded the North Jutland Lifeboat Service in 1852. There was still no harbour: the lifeboat stood on a wheeled carriage in a boathouse, was harnessed to horses, driven through the dunes and launched straight into the surf — in the same weather that had put the ship in distress.

“Redningsstation” — the rescue station — at Øhuse on Vedersø Klit, and behind the dunes Øby and Husby.
Image 1c · Survey sheets 1:20,000, sheets AA15, AA16, Ø15 and Ø16, surveyed 1872 · free map material · credit historiskekort.dk
12345678910111213

There is a photograph of the crew of the Vedersø lifeboat station — and behind it, in the archive, lies the handwritten slip on which someone has named every single man from left to right. The heading says “c. 1910-20”, and another hand has later written 1915 above it.

From the left · name · residence
1Mikkel Vandborg · Sund 2Niels Silkjær · Silkjær 3Anton Pedersen · Husby Klitvej 4Ole Pedersen · neighbour to Silkjær, now Husby Sommerland 5Johan fræ æ Havbjerge · “no further introduction needed” 6Poul Bank · Vesterhavsvej 45 · superintendent 7Poul Knak · Knak, now the camping farm 8Peder Kr. Gammelgård “Pe’ Kjærk” · south of the campsite 9Søren Jørgen Sørensen, Poulsgaard · coxswain for 35 years 10Peder Sand Pedersen · Vandværksvej 11 11Jens Kr. Gammelgaard · now Vedersø Klit Camping 12Anthon Stage · Stagegaarden 13Peder Pedersen “Skomager” (the shoemaker) · Ø. Husby

Notice numbers two and four. The man is called Silkjær and lives at Silkjær — name and place in the same breath; the house on the cadastral plot had by then been the family’s since 1855 (Appendix A). And his neighbour needs no other address than “neighbour to Silkjær”. On this slip the place has become a fixed point that the whole row takes its bearings from.

Who he was

The man in the photograph can be named from two sources. The family’s own records give Niels Thomsen Silkjær two occupations, not one: “Smallholder & fisherman, Økjær in Husby” — and “boatman, the lifeboat station, Vedersø”. So he was not in a group picture by chance. He was a regular member of the station’s crew. [S15, S21]

The lifeboat service’s own work of 1927 confirms his post, the date he was taken on and his length of service; there he stands with name and portrait. See the reproduction of the record below. [S58]

So the picture can say what it is: around 1915 — the archive’s dating — the boatman Niels Silkjær stood in the lifeboat crew at Vedersø, 60 years old and in his thirty-seventh year at the station. Thirty-seven years earlier his father had drowned on the same coast. The father came ashore and was given a grave in Husby; Iver Kristian Olesen was the only one of the five whose body never came ashore. [S67]

“The lifeboat crew at Vedersø, lined up in front of the boathouse. In the darkness behind them the bow of the boat with the name VEDERSØ can just be made out. Second from the left: Niels Silkjær.”
From the left: Mikkel Vandborg (living at Sund), Niels Silkjær “Silkjær”, Anton Pedersen (Husby Klitvej), Ole Pedersen (neighbour to Silkjær, now Husby Sommerland) and “Johan fræ æ Havbjerge” — Johan from the sea-hills. The archive dates the photograph to 1915; the personal details place it between 1908 and 1916.
Vedersø Lokalhist. Arkiv F33 · [S37] · arkiv.dk

What made him join just then, we do not know. But the sequence stands firm and is recorded with dates in the lifeboat service’s own book: the accident in November, the appointment at New Year — at the station that had tried in vain to come to his father’s aid. Looking back, the picture is hard to miss: the sea had taken his father, and he signed up to bring other men’s fathers home. The service was not heroics; it was neighbourliness, made into a system.

The lifeboat service’s record of 1927

Niels Silkjær’s service

In 1927 C. P. Eisenreich, a senior clerk in the Lifeboat Service, published the official work on Det Nørrejydske Redningsvæsen, the North Jutland Lifeboat Service — each station in turn, with its history, its list of strandings and, at the end, a row of the men who had served there. The chapter on Vedersø runs to five pages. It ends with seven portraits under the heading “Of the men who have served at the Vedersø station, the following must be mentioned”.

The third man on page 314 is ours. With a portrait. And with the Cross of Honour on his breast.

Niels Silkjær was taken on as Boatman on 1 January 1879 and retired on account of age on 1 October 1916, and shortly afterwards was decorated with the Cross of Honour of the Dannebrogsmænd. He took part 7 times with the Lifeboat and 8 times with the Rocket Apparatus in the rescue of 195 shipwrecked persons.
Five lines · six facts
Post
Boatman at the Vedersø station
Taken on
1 January 1879 · 23 years old
Retired
1 October 1916, on account of age · 61 years
Length of service
37 years and 9 months
Launches
7 with the lifeboat · 8 with the rocket apparatus
Decoration
The Dannebrogsmænd’s Cross of Honour, conferred 10 November 1915
195
shipwrecked people brought ashore in the rescues he took part in. It is not his merit alone — but he was there.

The record establishes three things: his title, the decoration and the date he was taken on.

The title. The book writes Baadmand, boatman — the ordinary post in the crew, not the coxswain’s. He sat at the oars and did not command the boat; the family’s word “bådsmand” covers the same post.

The decoration. The book says he was decorated shortly after he retired — but the protocol of the Chapter of the Royal Orders shows otherwise: he was appointed on 10 November 1915, while he was still in service, recorded as “serving boatman at the Vedersø lifeboat station”. The grounds are not preserved in the Chapter’s files, but it was not a medal for bravery on one particular night — it was an honour for long and faithful service, given in his thirty-seventh year at the station. He signed the oath of loyalty at Vedersø on 30 November 1915. He wore the cross for the last twelve and a half years of his life, and it is what you see in the portrait. [S110, S111]

The date. And then there is the first line, which is the one that hurts.

Fifty-three days

His father drowned on 9 November 1878 and was buried on the 17th. On 1 January 1879 the son was on the lifeboat service’s payroll. Fifty-three days passed from the accident to the appointment — forty-five from the parish register’s date.

And he did not sign up just anywhere. The newspaper wrote in 1878 that the accident happened “close to the Stage lifeboat station”, and that both the lifeboat and the rocket apparatus were brought there in vain. The station at Stage is Vedersø, as chapter 5 tells. So it was the station that could not reach his father that he joined at the turn of the year. And he stayed there until they sent him home on account of age.

And then there is his own voice. Every Dannebrogsmand had to send a life account to the Chapter of the Royal Orders, and Niels Silkjær’s is still there: two handwritten pages from November 1915, together with the photograph he enclosed and the printed oath of loyalty he signed at Vedersø on 30 November. [S111]

His own voice · the life account of 1915

“I was born on 9 July 1855 in the home where I still live. As my parents were very poorly off, I had to go out into service early. From my 10th year I served with the farmers, and as soon as I was grown I went along on the fishing. At 23 years of age I married and at the same time, on my father’s death, took over my father’s home, a little property for 2 cows; but as this could not feed the family, I had still to go to work for the farmers and to the fishing when the North Sea was calm. After barely 2 years of marriage my first wife died, leaving me and a little girl. A year later I married for the second time, my wife who is still living, and in this marriage we have 10 children. I was taken on as boatman at the ‘Vedersø’ lifeboat station in 1879, the first years as a reserve and permanently employed some 4 years after, which post I still hold. It has often been very hard to provide our bread, as the day wage was small and the fishing often failed, and the pay in the lifeboat service was also small — it has now been raised over the years, which has been a good help to me that I have been glad of, and now all the children but one are grown, so now it goes tolerably well. My photograph is sent herewith. Most humbly, Niels Silkjær.”

Everything the chronicle has had to gather from scattered sources stands here in his own words: service with the farmers from the age of ten, the father’s home with two cows that could not feed the family, the first wife who died leaving him and “a little girl” after barely two years of marriage — and his father’s death and his wedding in one and the same sentence. One number sticks out: he writes ten children in the second marriage, where the parish registers know nine. The number matches the whole family of children if the daughter from the first marriage is counted — she grew up in the same household — but whether that is the conflation he made himself cannot be decided. And one piece of information is new: the 1879 appointment meant the first years as a reserve; the permanent post came only some years later. The book’s clean date covers a slower beginning.

The protocol in the Yellow Palace records him on page 510 — “Grounds not received by the Chapter of the Orders”, so what brought the cross just then is written nowhere. But it also records the end: a stamp about the death in June 1928, and beside it: Dek. indk. 9/7 1928 — decoration received. Three weeks after his death the Cross of Honour was sent back to the Chapter of the Orders, as the rules required. The cross in the portrait was on loan — the service was his own. [S110]

The photograph, which the archive dates to 1915, shows him in his thirty-seventh year of service — the year the cross came. The year after, he was done.

The fifteen strandings of his years of service

The book gives each station a complete list of the rescues that succeeded. At Vedersø a total of 300 shipwrecked people were saved, and the apparatus had been set in motion a further 55 times without being used by the shipwrecked. Lay Niels Silkjær’s years of service over the list, and there are exactly fifteen strandings — as many as he is credited with.

3.11.1879Galeas “Oscar” of Kerteminde5rocket 12.12.1880Schooner “Alpha” of Thisted4rocket 22.2.1882Cutter “Ondine” of Ostend5boat 11.6.1885Brig “Speed” of Drammen12rocket 14.10.1887Schooner “Vilhelmine” of Frederiksstad6rocket 21.11.1888Schooner-kuff “Ente” of Leer4rocket 30.12.1888Schooner “Haabet” of Nyborg5boat 3.12.1891Steamship “Ætna” of Copenhagen22rocket 16.12.1892Barque “Rothesay” of Tønsberg12rocket 15.1.1898Steamship “Vesta” of Gävle15boat 14.3.1902Steamship “Wanda” of Odessa29boat 2.4.1902Three-masted schooner “Margrethe” of Harburg6rocket 11.—13.11.1902Steamship “Probus” of Stockholm37boat 23.11.1906Steamship “Ophelia” of Helsingør19rocket 10.1.1907Steamship “Gustaf” of Motala19boat

The last nine years of his service, 1907—1916, stand empty in the list. The station turned out in those years too — the apparatus was set in motion — but the list records no new successful rescues in his last years of service.

The accounts do not quite add up, and that must be said. The station list divides the fifteen into six boat rescues and nine by rocket, where the book says seven and eight of him; at the “Speed” in 1885 the boat was in fact launched and worked for two hours before they gave up and saved the men by rocket, which may explain the one. The main figure is harder: the fifteen strandings add up to 200 saved, not 195. The difference of five cannot be settled from the two sources; the chronicle follows the book’s own figure. [S58]

The work Niels Silkjær was part of
The road to the scene of the wreck. The boat on its carriage, harnessed to teams of horses, along a sandy track through the dunes — in the weather that had put the ship in distress.
The crew follows the boat on foot. No uniforms — just fishermen and smallholders from the parish in their own clothes.
The last stretch down towards the surf. From here the boat had to be launched straight from the open beach.
What it was all about: a stranded steamship, and a line shot out with the rocket apparatus. The figure on the right stands on the beach, hauling.
The boathouse with the crossed oars on the door. Here the boat stood waiting, all year round.
The station in the dunes: crew building and boathouse, later extended. All of it a few hundred metres from the water’s edge.
Image 6 · Vedersø Lokalhist. Arkiv F33 · photographer unknown · arkiv.dk
Read more: how a rescue was carried out

If the boat could not get out, they used the rocket apparatus: a line was shot out to the stranded ship, after which the crew hauled out a heavy hawser and made it fast round the mast, a good two feet above the tail block. Along the hawser a breeches buoy was sent out, one man at a time. The instruction board that went out with the line was printed in Danish and English. The rule was clear: women, children, passengers and helpless persons ashore first.

A station’s crew consisted of a coxswain and boatmen; the superintendent kept the records and decided when to raise the alarm. The coxswain was elected by the crew themselves and had undisputed command during rescues. The pay was a fixed yearly fee — until 1876 it was 32 kroner for a coxswain and 24 for a boatman, plus extra pay for exercises and launches. On this list Poul Bank is the superintendent, and Søren Jørgen Sørensen of Poulsgaard was a coxswain in the lifeboat service for thirty-five years. In all of Niels Silkjær’s time Vedersø had only two superintendents: Morten Th. Stage until 1908 and then Poul Pedersen Bank. Morten Th. Stage had succeeded beach bailiff Chr. M. Stage in 1864; both came from the farm the district named the station after. [S58]

In that order of rank Niels Silkjær was one of the boatmen — bådmand, an ordinary member of the crew, from 1879 to 1916. [S58]

Vedersø was one of the original stations: the rocket apparatus came from England as early as 1851, the station was founded with the lifeboat service in 1852, and in 1854 a lifeboat built in Copenhagen arrived together with the first boathouse. On 23 November 1906 the steamship Ophelia of Helsingør stranded south of Thorsminde with a cargo of oilcake; the boats from Vedersø and Tuskjær were called out, and the Vedersø boat arrived at one o’clock. Nineteen men came ashore, by the rocket apparatus. Those are the kind of days the crew in the photograph were chosen for.

The figures say something about why it went on: in the period 1852—1925 10,500 seamen were brought ashore alive by the Danish lifeboat service. From 1914 came the first motor boats; from 1965 the boats were drawn by tractors, and in 1973 the small stations were closed.

The lifeboat “Vedersø” was built at the naval dockyard in 1924 as the last without an engine. It turned out 38 times and was last in action in 1933, when the kuff “Farø” of Copenhagen stranded in fog with 13 men aboard — nine were saved by the boat, four by the rocket apparatus. The boat still exists; it was found in Nexø harbour and came back to Nr. Lyngvig in 2013.

8
Chapter 8 · 1880—1902

The children from Økjær

Niels Thomsen Silkjær had a large family of children, who grew up in and around Økjær. All of them carried Silkjær in their names, in varying forms: Nielsen Silkjær, Jensen Silkjær, or simply Silkjær. The first time anyone in the family is themselves recorded with the name in a census is in 1890, when the five eldest appear as Nielsen Silkjær, while the parents still appear as Niels Thomsen and Ane Jensen. That turns out to be decisive for everything that follows — for the name did not go only to the one who stayed. It went out into the world with every single child.

The eldest of the brothers and sisters has her own entry in Vort Sogns Historie — under her husband’s name. Ole Lauridsen was born in Husby on 29 May 1861 and died on 11 July 1916; so he was almost nineteen years older than his wife. They had eight children. The youngest, Ole, was born on 14 May 1916 and was barely two months old when his father died on 11 July. Ane Marie was then thirty-six and was left alone with the children — about the same age as her grandmother Anne Marie Jansdatter had been when death took her from her own children in 1863.

She stayed on the farm for almost forty-four years after his death. Around 1950 it says of the place:

“Mrs Lauridsen has the farm here today, but all the land is let, and in summer Mrs Lauridsen lets part of the farmhouse to summer guests.”

Read that sentence together with chapter 2. The landscape that was not holiday country — poor soil, drifting sand, fishing from the open beach — was becoming it. And the first of the family to live off it was a widow who let out her fields, and her rooms to guests from the town. The land no longer gave enough. The view did.

Vort Sogns Historie, Husby parish, p. 334 · Ulfborg-Vemb Lokalhistoriske Arkiv [S27]
The boy from the school photograph, grown up

The parish book includes him as a smallholder at Damhus, Sønder Nissum: Niels Silkjær Lauridsen, born in Husby on 9 August 1911, son of Ole Lauridsen and Ane Marie. Under grandparents it says simply: MF Niels Silkjær, smallholder, Husby — his mother’s father, the man from chapter 6.

Married to Elin Kamma Lillelund, one daughter: Henny, born in 1940. He took over the property from his father-in-law in 1938 — eight tønder of land, two of them scrub, and a farmhouse that was 80—100 years old.

It is the same movement as with Ane Johanne: the name is carried on by a man who is officially called something else.

Entry from Vort Sogns Historie, c. 1950 [S27]
Part III

The wreck, the revival and the prison

Chapters 9—13 · 1873—1963
9
Chapter 9 · 1873—1963

The widow
from Årgab

There was no harbour at Årgab. There was a beach, a line of dunes and an open, restless sea.

The boats were launched into it by hand and hauled out of it again by hand. Årgab was one of the four old fishing hamlets on the narrow Holmsland Klit — together with Haurvig, Brunbjerg and Kokkedal, which are named together in a royal letter as early as 1553. In the dunes stood the fishermen’s huts — frame huts of turf, reed and marram — where the fishermen and the baiting girls stayed from April until Midsummer, with one double bed for the men and one for the women.

The local literature makes the women’s share of the work concrete: sorting out the fishing lines, mending, washing and drying them, baiting the hooks — ese — cleaning cod and boiling train oil from the livers, and on top of that cooking and keeping the hut clean. At Nymindegab a baiting girl’s day’s work is reckoned at around 2,400 hooks, four tubs of 600 — what one fisherman could set on a trip, and so there was one baiting girl to each fisherman. Fishing from the open beach, in other words, was not the men’s work alone; it rested on the women’s labour too. [S116]

It was here that the family lived into which the fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkjær — Niels Thomsen’s eldest son, whom we have just met among the children from Økjær — would later marry. Kristiane Enevoldsen — in the sources also written Christiane — was born on the dunes on 27 March 1873, daughter of the farmer Simon Enevoldsen and Ane Marie Christensen in Haurvig.

On 1 April 1892, in Haurvig Church — whitewashed, neo-Romanesque and built four years before her own birth — she was married to Christen Olesen Enevoldsen, smallholder, fisherman and boat skipper at Årgab, born in the same place on 17 October 1871. They bore the same surname but belonged to two different Enevoldsen families on the dunes — in both cases the name came from a distant ancestor called Enevold.

As boat skipper Christen was responsible for the boat and its crew when it was launched through the surf and hauled up again. The boat was called “Forsøget” — the Attempt.

Holmsland Klit from Renderne to Havrvig: Årgab in the middle, the sea to the west and the fjord to the east.
Image 1d · Survey sheets 1:20,000, sheet AA11, surveyed 1871 · free map material · credit historiskekort.dk
Four years after the wedding · 1 April 1896

Exactly four years after the wedding the boat was wrecked. She was called “Forsøget”, had been built the year before and was reckoned one of the soundest on the coast. She came in over the outer bar — and then the breaker rose behind her.

Four boats were out that morning — two from Årgab, two from Lyngvig — on the first trip of the year in the spring fishing. The other three came safely ashore. According to the account Ringkøbing Amts Dagblad carried in the days that followed, the sea lifted the stern so high that the boat went almost vertically down onto the bar and struck the sea bed.Ringkøbing Amts Dagblad has not been obtained. The course of events is known from Sigurd Enggaard Poulsen’s summary of the newspaper from 1977 and from Klinting’s account; the two agree with each other about the breaker, the stern and the blow against the sea bed. See caveat 41. [S134, S177] All caveats →

Five men were on board. Christen stood first on the list, because he was the skipper:

1Skipper Chr. Olesen Enevoldsen24 · married · smallholder at Årgab · b. Årgab 17 October 1871lost
2Peder Enevoldsen25 · married · smallholder at Årgab · b. Haurvig 8 August 1870lost
3Jens A. Larsen20 · bachelor · b. Klegod 3 September 1875lost
4N. Marius Christensen23 · bachelor · b. Sønder Bork 4 May 1872lost
5Fisherman Søren Andersen Jensen26 · married · smallholder at Årgab · b. Årgab 17 November 1869came ashore alive

The list hides a divide. Three of them — Christen, Peder Enevoldsen and Søren Andersen Jensen — were married smallholders at Årgab and owned the boat together. The other two were young farmhands from Klegod and Sønder Bork; they had no gear with them but were hired at a fixed wage for the trip. So the accident struck unequally. At Årgab both the breadwinners and the capital the boat represented were lost; the two young men left parents, not widows. [S177]

The fifth is the one to remember. Søren Andersen Jensen clung to an oar and drifted some six thousand alen south in the surf, followed by a crowd of fishermen on the shore who tried in vain to reach him. Then his strength failed too; he lost consciousness and let go of the oar. At that Enevold Enevoldsen leapt out after him with a line round his waist and caught hold of the unconscious man. He was taken for dead until the attempts to revive him worked — he came to life before the doctor from Ringkøbing arrived.

He was not the only one to catch hold of something. Peder Enevoldsen got a grip on a piece of the broken mast and drifted some 2,500 alen south with the current, while people followed along the beach. Then his strength gave out. He let go of the stump of mast and drowned.

The man with the line round his waist was Peder’s brother. That is the fact that ties the two fates together: the same family lost a son in the surf and pulled another woman’s husband out of it alive, a few thousand alen apart. Enevold Enevoldsen was later awarded the medal for saving life.The relationship and the medal are given by Klinting, whose informant for the account was, according to the text, Enevold Enevoldsen himself. He must not be confused with the boat skipper’s father, the fisheries inspector Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen — they are two different men in two different Enevoldsen families. The medal has not been searched for in Statstidende. See caveat 41. [S177] All caveats →

The bodies came ashore the next day, Maundy Thursday, 2 April. Three of them had drifted up off Gødelen — Christen, Peder Enevoldsen and Jens A. Larsen. Christen lay on the strandlen in Bjerregaard that belonged to Peder Christian Nielsen, known on the dunes as Dahl. A strandlen was an allotted stretch of the coast where a particular farm had both the right and the duty over what the sea threw up — wreckage, timber and the drowned.The name rests on A.K. Sørensen’s family book, which writes “Peder Christian Dahl’s strandlen”, compared with Vragwiki’s list of strandlen on Holmsland Klit, which for Bjerregård gives “1885—89 P.C. Nielsen (Dahl)”. Dahl was the farm name, not the surname. Klinting instead names beach bailiff Jens Dahl, Bjerregaard, as the one who found the bodies. See caveat 42. [S56, S177, S180] All caveats →

Christen was buried from Haurvig Church on 6 April 1896 — Easter Monday — twenty-four years old, and Peder Enevoldsen followed in the same place. Jens A. Larsen was buried at Nørre Lyngvig. Niels Marius Christensen’s body only drifted ashore a couple of months later off Hovstrup and was buried in Sønder Bork. The boat itself came ashore smashed at the same spot. [S177]

Six weeks later, on 17 May 1896, Kristiane gave birth to a daughter: Kristine Oline. She never saw her father. She is a posthumous child — and we meet her again in chapters 12 and 13.

Whit Sunday · 24 May 1896

The stone came a month and a half after the wreck — and seven days after Kristine Oline was born. It was raised close to the road in Årgab village, on a fenced plot given by Knud Andersen, and it was paid for by the fishermen of Esbjerg.

Off the coast lay the gunboat “Grønsund”. Its commander, Captain Brædstrup, and First Lieutenant Reinhardt came ashore for the unveiling. At three o’clock they began with “Dejlig er Jorden”. Then Brædstrup handed over the stone on behalf of the Esbjerg fishermen to the fishermen of the dunes and asked the people of the dunes to protect it.

Some 500 people had come to the unveiling, surely one of the largest gatherings ever held down there on the dunes.
Dagens Nyheder · 28 May 1896 · after Ringkjøbing Avis [S178]

The harbour town gave the stone to the open beach. Esbjerg had a harbour, a mole and a fishermen’s association; Årgab had sand and muscle. It was the town with means that set up the memorial over those who had none.

Kristiane had given birth a week before. Whether she stood among the five hundred, the source does not say.The newspaper page has not been seen. The report was received in transcript from Hardy Sørensen and is given in the transcript’s spelling, not the paper’s own. Dagens Nyheder itself is reporting Ringkjøbing Avis — that paper has not been checked in Mediestream, where the volume is freely available. [S178] All caveats →

Kristiane was then 23 and had two small sons: Enevold Jepsen, born on 13 October 1892 and named after his paternal grandfather, and Simon, born on 2 May 1894, named after his maternal grandfather.Both sons appear in the sources: the prison register of 1913 records Thomas as stepfather to “3 stepchildren”, and Enevold Jepsen, b. 13.10.1892, bears his paternal grandfather’s name. The birth entries have not been read in the original in Ny parish (Haurvig church district), births 1892—1894. [S31, S32, S44, S45] All caveats →

Ten years passed.

In 1906 she married again — the fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkjær from Husby, almost nine years her junior. That marriage, and all that followed from it, are chapters 11 to 13.

In that marriage two families met who had each given the sea a man. Kristiane’s first husband drowned off Årgab in 1896. Thomas’ own grandfather, Thomas Jensen, drowned capsizing with a sea-boat off Husby in 1878.

A generation later the sons of that home sailed out on the same North Sea — during the war, with weapons for the resistance.

Kristiane Enevoldsen lived long. She died in Esbjerg on 31 July 1963, 90 years old.

Kristiane Enevoldsen — widowed at 23, married again at 33, died at 90 in Esbjerg.
The family archive
“Haurvig Church, built in 1869 — the tower only in 1947, and both years are painted on the wall. Here Kristiane Enevoldsen was married on 1 April 1892, and here Christen was buried on 6 April 1896.”
In the churchyard in the foreground stand stones with the name Tarbensen — the family Ane Kirstine Silkjær married into on New Year’s Day 1920.
Photo: ClausNe · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons [S36]
“There was no harbour. The boats were launched and hauled up on the open beach — the work Christen Olesen Enevoldsen was responsible for as boat skipper. J. Chr. Fjord’s painting of 1924 shows a sea-boat home from fishing: the fish has been sorted and laid out on the sand, and a farmer with a horse and cart is on his way to buy.”
The painter’s own inscription: “Fiskeri med gl. Havskibe” (fishing with old sea-boats) — exactly the type of boat Thomas Jensen capsized in in 1878.
J. Chr. Fjord, 1924 · painting in private ownership
The other widow

There was one more widow at Årgab after 1 April. Peder Enevoldsen’s wife was called Ane Marie, was born in 1868 and had two small children: Jensigne, born 1893, and Kresten. She stayed on in the little thatched house by the road, and she never married again.

The two women lost their husbands in the same boat, on the same afternoon, in the same little village. From there their lives went separate ways. Kristiane was widowed at twenty-three and married again at thirty-three and followed her new husband into everything chapters 11 to 13 are about. Ane Marie remained a widow for fifty-seven years. She died in 1953, eighty-five years old, and lies in Haurvig churchyard, where her husband was buried.

The sea took her son too. In March 1918 Kresten came home on Easter leave from military service in Copenhagen and went down to the harbour in Ringkøbing to find a boat across to Årgab. He sailed with two young men from the town in a south-westerly gale. They were warned, set sail all the same and capsized not far from the harbour. All three drowned and were buried at Easter.

Ane Marie does not belong to this family. She stands here because she is what Kristiane might also have become.This section is based on an account by Søren Rinder Kristensen, Årgab, with additions from Hardy Sørensen. Søren Rinder is a grandson of the survivor Søren Andersen Jensen; Hardy Sørensen is of Peder Enevoldsen’s family. It is family tradition written down in our own time, not archival record — neither Ane Marie’s dates, the children’s births nor the accident on Ringkøbing Fjord in 1918 have been checked in parish registers or newspapers. See caveat 43. [S179] All caveats →

10
Chapter 10 · 1896—1899

The wreck and the revival

Four men drowned off Årgab on 1 April 1896. Three and a half years later a mission house stood on the dunes. Between the two dates lie a funeral, a sermon and a community that remade its life.

Before the revival · Årgab, the 1860s
The sou’westers

More than sixty years later an old man sat down to write down how things had been before any of this happened.

Christen Christensen Sørensen — known in the district as Kræ Krænsen — was born at Årgab in 1857 and grew up at the place called Hummelbu south of Revsgård. In 1880 he married and moved across the fjord to Nr. Bork. In 1931 he set down his memories. Of his parents he wrote:

How deep their Christianity otherwise was, I shall not judge, but on occasions I had a feeling that they bore a deep reverence for what was holy. So I remembered from the time I was a little lad that I went along to the sea when the “sea-ship”, as it was called, was to go out. Father was with them. When they had first carried the heavy boat down, so that it stood with its stem out towards the surf, and shovelled in the ballast and set the tubs in place, each man stood beside the boat, ready to jump in as soon as it floated. The skipper stood at the stern. Then it was a holy moment, when all these 7 men, weather-bitten faces and tanned fists, bowed, took off their sou’westers, folded their hands for a little while, until a faint “Amen” was heard. And after that the command was given, and the boat slid quite quietly out towards the surf, and each man jumped to his oar.
Kræ Krænsen · memories set down in 1931, of a childhood at Årgab [S134]

The prayer was short and had no words but the last. It had no congregation and no pastor. Only the boat’s crew and the little boy who remembered it many years later. And it took place at exactly the moment when the men knew their strength might not be enough.The memory was set down in 1931 about a childhood in the 1860s — at a distance of some sixty to seventy years. Kræ Krænsen makes his own reservation in his first sentence. See caveat 35. [S134] All caveats →

Then comes the sentence that turns the memory into history rather than mood:

But as time went on, yes, also in the time when I myself was a sea fisherman, the quiet moment before they began disappeared.

The man watched it happen. The quiet moment had not survived unbroken until 1896. It was on its way out while he himself stood in the boat.

Where that faith came from, another man of the dunes has explained. The later pastor H.P. Kristensen remembered the old dune people’s Christianity as a “living inheritance” from home: the mother’s prayers, the hymns, the book of sermons brought out on a winter Sunday. The North Sea he called their second pastor — the one they listened to on weekdays. Normally the dune people did not speak of their relationship with God; modesty kept the mouth shut, and only the direst need could force it open.Kristensen’s words are given at two removes: Poulsen quotes P. Pedersen’s “Klittens historie”, in which Kristensen speaks. The original has not been seen. [S135] All caveats →

The words give a language for what happened on the dunes in 1896. The accident did not create the fear of God. But the direst need forced out what was otherwise carried in silence.

Christmas at Hummelbu · Årgab, the 1860s

By four o’clock on Christmas Eve everything was in order. The animals had had their Christmas feed, the children were scrubbed and in their good clothes when the lights were lit. There were Christmas cakes, and then came the soup with meatballs “as at a wedding”, roast duck, roast chicken, fruit soup. Father began by saying: “Well then, in Jesus’ name”.

Afterwards he took the hymnbook and read the Christmas gospel, and then almost all the Christmas hymns had to be sung. Father was no singer; mother was a songbird. The boy fell asleep in the middle of “I denne søde juletid”, and the hymns they did not get to, Father sang himself early on Christmas morning.

“When we had sung on Christmas Eve, the new cards came out, then we were to play Sevinsel for an hour or so, and then we drank coffee and so to bed.”

The hymnbook and the cards lay on the same table on the same evening. A generation later, in the revival’s homes around the fjord, they were placed on opposite sides of a line. Not yet.The line could be funny, too. Anders Poulsen of Enggården in Nr. Bork — Sigurd Enggaard Poulsen’s grandfather — had become “helfe”, holy, and held a Christmas-tree party for the Sunday-school children. His old drinking fellows teased him with a brand-new pack of cards as a Christmas present; he promptly had the purchase reversed at the grocer’s and sent the money to the Inner Mission. So in the movement’s accounts, under “Gifts received”, it came to say: Received from the sale of cards: kr. … [S134]

Sevinsel was a card game. The Christmas parties in the district went round in turn from farm to farm with aquavit, coffee punch, cards for the old and dancing in the best room for the young. [S134]

1 April 1896
The breaker

The boat had almost come over the bars when the sea rose behind it. Four of the five fishermen were lost, among them the skipper Christen Olesen Enevoldsen — Kristiane’s husband and father of a child not yet born. The course of the wreck, the crew and the memorial stone at Renderne are in chapter 9.

Here begins the story of what the accident set in motion.

April 1896
The funeral at Haurvig

Forty-eight years later an old man sat in Esbjerg and was asked whether he remembered any particular events from his time at Haurvig. Chr. Sørensen — formerly a lifeboatman at the Haurvig lifeboat station for thirty years and beach bailiff for forty-eight — turned ninety-five on 6 May 1944 and was interviewed by Vestkysten. The conversation was reprinted in Tidsskrift for Redningsvæsen, the lifeboatmen’s journal.

The journal gives him only an initial, but everything in the profile fits Christen Olesen Sørensen, born at Aargab on 6 May 1849, fisherman and beach bailiff in the same place. He must not be confused with the drowned skipper Christen Olesen Enevoldsen; they are two different men in the same small parish.The identification rests on birthday, age, occupation and residence, which all coincide. The interview text itself names him only as “Chr. Sørensen”. He married for the second time in 1892, four years before the day he describes as his and his wife’s conversion, and died in Esbjerg on 25 March 1948. [S49, S53] All caveats →
