— Yes, the revival that came in 1896. A couple of fishermen had drowned, and that gave the push to the revival. Before that time there was much drinking and card-playing up there, and people did not know about keeping the Sabbath. But I remember so clearly what old Pastor Nedergaard, whose son is now pastor at the Elias Church in Copenhagen, said at the funeral: “You will not hear what the Lord speaks in the church; but what he speaks from the sea, that you shall hear!” From that day many were converted, my wife and I too.
Chr. Sørensen, 95 · Tidsskrift for Redningsvæsen, vol. 11, 1944 [S49]

Sørensen’s aside about the son at the Elias Church points to one particular home — and so to the pastor’s name: Peder Christensen Nedergaard, resident curate on Holmsland. “Old Pastor Nedergaard” is seen from 1944, not from the funeral: in April 1896 he was twenty-eight, had been on Holmsland for a couple of years, and his own child had been born at Årgab the year before. The man who interpreted the sea as God’s speech lived as close to the accident as a pastor could.The identification goes through the son: Paul Theodor Nedergaard, born at Årgab on 23 June 1895, became resident curate at the Elias Church in Copenhagen in 1924, and Dansk Biografisk Leksikon records him as the son of “resident curate on Holmsland, later parish priest at Gerslev, member of the Landsting Peder Christensen Nedergaard” (1868—1945), raised in a home shaped by the Inner Mission. That the father was curate on Holmsland in these years is in the lexicon; that it was he who took the funeral on 6 April 1896 is only in Sørensen’s memory — the officiating pastor is recorded in Ny parish register, deaths 1896. [S49, S52] All caveats →

At the same time the memory has its limits. Sørensen is wrong about the scale — he says a couple of fishermen, and there were four. The memory was written down almost half a century later, so the quotation from the pulpit cannot be treated as a verbatim record.The revival on the dunes was under way from around 1890, and there was Inner Mission activity before the wreck. Sørensen’s figure and his rendering of the funeral address are both treated as memory. See caveat 13. [S49, S51] All caveats →

But as testimony to how the dune people themselves remembered the connection, it is strong. The wreck did not create the revival. It gave it its breakthrough.

Three years earlier · Harboøre, November 1893

The sentence about the sea was not Nedergaard’s invention. Fifty kilometres to the north, twenty-six fishermen from Harboøre had drowned in November 1893, and at the joint funeral the Inner Mission pastor Carl Moe interpreted the disaster as a call to those left behind. The address set off a nationwide controversy over the Inner Mission’s view of Christianity and made an impression all along the west coast.

But the distance to Harboøre was also a distance in experience. Sigurd Enggaard Poulsen, who grew up by the fjord as a grandchild of the revival’s people, weighed the two against each other: “It was more ‘the other pastor’, the sea, that had spoken than it was the pastor at Harboøre.” The phrases from Harboøre recurred, and the songs with them. But the disasters were the dunes’ own.

On 20 May 1894 a sea-boat was wrecked on the inner bar off Søndervig; five men drowned, two were saved. The same day Trækfuglen (the Migrant Bird) from Nymindegab was lost a couple of nautical miles out with all her crew, four men. On 1 April 1896 came Forsøget. Thirteen men in two years — “everyone knew everyone on the dunes, and in one way or another almost everyone was related to one or more of them.”

The words could come from Harboøre. The experience was their own. [S134]

The contested question in the Denmark of the 1890s was whether a disaster should be met with unconditional comfort — or whether the pastor must also interpret it as God’s warning to the living.

No source shows that Nedergaard knew or imitated Moe’s address. The words in Sørensen’s memory belong to the same form of preaching, but the kinship between the two funerals is an interpretation, not a documented connection. [S54]

23 October 1899
Getsemane
Harboøre26 drowned · 1893Årgabthe wreck · 1896HaurvigGetsemane · 1899HolmslandThabor · 1899LyngvigEbenezer · 1910

The revival began with meetings in private homes. So many came that the parlours could no longer hold them, and three and a half years after the wreck the mission house Getsemane (Gethsemane) stood finished at Haurvig. The master mason Kristen Jensen had built it, and on 23 October 1899 it was consecrated by the Bishop of Ribe, Carl Viggo Gøtzsche. It became the centre for meetings, mission weeks, youth work and Sunday school on the southern dunes.

That a bishop came and consecrated the house says something about what it was. Getsemane was not a breakaway congregation but an Inner Mission meeting place with the church’s sanction — a house beside Haurvig Church, not instead of it. The church had baptism, communion and burial; the mission house had the weekdays, when lay people could themselves speak, pray and sing several times a week.

The name was hardly chosen by chance. Gethsemane is the place of prayer and of deep distress — the garden where the cup did not pass. The same year Thabor was built inland on Holmsland, and in 1910 Ebenezer followed at Sønder Lyngvig. The movement spread along the dunes.

In parallel · Nr. Bork Fælled, the 1890s—1901
A home on the other side of the fjord

The revival was not a single event in April 1896. It moved from home to home, and it went both ways across the fjord — known on the eastern side as early as the 1870s, and fed anew from the dunes in the 90s. How it came into a home, there is no description of from Årgab. But there is one from the other side of the fjord, where Kræ Krænsen had moved.Everything in this section takes place at Nr. Bork Fælled east of the fjord, not on Holmsland Klit. It stands here as a parallel to Kristiane’s parish, not as a description of it. The connection between the two sides is documented through the brothers. See caveat 35. [S134] All caveats →

The influence from Årgab reached the home through one particular channel. Kræ Krænsen’s brother Chr. Sørensen had stayed over there and was awakened before them; he had “often, before the conversion, written about his awakening and said that now Father must also make it earnest”.The brother at Årgab is probably the same Christen Olesen Sørensen who was interviewed about the revival in 1944 — but the identity has not been settled in the parish register. See caveat 36. [S49, S53, S134] All caveats →

The 1890s. The “præstbal”, the round of dances, went from farm to farm in turn, and one evening it was Kræ Krænsen’s turn. His daughter Line had begun going to Sunday school down at Enggården. When there was to be dancing at their home, Kirstine, the daughter from down there, would not stay with them any longer.

That is the whole scene. A friend who went home.

After the party Line’s mother said to Line’s sister: “I wish you could have it like Kirstine!” The home still stood outside. True, they read Vilhelm Beck’s sermons on Sundays — “the long ones, that is” — but Line did not count that as revival. “No, that came later.”

1901. Line was sixteen. Her mother caught diphtheria, and the doctor said she must go to the hospital in Varde. They got hold of a fast team, and she was laid on a bed up on a sprung cart. It was thirty kilometres, and she had a high fever. Father drove with her. “We never thought she would come home again.”

She came home.

Both father and mother knelt down and stayed kneeling a long time, and we stayed sitting each in our place. Later we could find Father lying on his knees out in the cowshed and the barn. He was in great spiritual trouble. That is how the conversion came, as I remember it.
Oline “Line” Holm, 92 · in conversation with Sigurd Enggaard Poulsen, 1976—77 [S134]

Afterwards Father could come home from a visit to his brother and say in the doorway: “Well, little girls, now we shall sing. Now I have learnt a new one!” The revival songs were learnt by word of mouth and carried across the fjord by a brother.

And then the thing later generations have found hardest to include: the conversion did not make them faultless. Line remembered that her father could afterwards have the odd “slip” and come home unsteady across the fields, and Kræ Krænsen wrote it himself, without beating about the bush: “But then we must again confess with shame on our faces that we have suffered one defeat after another.” The deepest change was a new way of seeing — themselves, their defeats and God’s grace. “Most of all I remember the joy after the conversion,” said Line. [S134]

Back on the dunes · 17 May 1896
The child born into the revival

When Christen was buried, Kristiane was heavily pregnant. Six weeks after the wreck she gave birth to a daughter: Kristine Oline Enevoldsen. The child had been conceived before the wreck and was born into the revival.

She was not the only pregnant wife in the boat’s partnership. Søren Andersen Jensen’s wife Larsine gave birth to their daughter Sørine Andrea on 21 June, not quite three months after the wreck. Two wives in the same small circle went with child through that April: one had got her husband back after he had been given up, the other had had hers brought home as a body from a strandlen in Bjerregaard.Larsine’s confinement is given in a genealogical compilation, not in an original parish register. No source names the women who followed the boat from the dunes on 1 April; whether these two stood there cannot be documented. [S55]

Three men from this part of the story return: Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen had lost his son. Søren Andersen Jensen was the only one to come ashore alive from the boat. And a fourteen-year-old boy in Husby, Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, had as yet nothing to do with Årgab.

Whether Kristiane herself was awakened, the sources do not say. She does not appear in the material examined from the mission houses — but she lived in the midst of it: first as the wife of one of the dead, then as a widow in the small community where the wreck was given a religious meaning, the homes filled with meetings, and the house was built.No available material on the mission houses on the dunes mentions Kristiane Enevoldsen, and the name Silkjær does not appear either — neither among the first awakened, on the building committee nor on the board. The connection between the family and the revival runs through the wreck, not through the house. [S50, S51]

But Kristine Oline grew up in the parish where her father’s death had been interpreted as God’s speech, and where the itinerant preachers later came along the dunes. Seventeen years after the wreck, one of them became the adult outside the house whom she dared to write to. That belongs in chapter 12.

11
Chapter 11 · 1882—1956

Havnegade 179

From Økjær to Esbjerg. This chapter is about one house on the harbour — the fishing skipper’s home, where the generations from the marsh at last came together under one roof.

ØkjærEsbjergÅrgab

The road to the house begins back at Økjær — with the boy born there on 10 January 1882. Thomas Nielsen Silkjær was Niels and Ane Jensen’s eldest son. Where several of his sisters went inland, he went out towards the sea — all the way to Esbjerg, the town that in a single generation had grown from a flat field into Denmark’s leading fishing town.

He came earlier than you might think. As early as 1905 a T. N. Silkjær, fisherman, is assessed for tax in Esbjerg — twenty-three years old, unmarried, with no house number. Where the address should be there is instead a name in quotation marks: “Robert Skov”. By all appearances it is a boat. A young man with no lodging in the town was entered under the vessel he sailed in.See caveat 27. The order of the initials separates father from son — the father is Niels Thomsen, the son Thomas Nielsen — and the occupation fisherman, not fishing skipper, fits a man who only took his examination in 1916—17. But it is a single entry with initials and no address, and that “Robert Skov” is a vessel is a reading of the quotation marks and the empty house-number field, not a statement in the source. [S94] All caveats →

Then the tax books fall silent about him until 1922. Meanwhile the family moved back and forth between the dunes and Esbjerg: Anna was born in Esbjerg in 1907, Niels at Årgab in 1910 and Ejlert in Esbjerg in 1915. Together with Christian Lauritsen, born at Årgab in 1904, the four births trace the family’s movement between dune and harbour town.

Anna’s baptismal entry gives the first address we know for the family in the town. She was born in February 1907 at Helgolandsgade 22 and baptised in church on 10 March by Pastor Berg. The father is recorded as fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkær, the mother as Christiane Enevoldsen, with a reference to the marriage on Holmslands Klit on 5 May 1906. Two of the four godparents came from Husby: smallholder Niels Silkær and his wife — the child’s paternal grandparents, who thus travelled to the harbour town for their grandchild’s baptism. The other two were fisherman Georg Gaardestrup Thellefsen and his wife, whom we do not know. No one from the mother’s Enevoldsen family stands in the circle — the exact opposite of Arne’s baptism at Haurvig six years later, where all four godparents came from Årgab and none bore the name Silkjær. The name is spelled Silkær throughout, two years after the name certificate had made it legal.

And the street is not just any street in this story. Nine years later, in September 1916, Kristiane’s daughter from her first marriage, Kristine Oline, married from Helgolandsgade 14 — four numbers down the same street, in her future in-laws’ property. She had been ten years old and living in the house when her sister was born at number 22. [S104]

In 1922 Thomas reappears in the tax book, now as a family man at Gl. Færgevej 7. That address remains the household’s for at least eight years, and the census of 1925 records the owner of the house as “Th. Silkjær” — the fisherman from the dunes owned his front house in Esbjerg. [S101] It is not one move but a commuting between two coasts that slowly became a home.

We know him unusually well, for he appears with a full biography in the contemporary work Dansk Fiskeristat of 1935—36.

Dansk Fiskeristat 1935—36, pp. 116—117 · [S8]
Thomas Nielsen Silkjær
Born10 January 1882 in Husby Fatherfisherman and Dannebrogsmand Niels Silkjær Married5 May 1906 to Kristiane, née Enevoldsen TrainedThe Fishing Skippers’ School in Esbjerg 1916—17 Vesselmaster of the cutter “Anne Kirstine”, E.94 · 33.61 tons · 48 hp ResidenceHavnegade 179, Esbjerg

Notice two things. One is the father’s title: Dannebrogsmand. Niels Thomsen Silkjær had been honoured with the Dannebrogsmænd’s Cross of Honour, and he wears it in the portrait — the story behind it is in chapter 7. When the son was registered in Dansk Fiskeristat in the mid-thirties, the father was dead — but the title went with him into the entry.The title is in Dansk Fiskeristat [S8], the decoration can be seen in the portrait [S41], and the occasion is printed in Eisenreich 1927 [S58]. The date of the award — 10 November 1915 — is in the Chapter of the Royal Orders’ protocol of Dannebrogsmænd; see chapter 7. [S110] All caveats →

The other is the address. Havnegade 179 is the bridge between the family’s two worlds. Here Thomas lived. Here too his son Christian Lauritsen Silkjær is registered — baptised in the parish register as Kristen Lauridsen Silkjær — born on 4 May 1904 at Årgab on Holmsland Klit, who took his skipper’s examination in 1924 and commanded the cutter E.426 BERGIT. And here Niels Thomsen’s widow, Ane Jensen, died on 28 June 1936. The tax books record the household there from 1932 until the book ends in 1956, and they show whom the house held. In 1932 the book records six at the address: Thomas, his mother, his daughter Anna, his sons Christian Lauritsen and Ejlert — and the step-grandchild Arne, entered as serial number 33944 immediately after the father; his story is told in chapter 13. [S89, S144]

Think of the arc of that woman’s life: born at Landtingmark in 1858, married into a widower’s home at Økjær in 1881, a large family of children by dune and marsh — and her last years in a fishing skipper’s home on the harbour in Esbjerg, where she died at 78.

There were also two daughters, and they appear nowhere else in this chronicle. Anna Silkjær, born on 17 February 1907 — the year after her parents’ wedding — stays in the house the whole way. The tax books follow her through twenty-three years: sewing apprentice on Gl. Færgevej in 1928 and 1930, domestic help in 1932, and from 1935 to 1951 shop assistant at Havnegade 179. The census of 1940 records her at the address.The tax books give only initials, and for several years there are two A. Silkjær at the same address. The occupation field separates them: in 1935 one is an old-age pensioner — Ane Jensen, who dies the year after — and the other a shop assistant. That the shop assistant is Anna rests on the census of 1940, on the unbroken sequence from the same household — and on the baptism in Zion’s Church in April 1945, where she stands as godparent with name, title and address: Miss shop assistant Anna Silkjær, Havnegade 179. There were, moreover, two Annas with Silkjær in their names in the same street: the census of 1940 records Anna Silkjær, b. 17.2.1907, at no. 179 and her cousin Anna Kirstine Silkjær Torbensen, b. 15.4.1929, at no. 132 with her parents. The godparent in 1945 is the elder — the address, the surname and the title all point to her. [S151] Elna Elisabeth is already in the family file as Thomas Nielsen Silkjær’s youngest child, born on 20 January 1919, and the tax book’s year of birth fits [S40]. The family file calls her the sixth child, but it counts a twin sister Kirsten; the parish register has only one birth on 4 May 1904, so Kirsten is treated here as a duplicate, and the couple had five children. [S40, S70] Anna’s parentage, on the other hand, stands in the original: the baptismal entry in Vor Frelser parish 1907 records the parents as “Fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkær and Christiane Enevoldsen” [S104]. Note too that there are two Elisabeths: the sister on Havnegade and an Elisabeth in Niels’ own household at Gormsgade 122 in 1940. They are not the same person — the sister is on Havnegade both the year before and the year after. [S40, S89, S94, S95, S101] All caveats →

The younger is called Elna Elisabeth, the youngest of the five, born on 20 January 1919 at Gl. Færgevej 7 and baptised in Zion’s Church on 9 February by Pastor Roesen — the same pastor who two and a half years before had married Kristine Oline. The parish register records the father as fisherman, not fishing skipper, and the mother as “wife Kristiane née Enevoldsen, 45 years”. She appears in the book in 1939 and 1941, twenty and twenty-two years old, at the same address as the others — and with one word in the occupation field, where her sister has shop assistant and her brother share fisherman: Miss. Then she disappears from the sequence — and the reason is the obvious one: on 10 October 1942 she was married in Zion’s Church to the clerk Holger Nielsen, a master tailor’s son from Strandbygade, born in Esbjerg the same year as herself. She appears in the entry as office assistant living at Havnegade 179, and her father was a witness.

Three years later, in March 1945, she gave birth to a son at St Joseph’s Hospital. He was baptised Kjeld Silkjær Nielsen. The name had stopped being a surname and become a middle name — but it was there. At the baptism her father, fishing skipper Thomas Silkjær, and her sister, Miss shop assistant Anna Silkjær, stood as godparents. Both with the address Havnegade 179.

Five years later came the second son. Thomas Silkjær Nielsen was born on 19 February 1950, while the family was living at Spangsberggade 44; the father now appears as forwarding agent. The boy was baptised in church on 6 April.

Seventeen days before, the child’s grandfather had died. Thomas Nielsen Silkjær had stood godfather to the eldest boy in 1945; at the youngest he was gone, and in his place his own children stepped in: Miss Anna Silkjær, Havnegade 179 — who had carried the first one too — fishing skipper Niels Silkjær, Strandbygade 67, and fisherman Kristian Silkjær, Havnegade 179. Three of the brothers and sisters from Havnegade around their sister’s child, barely two weeks after their father had been laid in the ground. The boy was named Thomas.The child was born a month before his grandfather died, so the name was chosen while he was alive; that it was a naming after him, the entry does not say. The family did, though, name after the same pattern in the other branch: Niels’ first-born was given his maternal grandfather’s first names, Jørgen Georg, in 1931 [S154]. The addresses confirm the godparents independently: the tax books record Niels at Strandbygade 67 in 1946, 1949 and 1951 and Kristian at Havnegade 179 up to and including 1951 [S94]. [S157]

The third son came the year after. Mogens Silkjær Nielsen was born on 16 June 1951 at the same address and baptised on 12 August, by the same Pastor Brask. This time the godparents were neighbours and not family — a coal merchant and his wife from Kronprinsensgade.

He became a journalist on Esbjerg Ugeavis and died on 9 December 1997, forty-six years old. And when the cemetery’s register entered him, it did not write Nielsen under surname but Silkjær. What had been a farm name for his grandfather and a middle name for himself had become the name he was entered under in the end. [S158]

She lived longest of them all. Elna Elisabeth Nielsen, née Silkjær, died on 5 February 2015 at the Fanø care home, ninety-six years old. She outlived her youngest son by seventeen years and left at her death two sons, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. She was born into a fishing skipper’s home on the harbour in the year when her father was still a fisherman, and she lived through almost the whole of the century that followed.

Anna was in the house when her grandmother died there in 1936, when her father died there in 1950, and she is still at the address the year after, when her mother Kristiane is recorded as Mrs Silkjær. After 1951 none of them are there any more. In Anna’s case the reason is the simplest: she died on 10 October 1952, forty-five years old — the entry of 1951 is her last. Kristiane lived until 1963 and died at the Old People’s Home; where she lived in between, the books do not say. In the last two volumes, 1954 and 1956, only one Silkjær is left at Havnegade 179: her brother Ejlert. [S94] The name had moved through four generations — and one of them stayed where it was.

Ane Jensen · 1858—1936

She came to Økjær at twenty-three in November 1881 and stepped into a house where a wife had just died. On the table lay grief, and in the cradle lay a child of a year and a half, Ane Marie, who was not hers. From that day she was the child’s mother — the parish book afterwards calls her quite simply “wife Ane”, without distinction.

In the next twenty-one years she bore nine children in the same house: Thomas in 1882, Ane Johanne in 1883, Jens Klaus, Esper, Karen Marie, Ane Kirstine, Sidsel Kathrine, Jensine Kristine — and Ellen in 1902, when she was forty-four. Notice the name the first daughter was given. Ane Johanne was the dead first wife’s name. It was not a muddle in the papers but a custom: the new wife gave her daughter her predecessor’s name — in the house where the predecessor had lived and died. And the family had done it before. When Niels’ uncle Esper lost his first wife Johanne Cathrine in 1856, his first daughter with his new wife was named Johanne Cathrine the year after. The same course, the same choice, a generation apart — and it was the uncle who did it first. [S69] It is above all her children who carry the name out into the country.

And then they moved. Niels Thomsen Silkjær died on 17 June 1928 in Esbjerg and was buried in Gormsgade Cemetery — not in Husby, where he had been baptised, married twice and lived most of his life. The exact date of the move the sources do not give, but the frame is narrow: in the census of 1925 they are at Peder Skramsgade 2 in Esbjerg — he seventy, she sixty-seven, recorded with the dates of birth the parish registers of Husby and Ejsing give them. The tax book records him there again in 1928, now as an old-age pensioner, the year he dies.

So they did not move in with their son. They set up their own home at the other end of the town, half an hour’s walk from the harbour — and they did something more. In the household there is a third person: Niels Poulsen, born in 1917, recorded as foster son. He was not a stranger’s child. He was their grandchild.

The Husby parish register records the birth on 28 April 1917 at Økjær — in their own house. The mother is “unmarried Jensine Kristine Nielsen Silkjær, 20 years”, their second-youngest daughter, and named as the father is the farmhand Laurits Nikolaj Poulsen, 22, of Gudum. On Whit Sunday, 27 May, the boy was baptised in Husby Church; his aunt the girl Ane Kirstine Nielsen Silkjær carried him, and among the godparents stood his grandfather, smallholder and fisherman Niels Silkjær.

How large a place the father had in the boy’s life, we do not know — and he did not get many years to have it. A death certificate from Lemvig closes the trail: Laurits Nikolaj Poulsen died on 28 November 1923 at the county hospital, unmarried, 28 years old, still resident in Gudum parish — after fourteen days’ illness; the cause of death reads as furunculosis followed by blood poisoning. The boy, who was growing up with his grandparents, was six. Whether father and son ever saw each other, the sources do not say. [S115]

Eight years later the boy sat in a flat in Esbjerg with his grandparents, seventy and sixty-seven years old. They had not taken in a child from outside; they had kept their daughter’s son.

And that arrangement ended when the husband died. Niels Thomsen Silkjær died in June 1928, and at the census of November 1930 the household on Peder Skramsgade has broken up in two directions: the widow had moved in with her son Thomas at Gl. Færgevej 7, and the boy had moved home to his mother. The census finds him at Fjand in Sønder Nissum — thirteen years old, in a house with Jensine Kristine, her husband Martin Jeppesen Nørfjand and the boy’s half-brother Evald. He had lived eleven years with his grandparents and after that had a family with his mother in it.

He stayed in the parish and became a fisherman. On 6 December 1940 he was married in Sønder Nissum Church to Maria Nielsen, domestic help, born at Arnborg on 22 December 1919. The parish register writes out his parentage as it had in 1917: son of Jensine Kristine Nielsen Silkjær and the farmhand Laurits Nikolaj Poulsen — with the addition “the mother now married to smallholder at Fjand Martin Jeppesen Nørfjand”. The bride too is entered with her mother first. They had three children.

And then in the column for witnesses there is one word: The mothers. At every other wedding in this chronicle it is the fathers who sign — at Ane Kirstine’s in 1920 both fathers, at Elna Elisabeth’s in 1942 the bride’s father. Here it was the two women who had had their children outside marriage who stood up for their children. [S136]

It is the second time Ane Jensen takes a child she did not bear. In November 1881 she stepped into the house at Økjær and became mother to her predecessor’s daughter of a year and a half. Thirty-six years later a child was born in the same house whom her own daughter could not keep — and she kept him. And four years before, her daughter-in-law Kristiane had done exactly the same with Arne. Two boys born outside marriage, four years and a parish apart, raised by their grandmothers in the same family.The identification is certain: the census records Niels Silkjær born on 9 July 1855 in Husby and Ane born on 29 April 1858 in Ejsing — Landtingmark lies in Ejsing parish — and both dates match the parish registers. The foster son’s relationship is not given in the census but is established by the Husby parish register: he is the son of their daughter Jensine Kristine, born outside marriage. The census writes the birthday as 29 April; the parish register has the 28th. The sequence is documented: with his grandparents in Esbjerg in 1925, with his mother at Fjand in 1930. That the grandfather’s death in June 1928 was the occasion is an inference from the timing, not a statement in the sources. He married in Sønder Nissum in 1940 and had three children; the chronicle does not follow that branch further. [S105, S106, S136] Peder Skramsgade 2 does not appear in the census of 1930. [S94, S96] All caveats →

Ane Jensen was a widow for eight years and died in her son’s home at Havnegade 179, seventy-eight years old. She died on 28 June 1936 at three o’clock of heart failure; the doctor who viewed her that same morning recorded her as the widow of a smallholder and fisherman, old-age pensioner. She was the last of the couple from Økjær. On 3 July she was buried in the Gormsgade cemetery, in section Ø, row 11, no. 10 — the grave next to the one her son Thomas was laid in fourteen years later.

And the cemetery register writes her name in a way no other source in this chronicle does. Under surname it says Thomsen. Under first names it says “Ane called Silkjær”. Thirty-one years after the name certificate and fifty-eight years after her husband began writing Silkjær after his own name, the cemetery office still recorded her as Thomsen — with the farm name as something she was called.The family file has the date of death as 23 June 1936. The death certificate, issued by the viewing doctor on the day she died, gives 28 June at three o’clock, and the cemetery’s day register says the same. The certificate takes precedence, and the chronicle follows it. [S143, S144]

There is an older picture in this. Eighty years earlier the seller Niels Jensen had sat in the newly built house in the marsh as a “retired man, kept by the householder” (chapter 3). Now it was the family itself that had an old parent living in the household. The same district, the same custom — only the address was new: a fishing skipper’s home on the harbour. But the arrangement began only with the widowhood. As long as her husband lived, they had their own home.

It is a move that can be read in two ways. One: two old people who followed the work and the children into the town, as all of West Jutland did in those decades. The other: that the couple who had lived a whole life on a coast without a harbour ended their days at Denmark’s biggest fishing harbour — and that neither of them lies buried in the parish where the name was born.

The move from dune to town was not a break with the sea. It was a promotion: from open boats hauled up on the sand to decked boats with engines that could stay out for days. In the vessel register of the Fisheries and Maritime Museum Thomas appears as T. N. Silkjær, owner of E.94 ANNE KIRSTINE from 1923 to 1948.

“Havn” and “Forhavn” — the harbour and the outer harbour — below the streets of the town.
Image 1f · Survey sheets 1:20,000, sheet Z4, surveyed 1870, revised in the field 1896, drawn 1899 · free map material · credit historiskekort.dk
The Silkjær name among Esbjerg’s skippers

Three men, three cutters, one street. In fifty years the family had gone from open boats on Husby Klit to a fixed place in the country’s largest fishing harbour — and a name that stood in the trade’s own handbook.

12
Chapter 12 · 1904—1913

Vridsløselille

The trade’s handbook gave Thomas Nielsen Silkjær half a column: born, father, married, school, vessel, address. The court entered him in six registers, and the prison in four.

The case can be followed day by day: from journal number 48 in the district bailiff’s police journal, through the six court days of the examinations in the court books, to the judgment in the register of judgments and prisoner no. 240 at Vridsløselille. To this comes the criminal file itself — the folder from Ringkøbing with the prosecutor’s and the defence counsel’s pleadings and the series of exhibits A—K, from the constable’s report to the telegram about the arrest. The chronicle tells the case in the registers’ own words — even where they are hard to bear. The most important entries are given in transcription at the end of the chapter. [S174]

1904—1906
The second marriage

Ten years after the wreck Kristiane married again — the fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, almost nine years her junior. But the story begins two years before the wedding. On 4 May 1904 she gave birth to a son, Kristen Lauridsen Silkjær, at Årgab. She was a widow of thirty-one; the parish register recorded Thomas Nielsen Silkjær as the named father. So the boy bore his father’s byname from birth. [S70]

The godparents at the baptism all came from Kristiane’s own world on the dunes: her father, the farmer Simon Enevoldsen of Haurvig, the girl Sidsel Enevoldsen, the fisheries inspector Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen of Bjerregaard and the bachelor Niels Christian Jespersen of Årgab. It was her parish, and they were her people — godparents were taken from the parish’s own circle, and Husby lay a day’s journey away. Then notice the fisheries inspector: Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen was the father of her drowned first husband. He stood godfather to the child, was a witness at her new marriage two years later, appeared in court in 1913 as Kristine Oline’s guardian and the same year again stood godfather in the family (chapter 13). Four times in nine years, across a child born outside marriage, a new marriage and a criminal case: her former in-laws did not turn their backs on her. [S70, S71, S119]

Thomas was then a young fisherman from Husby. The levying roll follows him: he stood without a break in the Husby levy district until 1906 and fished — as the prison register later summed it up — partly at Esbjerg, partly at Ringkøbing. The census of 1 February 1901 finds the nineteen-year-old as a farmhand with Peder Sand Pedersen on cadastral no. 67 in Klit By in Vedersø parish — the enumerator wrote him down as “Tomas Nielsen Silkær”, unmarried, born on 10 January 1882 in Husby. In September 1903 he was given a seaman’s book and went to sea, and at the draft board he was called up for the Navy, where he did his national service from September 1905 to April 1906. So both registers recorded the son with the farm name — the roll as Silkjær, the census as Silkær — while the roll at the same time records the father patronymically as Thomsen. The state’s own registers used the byname years before the name certificate. [S72, S74]

Twelve days after his discharge, on 5 May 1906, they were married in Haurvig Church. She stood as a widow at Årgab, he as a bachelor in Esbjerg; the witnesses were her father and her former father-in-law. A week later he was given a removal certificate, and on 21 May he registered in the Esbjerg levy district. Four weeks from man-of-war to husband with an address in the town. [S71, S72]

He came into the house as stepfather to three: Enevold Jepsen, b. 1892, Simon, b. 1894, and Kristine Oline, b. 1896. She was nine — twelve days from turning ten.

The couple settled first in Esbjerg — their daughter Anna was born there in 1907 — and then came to Årgab, where they took over her in-laws’ property. He himself put a date on it in court: settled residence at Årgab from 1 April 1908. The levying roll only transfers him to the Holmsland Klit levy district in 1910, the same year their son Niels was born at Årgab — notices of removal often lagged behind the moves, and his own statement is the dated source for the takeover itself. [S72, S119]

The place was not large: room for four cows and two small horses, bought for 5,000 kroner and — in the register’s words — on condition of taking over a larger retirement settlement that rested on the property. It was mortgaged for the same amount as the purchase price; if it were sold, nothing would be left. On top of that a share in a motor boat, bought on a guaranteed loan and used for fishing and freight between Årgab and Ringkøbing, and a share in pound nets and gear that were wearing out. He put the income himself at 1,000—1,200 kroner a year. This is the house the rest of the chapter takes place in: a household with children of two marriages, debt on everything and one breadwinner. [S119]

14 December 1912
The flight

The collapse became visible before the case. The neighbour on the dunes was the smallholder Thyge Nielsen, and his daughter was called Nielsine Nielsen — born at Årgab on 23 November 1887, unmarried, twenty-five years old in the autumn of 1912. In late summer Kristiane had noticed that her husband often called at Thyge Nielsen’s, and there was talk in the district. She asked him straight out whether there was anything between him and the daughter; he firmly denied it, and she believed him. There was something: he later admitted in court that he and Nielsine had already had intercourse several times by then — in her room at her parents’, while the families lived as neighbours. [S119, S129]

On 14 December 1912 he left home in secret together with her. They went first to Kiel, where he looked for work but was expelled before he found any, and then to Copenhagen, where they lived together — the register’s words are “as man and wife”. In court he later declared that it had been his intention not to return to his wife or his home. [S119]

The police report in the criminal file tells what the registers do not: the families searched themselves before the police did. Nielsine’s father, Thyge Nielsen, went after the couple and found them between Christmas and New Year in Kiel, where Thomas had taken lodgings as “fisherman Thomas Nielsen and wife from Esbjerg”. When it came out that this was not true, the police expelled him, and they both went back with the father to Vamdrup — but there they left him and bought tickets, apparently to Fredericia. From there they went on to Copenhagen. The closest anyone from home later came to them was a chance in the dark: a marine from Bjerregaard — the report records him as Otto Hejde — saw them one evening around New Year pass by in the street while he was standing guard at the Yellow Palace. Seen and gone again; where they were living, no one at home knew. [S174]

Back at Årgab Kristiane was left with the children, the debt — and a stepdaughter carrying something no one in the house had yet put into words.

January—February 1913
The letter to Randers

Kristine Oline was sixteen, pregnant and alone with it. The man who had made her pregnant was her stepfather, and he had gone. Her mother knew nothing. The adult outside the house she chose to confide in was not from the dunes.

Pastor Hornbech of Randers was an itinerant preacher and had in recent years visited the dunes several times — and had talked with her along the way. Behind the register’s name stands in all probability Carl Marius Hornbech: a pastor’s son, a graduate of Randers grammar school, a missionary in India from 1902 until his wife died out there in 1908 — the year after, he came home as an itinerant preacher and lived in Randers in exactly the years the register speaks of. The police report in the criminal file records him precisely as “itinerant preacher for the Danish Missionary Society” — the society Hornbech travelled for. A man who had himself known loss. The church mission milieu that the revival on the dunes had made part of her world reached far beyond the parish. Through it she had met him; now that connection became her way out. Without her mother’s knowledge she wrote to the pastor in Randers and confided in him — about the pregnancy, and about who the father was.

Hornbech answered with a letter in which he charged her to confide in her mother. How it then came about, Kristiane herself told in court on 7 March, and the register has preserved the scene: the daughter handed her the pastor’s letter and left the room. The mother read it and went in to her. The police report in the criminal file puts a date on the evening: Thursday 13 February 1913. [S174]

…after the deponent had read the letter, she went in to her daughter, who thereupon, with strong emotion and in tears, confirmed to the deponent what she had told the pastor, and on the deponent’s express question firmly declared that she had had nothing to do with other men and that the prisoner was therefore the father of the expected child.
Police register p. 153 · Kristiane’s statement, 7 March 1913 · deponent (Cpd.) = Kristiane, prisoner (Arr.) = the accused [S119]

That is how the case came to light: not by a report from neighbours, not by a midwife or a doctor — but because a sixteen-year-old girl wrote a letter to a pastor, and the pastor answered her seriously and pointed her home to her mother. The mission milieu’s network had given her an adult outside the house to write to.

Hornbech’s letter itself has not been found — not among the exhibits of the criminal file either — but report A independently confirms that the pastor had “received a letter from the girl made pregnant about the matter”; on the letter and on the identification of the pastor, see caveat 31. The scene stands as Kristiane told it in court, reported by the clerk of the court. [S119, S172, S174]

17 February — 26 March 1913
Journal number 48

The birth of the case itself can now be followed to the day — it is in the constable’s report, exhibit A of the case. On the evening of Thursday 13 February Anders Hejde came home to Bjerregaard from Randers. There he had met Pastor Hornbech, and the pastor had told him what he knew from the letters: that Thomas Silkjær’s stepdaughter was pregnant, and by whom. Hejde took the message to Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen — Kristine Oline’s paternal grandfather, who was staying in Bjerregaard just then. That same Thursday evening, in the house at Årgab, Kristine Oline handed her mother the pastor’s letter. The next morning the grandfather travelled to Årgab “to have the matter looked into more closely” — “but Christine had by then already confided in her mother”. What had been hidden since the summer of 1911 became shared knowledge in a single evening. [S174]

On Monday 17 February Constable Jensen was at Årgab. His report opens in the formulaic language of the time — and with one fact the registers do not have: “… and the proper persons concerned have moreover wished the matter to be made the subject of public investigation”. The family itself asked for the investigation. Four statements were taken that same day — the grandfather, Kristiane, Kristine Oline herself and Thyge Nielsen — and, for use in the search, a description of the man who had left: “a little under middle height … very fair moustache; he is ruddy and speaks West Jutland dialect”. [S174]

The same day the district bailiff’s office gave the case journal number 48. In the journal’s column for the nature of the case the clerk wrote: “Breach of Penal Code § 162 (impregnation of stepdaughter)”. From there every step can be followed in the journal’s column of dispatches: the next day a letter went to the Copenhagen police, and on 21 February the answer came by telegram — arrested. [S123]

The letter of 18 February lies in the file as exhibit B. The bailiff asked the Copenhagen police to search for the accused, “if need be circulated in P. E.” — Politiets Efterretninger, the police’s own nationwide gazette — and if found, to arrest him, question him and telegraph. And then he added something that stands in no register: Thyge Nielsen intended to travel to Copenhagen himself that same evening to help with the search — and to be present when the couple was found. The bailiff wrote why: [S174]

…as he has expressed to me his fear that the daughter, who is said to be nervous and overwrought, and who is said to have threatened to take her own life if the relationship between her and the accused is interfered with, will carry out this threat if the accused is found and arrested.
The arrest requisition of 18 February 1913, exhibit B · the bailiff to the Copenhagen police [S174]

So the father, who in December had fetched them in Kiel and lost them again at Vamdrup, got on the train once more — now with the police case behind him and his daughter’s threats on his mind.

The arrest itself is in exhibit C of the case, the extract from the register of the Copenhagen Criminal and Police Court. On Friday 21 February at a quarter to seven in the morning he was found on the corner of Strandgade and Torvegade in Christianshavn and taken to the police station. He was then living in Mathæusgade in Vesterbro and working at Copenhagen Floating Dock; Nielsine is entered in the papers as a seamstress. At 8 o’clock he was handed over to the Nytorv jail, and at half past eleven — barely five hours after the arrest — he had been brought before the Criminal and Police Court as examination no. 575. He confessed at once: he had had intercourse with his stepdaughter many times, and “he dare not deny that he has made his stepdaughter pregnant”. The court closed the case “for transcription, to be sent together with the arrested man to the bailiff in Ringkjøbing” — the man and the papers were to go the same way. The same day the telegram arrived in Ringkøbing, written in pencil on the state telegraph’s form, exhibit D of the case: “Thommas Nielsen Silkjør found brought before court arrested to be collected here.” [S174]

And then it became public. Politiets Efterretninger — the gazette the bailiff’s letter had pointed to — carried him the day after the arrest, in no. 23 of 22 February, under the heading “Arrested for crimes etc.”; three days later, in no. 24 of 25 February, he stood again under “Handed over to other jurisdictions” with the addition “To Ulfborg-Hind Hundreds” — the transfer to the jail in Ringkøbing, set in print. Two lines in a gazette that went out to every police station in the country: the case from the dunes was no longer anybody’s secret. [S175]

On 24 February at half past eleven he was brought before the police court at the court house — in the absence of the regular judge the examination was conducted by the acting deputy H. Gronenberg. He repeated his confession, and the judge decreed custody. Here the register has a note that was later struck out: under D a service book (skudsmålsbog) for Kristine Oline was filed — the entry is struck through with wavy lines. In the preserved criminal file, however, D is the telegram about the arrest; so the service book did not go into the final series of exhibits, and the letter was reused. The case was given the police court number 26/13, and the list of cases then records six court days: 24 and 28 February, 7, 17, 22 and 26 March. [S119, S120, S174]

On 28 February — now before deputy Th. Edsberg, in the judge’s absence — he gave his detailed statement. The marriage could by his account be said to have been happy until last summer, when the connection with Nielsine began. About his stepdaughter he admitted everything: intercourse many times since the summer of 1911 — the first time one evening at harvest time, in the barn of the property at Årgab. She was fifteen, just turned. He maintained that she had never been forced — and in the same statement admitted something that turns his own claim around: [S119]

The prisoner must admit that his stepdaughter drew his attention to the danger in their relationship, but that he always brushed it aside and reassured his stepdaughter that it did not matter, as long as the relationship did not get out among strangers.
Police register p. 149 · Thomas’ statement, 28 February 1913 [S119]

She warned him. He brushed it aside. It stands in his own statement, entered in the register by the court — the girl of fifteen understood the risk, and the grown man talked her out of it.

7 March was Kristiane’s day in court, and her statement is the longest in the case. She described her daughter as physically early developed, but mentally like others — “always a good girl in her home”. She told of her marriage: ten years as a widow with three children, “quite without means”, and as a widow she had received support from the Harboøre Fund — the fund from the disaster of November 1893 whose funeral address chapter 10 compares with the words at Christen’s funeral. So Harboøre appears twice in the story: as a parallel in preaching and, quite concretely, as her support in the years of widowhood. The marriage to Thomas had not been entered into for the sake of support, she said, but grounded in “a strong and deep love”, and it had been happy until the collapse in the autumn. And then she declared something the court expressly asked about: she did not wish charges to be brought against him for adultery. [S119]

One of the questions from the bench that day is worth pausing at. The judge asked whether there was in the man’s nature “something that affects women particularly strongly”, and whether that could explain why the daughter “at once fell for his first attack”. Attack (Angreb) — that is the register’s own word for the first intercourse, chosen by the court in 1913. Kristiane answered that she could not say. [S119]

The same court day the maintenance case was settled — while he was in custody, Kristiane had applied to the county to have him ordered to pay maintenance. He admitted liability, offered 300 kroner a year to her and 90 kroner a year to each of the three children of the marriage until they reached eighteen, and she accepted. Raised, heard and settled in one day. [S119, S120]

Kristine Oline herself had been summoned to appear that day but could not: she was then a good six months gone, and her mother informed the court that her daughter “on account of her condition” did not feel able to appear in Ringkøbing until after the birth. Three days later the midwife’s certificate came from the district midwife A. J. Paulsen. [S119, S123]

So the court travelled out to her. On 17 March at half past three in the afternoon the Police Court of Ulfborg-Hind Hundreds was convened on Thomas Silkjær’s property at Årgab — the judge himself, with two witnesses summoned to the court, in the house on the dunes. The travelling police register, the book the judge took with him on official journeys, explains why: [S163]

The judge observed that the court was convened here because the girl Christine Oline Enevoldsen cannot appear in court in Ringkøbing in her advanced state of pregnancy, and that the weather in the past week has made it impossible for the judge to travel to Aargab before today.
Travelling police register p. 72 · the court session at Årgab, 17 March 1913 [S163]

Here, in her own home, she gave her statement — the full transcription is at the end of the chapter. Her first statement lay in Constable Jensen’s report of 17 February, exhibit A of the case; it was read out to her, and she confirmed it. Then she gave her own account. She knew very well that what had happened was wrong — “as much against the commandment of religion as against human morality”, as the register reports it, and particularly reprehensible between stepparents and stepchildren. But above the line the clerk has inserted a sentence with an insertion mark: on the other hand she did not know before that such intercourse was punishable. She knew the shame to the bottom. The law under which she was sentenced a month later she did not know.Report A lies as exhibit A in the criminal file (B-410, folder 408) — Constable Jensen’s report of 17 February 1913 with statements from the grandfather, the mother, Kristine Oline herself and Thyge Nielsen. The whole report is given in transcription at the end of the chapter. Some readings in the travelling police register are uncertain. See caveat 29. [S119, S123, S163, S174] All caveats → [S119, S123, S163]

The statement also fixes the scene where it began: the approach came in the cowshed, one day when her mother was not at home — and until then, she says, he had never behaved towards her other than as “the one who stood in a father’s place to her”. And it tells who was told first. When in October 1912 she herself understood that she was with child, she did not confide in her mother but in an eighteen-year-old son of Anders Hejde in Bjerregaard, “who has always been her confidant” — Søren Mathiasen Heide, born 17 November 1893, eighteen in just that month and nineteen a few weeks later. He asked leave to tell her mother; she asked him to keep quiet, and he kept his word. A girl of sixteen with one confidant in the world: an eighteen-year-old from Bjerregaard, the settlement south of Årgab.The travelling police register does not name the son, only the father and the age. The parish register for Ny parish records the birth: Søren Mathiasen Pedersen Heide, born 17 November 1893 at Bjerregaard, son of smallholder Anders Hejde Pedersen — eighteen in just October 1912, nineteen on 17 November. The age fits only in the weeks the statement is about. See caveat 29. [S163, S170] All caveats → [S163, S170]

Then the December scene, days before Thomas left. She was not well, and he asked whether anything was wrong with her — “to which she replied that it was he who was to blame for her being poorly, and then nothing more was said about it”. Whether he understood that she was with child, she did not know. Shortly afterwards he was gone. And in January she wrote to Pastor Hornbech. [S163]

At the foot of the page the judge and the two court witnesses signed. One name is Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen — the guardian, who nine days later appeared in Ringkøbing in the same capacity. The other reads “Chr. Silkær” — in all probability Christiane herself: the court was sitting in her home, and her legal name was Silkjær. If the reading stands, the mother sat in the room as the court’s witness while her daughter gave her account.The witness signature is a reading and the identification an inference — the abbreviation of the first name is not quite certain. See caveat 29. [S163] All caveats →

On 22 March, back in Ringkøbing, the judge went through all the statements with the prisoner — hers from Årgab five days before as well. And here, on page 174 of the register, stands the moral core of the case — in his own words, entered in the register:

The prisoner admits that he knew very well that the girl was only 15 years old when he first had intercourse with her, and he admits that in view of her young age and his particular position towards her as her stepfather he must be said to have seduced her into the lewdness that took place between them, even though her resistance to it was only weak and brief.
Police register p. 174 · the examination of 22 March 1913 [S119]

The prison’s register later wrote simply intercourse and left the relation of power unsaid. Here the man says it himself, in court: her age and his position as stepfather make it seduction. Utugt, lewdness, is the register’s word — the period’s, not the chronicle’s.

The judgment later summed up her statement in the court’s own language: the first time she made “some weak objections”, but gave in when he reassured her that he would see to it that the relationship had no consequences, “and that it did not matter when no one knew”; she repeated her objections before the next occasions, likewise gave in — and gradually gave up “entirely every objection”. Here too her words are filtered — written down by men, reported in the third person, confirmed by him. The nearest the sources come to her own voice is the statement from her own home on 17 March. Before the first intercourse she had told him that it was wrong and that she could become pregnant. He answered, and he went on. [S121, S163]

On 26 March the examinations ended. For the last court session the judge had expressly summoned the former fisheries inspector Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen — the register calls him Kristine Oline’s natural guardian — guardian by virtue of kinship, as the nearest male of age on her late father’s side. He and Kristiane declared in agreement that they did not ask for charges against Thomas for breach of § 174 of the Penal Code — the provision on the seduction of a girl between twelve and sixteen, which could only be prosecuted at the request of parents or guardian. The case under § 162, which concerned the sexual relationship between stepfather and stepchild, continued as a public prosecution. They each received travel expenses and two kroner for lost earnings, and the case went for transcription. Two days later the recommendation to prosecute lay with the county — the district office’s letter of 28 March recommends officially “that the persons concerned be charged with breach of § 162 of the Penal Code” — and on 31 March the order to prosecute came back from Rindumgaard, the prefect’s residence near Ringkøbing: that same day proceedings had been instituted against Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen for breach of § 162 of the Penal Code, and two attorneys had been appointed to conduct the case — High Court attorney Grove and attorney Kamp, “the former as prosecutor, the latter as defence counsel”, with instructions that the defence counsel be notified. The letter bears the signature of the county prefect H.C. Dons, the county’s journal number D 698 and the endorsement with one word saying what it was: “Prisoner case”; at the bottom the district office put its red 48/13 — the journal’s own number for the case. [S119, S123, S165, S166, S171]

11 and 14 April 1913
The judgment

The trial took place in the extraordinary court at the court house on 11 April at half past ten — the heading of the session calls it a justitssag, a criminal case, with appointed prosecutor and defence counsel. The case now bore its third and last number: 6/13 in the extraordinary court, after the journal’s 48/1913 and the police court’s 26/13. The prosecutor, High Court attorney Grove, appeared and filed his pleading. The defence counsel, attorney Kamp, did not appear himself but through attorney Hammersø, who filed a pleading with the remark that the documents of the case had been lent to him “privately”. Thomas had been brought from the jail and declared that he had nothing further to say. And then the third name in the case: “The accused Christine Oline Enevoldsen did not appear when called.” She was heavily pregnant and at home on the dunes. No witnesses were heard during the trial itself; the court decided the case on the basis of the recorded statements, the confessions and the written exhibits. [S122]

The two pleadings lie in the criminal file, handwritten on each attorney’s notepaper. The prosecutor was finished first: the summons is dated 1 April — the day after the order to prosecute — and the pleading 2 April. Grove’s account of the case is dry and precise, and his demand reaches straight for the top of the law: both accused to be “sentenced to the law’s severest penalty for breach of Penal Code §162”. Both. The sixteen-year-old too. [S174]

Kamp’s pleading, dated 3 April, is twice as long and goes the opposite way — for both of them. For Thomas he looks for explanations where the period had any language for them at all: the age difference in the marriage, a sexual drive “more than normally developed”, and that the Penal Code did not take “the right and rational account” of what he calls mental abnormalities — but also that the man was otherwise “a capable and honourable man”, no “sexual criminal of the sinister kind”: the law’s mildest penalty. And for Kristine Oline he wrote the lines that read like the case’s only speech in her defence: the offence had “carried its punishment in itself”; the disgrace falls “most heavily on the woman”; it was the stepfather “who is thus the one who has seduced her”; had she known that the relationship was punishable, that knowledge would have “torn her out of it” and made her resist. And then the sentence that points a hundred years ahead: “Forced labour or imprisonment will here do more harm than good.” His demand for her: a suspended sentence with the mildest penalty. The whole pleading is given in transcription at the end of the chapter. [S174]

Severest penalty against mildest, filed side by side in the same court session, a week between the two signatures. The court came down in the middle for him — eighteen months is neither the top nor the bottom of the law — and followed Kamp for her.

The judgment was pronounced three days later, on Monday 14 April at four in the afternoon, in the extraordinary court at the district office: [S121, S122]

It is therefore adjudged: Thomas Nielsen Silkjær shall be punished with hard labour in the house of correction for Eighteen Months. Christine Oline Enevoldsen shall be punished with simple imprisonment for one month, but the execution of the sentence is suspended and the sentence lapses after the expiry of 5 years from the pronouncement of this judgment, provided the conditions laid down in § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911 are fulfilled.
Register of judgments fol. 102 · 14 April 1913 [S121]

The judgment repeats the admission of seduction almost word for word — “must be said to have seduced her into the immoral relationship that took place between them” — and establishes that neither of them had been charged before. The legal basis is § 162 of the Penal Code for both of them; in her case “taken together with §§ 21 and 37”. The two sections are the law’s provisions for the young, from 1866, and the arithmetic comes out exactly: § 162 set the minimum penalty for a stepchild at two months’ simple imprisonment in mitigating circumstances, and § 37 allowed the penalty for anyone between fifteen and eighteen at the time of the offence to be reduced “by up to half” — one month, exactly what she was given. § 21 at the same time forbade putting anyone under eighteen in prison on bread and water. And the suspension on top is the suspended sentence — introduced in Denmark in 1905 as something new and continued in the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911, whose § 20 the judgment cites. The court expressly grounded it in her young age. In other words, the judge went to the very bottom of what the law allowed at all. [S121, S127]

The court’s own draft of the judgment — the draft preserved among the documents for the justice registers — shows that precisely those lines came into being along the way. The reference “in the accused’s case taken together with §§ 21 and 37” has been added in the margin with an insertion mark. And in the operative part the clerk began on a single joint sentence — “Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen shall be punished …” — before her name was struck out and she was given a sentence of her own, the one with the suspension. The mild outcome was not there in the first stroke of the pen; it was written into being, correction by correction. [S164]

One more line should be read slowly. The costs of the prosecution — a fee of 30 kroner to the prosecutor, 25 to the defence counsel — were laid on them both “one for both and both for one”, in solidum. The sixteen-year-old was jointly liable for the costs of prosecuting her own stepfather. [S121]

She was not there when the judgment was given. But the file’s endorsements of service show how it reached each of them. The next day, 15 April, the town’s process servers served the judgment on Thomas “in person outside his cell” — he declared himself satisfied with the judgment and did not wish to appeal. On 19 April the process servers for Haurvig, Aargab and Bjerregaard went out to her: the judgment was served on Kristine Oline and her guardian, Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen, “in person at their residence in Aargab” — and they too declared themselves satisfied and waived appeal. The journal’s dispatch to the parish constable at Haurvig, sent on the 15th and returned on the 22nd, was thus the judgment on its way out there and home again. [S174]The journal records “15/4 to parish constable Haurvig[?]”, returned 22/4 — and the file’s endorsement of service of 19 April shows what the dispatch contained: the judgment, served at the residence and on 22 April laid before the county with the file. See caveat 30. [S123, S174] All caveats → The judgment was accepted without appeal — in the county’s journal case the sheet bears the chief constable’s endorsement “acquiescerer”, acquiesces, and the order of execution went out on 24 April. At eight in the morning on 27 April Thomas began serving his sentence in Ringkjøbing jail, and on 3 July he was delivered to Vridsløselille — the prison’s own stamp on the last page of the file acknowledges both dates. [S87, S123, S165, S166, S174]

The period · why was she sentenced too?

The Penal Code of 1866 punished both parties in what it called incest — even when one was a child in the other’s care. The logic was the period’s: if the girl had not resisted, she was complicit. Only the Penal Code of 1930, in force from 1933, took the younger party out of criminal liability; until then she could be sentenced if she was over the age of criminal responsibility — and mitigation had to be found in the law’s provisions for the young and, from 1905 and with the provisional Penal Code of 1911, in the suspended sentence. Those were exactly the tools this judgment used. [S125, S127]

The criminal statistics put figures on it. The decades around 1900 were the provision’s peak: the Statistical Yearbook records between 12 and 18 persons convicted of incest a year nationally in the period 1903—07. The figures count persons, not cases; when both the man and the girl were sentenced, both appear in the statistics — as here. Around the turn of the century about a third of those convicted in cases involving parents and stepparents were women — the great majority of them daughters and stepdaughters, not mothers. [S125, S126]

The sentence was mild measured against the courts’ practice of the time. A legal-historical study of incest cases has shown that convicted daughters typically received between eight months and a year in the house of correction — up to two years — and that it was usually the girls whose “morality” the court found something to criticise who were sentenced most harshly. She received one month’s simple imprisonment, suspended, with the law’s provisions for the young and § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911 behind her. And she was among the very few of the very young it struck at all: from 1906, when the age of criminal responsibility was raised to 14, until 1932, only about fifteen persons between 14 and 18 were punished for incest in the whole country. She was one of them. [S125]

That the judgment was mild by the standards of its time does not make it reasonable by ours. The law treated her as complicit; the registers themselves — the judge’s word “attack”, the man’s admission of seduction, the court’s reference to her age — show that the court could see perfectly well what it was. It sentenced her all the same, because it was in the law — a law that, by her own account, she did not even know existed. [S125, S127, S163]

27 April — 15 November 1913
The sentence · Ringkjøbing and Vridsløselille

At Vridsløselille the case became twelve lines. The register of inmates, entry Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, Husby — the same man as in the trade’s handbook, the same year of birth, the same occupation. Two hands, two purposes: one was to sell a skipper to his colleagues, the other to describe a prisoner for an institution.

The judgment
CaseThe prison’s judgment no. 19953 · prisoner no. 240. The court’s own numbers were the journal’s 48/1913, the police court’s 26/13 and the extraordinary court’s 6/13 JudgmentExtraordinary court of Ulfborg-Hind Hundreds, 14 April 1913 OffenceSexual offence, Penal Code § 162 SentenceHard labour in the house of correction for “Eighteen Months” — the register’s 1½ years Servingbegun in Ringkjøbing jail on 27 April 1913 at 8 in the morning Admitted3 July 1913, transferred from Ringkjøbing jail Expiry27 April 1914, as the register records it. The expiry date follows § 13 of the Penal Code on serving in a cell: a year and a half of hard labour in the house of correction was shortened by a third when served in solitary confinement — to exactly one year [S117] Released15 November 1913 — pardoned by royal resolution of the same day Previous convictions“None”
The description
Age31, b. 10 January 1882 · fisherman · last at Aargab AppearanceHeight 63¾ inches (c. 167 cm) · limbs medium · eyes blue · hair fair · complexion good · speaks Danish · 61 kg Distinguishing mark“Scar on r. thigh” Enrolled for sea serviceThe naval roll, Ringkjøbing · marine no. 3959, 1905—06 SchoolingLutheran · confirmed · can read and write Brought with him3 kroner 9 øre Family“Lawfully married, 1 child of incest and 3 stepchildren”

The three stepchildren are Kristiane’s three children from her first marriage. The fourth word in the sentence is the child the case is about.

Eight court sessions, six registers and an admission of seduction were boiled down in the prison to two almost identical entries, one in the register of inmates and one in the class register: since the summer of 1911 he had several times had intercourse with his stepdaughter Kristine Oline Enevoldsen and made her pregnant. Intercourse — that is all the register writes, and the relation of power goes unsaid. Even her suspended sentence is reduced to a subordinate clause in the column.

And the words hard labour in the house of correction should not be heard with modern ears. Vridsløselille was built on the isolation principle of the Philadelphia system, and in 1913 it was still in force: the sentence was served in a single cell, where the prisoner both worked and slept. Outside the cell the prisoners wore masks so that they could not recognise one another, all conversation was forbidden, and in church and school they sat in small stalls from which they could see the pastor and the teacher — but not each other. The mask was only made voluntary in 1924. In return the Penal Code of 1866 gave a reduction in the term for serving in a cell — the isolation was itself reckoned an aggravation of the punishment, and the time was reduced accordingly. [S117]

There is another trace in the entry that has nothing to do with the judgment. Nielsine is given no name in the prison’s register — she is simply the neighbour’s daughter. But the clerk notes what the prisoner was afraid of: particularly at the thought that the neighbour’s daughter may be with child. How well founded that thought was, the clerk did not know. The calendar did.

“F. seems very erotically disposed and has been bad towards her in her earliest youth … He is nonetheless fond of his wife and is rather unhappy and serious.”
The register sheet, “Information about the prisoner’s previous life”

The prison also kept a kind of conduct book. At first class the second teacher writes that the prisoner is pleasant and acknowledging, moved at the thought of the misfortune he has brought into his home — and then adds: but far too fond of women. On 4 October 1913, in second class, the tone has cooled: Neat and orderly, but without deeper acknowledgement. The column for letters has two strokes in all: he wrote home on 10 August and on 12 October.The teachers’ assessments are written in a hasty cursive, and some words — particularly kvindekær (fond of women) and ordentlig (orderly) — have been read from the context. All caveats →

The eighteen-month sentence ended in release after a good six and a half months served — and the way there took two attempts. The first was the defence counsel’s. In July attorney Kamp applied for a pardon for his client; the judge — the same district bailiff who had given the judgment — recommended the petition in a statement of 7 July, and the county passed it on to the Ministry of Justice with the remark that it could refer to the statement given. The ministry’s answer came ten days later, typewritten and short: [S165, S166]

In consequence of this, it is hereby communicated for your kind information and further notice, also to attorney Kamp, that the Ministry does not find grounds to seek any pardon for the person concerned.
The Ministry of Justice to the Prefect of Ringkjøbing County · 17 July 1913 [S166]

The refusal was passed on and entered in the institution’s journal. There the case could have ended: judgment, refusal, sentence served to April 1914. But 15 November 1913 was the fiftieth anniversary of the House of Glücksburg on the throne: Christian IX had become king on 15 November 1863, and although he had died in 1906, his grandson Christian X marked the day as the royal line’s jubilee — the prison’s journal itself calls it “the Lyksborg 50 years’ jubilee of the reign”. On 10 November Vridsløselille recommended seven prisoners for pardon on that occasion. Prisoner no. 240 was one of them, and the institution’s letter gives the reason: [S167, S168]

He behaves well and seems to repent his crime. At home he is sorely missed, and the judge has recommended a petition for pardon, which was refused on 17 July this year, though with reference to the judge’s recommendation.
Vridsløselille to the Director of the Prison Service · letter no. 131, 10 November 1913 [S168]

The same letter sums up his family in the prison’s own language: “married and has 3 legitimate children, 1 illegitimate child, 1 child of incest and 3 stepchildren”. The child of incest is Arne, and the stepchildren are Kristiane’s three children of her first marriage. But whom the letter counts as the illegitimate child remains open: Kristen was born in 1904, two years before his parents’ wedding — but if he is counted as the illegitimate child, the three legitimate children do not add up with the two younger ones, Anna and Niels; and if he was counted as legitimate by the marriage, the letter counts a child the sources otherwise do not know. Nielsine’s child cannot be meant — when the letter was written on 10 November, Else Margrethe was not yet born. The royal resolution came on the anniversary itself, 15 November: all seven pardoned, the three foreign prisoners with expulsion from the realm, all released the same day. At four o’clock he walked out of the gate — not because anyone had changed their view of the case, but because the royal house had been on the throne for fifty years.The register’s endorsement of release “kgl. Res. s.D.” (royal resolution, same day) and the class register’s “Ben. kgl. Res. 15/11” (pardoned by royal resolution 15/11) both date the resolution to 15 November. See caveat 40. [S44, S45, S167] All caveats → [S167, S168]

And then the thing no register explains. In February 1913 he declared in court that it had been his intention never to return to his wife. Yet we find them together again: the family reunited on Gl. Færgevej in Esbjerg, Elna born in 1919, and Kristiane as Mrs Silkjær at Havnegade 179 right up to 1951 (chapter 11). When and how they were reconciled, there is no source for. It is the last, unwritten sentence of the case — and they wrote it themselves, without a register.

Read the register entry in transcription
The register sheet · “Information about the prisoner’s previous life” · translated; the source’s abbreviations are kept where they carry meaning

Legitimate. The parents living. Father smallholder Niels Silkjær, Husby. 2 brothers, 7 sisters. Brought up at home until confirmation, though now and then in summer service. After confirmation in service and fishing, partly at Esbjerg, partly at Ringkjøbing. Married 1906 to the widow Christiane Enevoldsen, whose husband, a fisherman, was drowned, after which F. came to serve with her father-in-law, whose property at Aargab they got after having lived 2 years in Esbjerg, to which the wife has now moved again with the children, address Gl. Færgevej 7, now that the property at Aargab has been sold.

Since the summer of 1911 several times had intercourse with his stepdaughter b. 17/5 1896 and made her pregnant; she has now given birth to a child. The stepdaughter: Christine Oline Enevoldsen, 1 month simple imprisonment, suspended sentence. F. seems very erotically disposed and has been bad towards her in her earliest youth and in Dec. 1912 left home with a neighbour’s daughter. He is nonetheless fond of his wife and is rather unhappy and serious, particularly at the thought that the neighbour’s daughter may be with child.

The field immediately above on the same page: The crime for which the prisoner is sentenced: sexual offence, Penal Code § 162.

The class register · “Previous circumstances of life”

The class register’s entry repeats the register of inmates’ life history almost word for word — the same formulas, clearly copied from the same draft. It differs only in small things: the abbreviations are written out (brought up at home until confirmation for brought up at home until conf., Fg. for F.), the section on parents and brothers and sisters is left out, the stepdaughter’s date of birth and the words that she “has now given birth to a child” are missing — and the register’s “a neighbour’s daughter” has in the end become “the neighbour’s daughter”.

Three caveats. “Gl.” in Gl. Færgevej is the most probable reading, but the two letters are worn; the census of 1930 records the household in the same street. In 1916 the family had moved to Hjertinggade 13, so that census can neither confirm nor refute the reading. [S76] “simp. Fgs.” is undoubtedly simple imprisonment. F. and Fg. are the clerk’s standard abbreviations for the prisoner (Fangen). [S44, S45]
