15 November 1913
The neighbour’s daughter

The prisoner’s fear was well founded. Nielsine was pregnant when he was arrested — the date of birth is consistent with the child having been conceived during the stay in Copenhagen, around the time shortly before the arrest.

She did not give birth at home at Årgab. She gave birth in Aarhus — and the parish register records her as an “unmarried servant girl”: she was in service in the town, so the journey there was not only a flight to hide. The birth took place at Bethesda — a rescue and maternity home for unmarried pregnant women, founded in 1894 and run on Inner Mission funds, with a deaconess as matron. The home cared precisely for the “fallen for the first time”, as the period called them: young women expecting a child without a husband, who had few other places to give birth. In 1913 it lay on Skovvangsvej on Aarhus Mark, with room for twenty women and thirty children. [S128]

It is worth pausing at what that means. The mission movement appears twice in this case, and both times on the same side: through the itinerant preacher Kristine Oline wrote to — the Danish Missionary Society’s man, cf. caveat 31 — and through the Inner Mission’s institutional network, which gave Nielsine a place to give birth. The revival’s people in those years were not only the moral authority that put a name to sin; they were also the social safety net that caught those sin left behind. “Fallen girl” is the period’s phrase, not the chronicle’s — but the help was real enough.

The child came into the world on 15 November 1913 and was entered in the parish register of St John’s parish as birth no. 93:The censuses give the birthday as 13 November; the parish register, kept at the birth, has the 15th and takes precedence. See caveat 32. [S124]

Else Margrethe Nielsen of Aargab. — Unmarried Nielsine Nielsen and named father fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkjær. (Mother and daughter are staying with the grandparents: smallholder Thyge Nielsen and his wife Else Margrethe Nielsen of Aargab, Holmslands Klit.)
Aarhus St John’s parish · births, female, 1913, no. 93 [S124]

The girl was named after her maternal grandmother and baptised in St John’s Church on 14 December; among the godparents stood Johanne Nielsen — most probably Nielsine’s sister, four years older. The family was there, at the font in Aarhus too. And then the date again: on 15 November 1913, at four o’clock in the afternoon, Thomas walked out of the gate at Vridsløselille. His second child that year was born on the same day he was freed. So in 1913 he stood in two parish registers as named father — Arne in May at Haurvig, Else Margrethe in November in Aarhus — two children with two women in under six months. Arne was born while he sat in Ringkjøbing jail; Else Margrethe on the day he was released from Vridsløselille. [S44, S124]

Nielsine took the child home to Årgab. In the census of 1916 Else Margrethe appears as a foster child with her grandparents — the same discreet column Arne later had in his father’s household — in 1921 simply as child. In 1930 they both lived there — Nielsine unmarried and forty-three, her daughter seventeen. Nielsine later had children with another man, and the chronicle follows her no further: that story is hers.

The daughter grew up on the dunes. She went into service as a domestic help and lived in Hvide Sande, a couple of miles from Årgab. On 10 November 1938, five days before her twenty-fifth birthday, she died at the mental hospital in Viborg. The death certificate gives bronchopneumonia as the cause of death and at the same time records “morbus mentalis” — mental illness — without a closer diagnosis. The certificate tells no more. She was unmarried.

At the top of the certificate someone has written where she was to go: Nørre Haurvig churchyard. It is the church on the dunes — the one her half-brother Arne had been carried into as a baby in June 1913, five months before she herself was born in Aarhus. The two never met in any document. They ended in the same parish. [S124, S132]

Source appendix
The registers in transcription

The chapter is based on the court books from Ringkøbing and on the archives of the county and the prison, read in the originals at Rigsarkivet Viborg, and on the criminal file itself (B-410, folder 408), whose certified transcript reproduces the same examinations; see caveat 28. The most important entries are given here in transcription — unabridged, with the registers’ own abbreviations kept. These are hard texts, and they can be skipped without losing the thread of the chapter. But they are what the chapter stands on.

The abbreviations: Arr. the prisoner (Thomas) · Cpd./Cp. the deponent (the person examined) · Fkl. statement · F.R.m. appeared before the court · frl. was filed · gj. bek. m. made acquainted with · O.V. read out and confirmed. Some words have been read from the context, and […] marks only words that could not be read in the original; see caveat 28. In this English edition the entries are translated; where a statement describes the acts themselves in physical detail, that passage is summarised in square brackets rather than translated.

Thomas’ statement · the police court, 28 February 1913
Police register pp. 148—149 · case 26/13 · the examination conducted by acting deputy Th. Edsberg in the regular judge’s absence

The prisoner was brought before the court and states that his full name is Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and that he was born on 10 Jan 1882 in Husby, and he denies having previously been charged or punished. The deponent married in 1906 his wife, the widow of Christen O. Enevoldsen, Christiane Enevoldsen, with whom he has 3 children aged 8, 6 and 2 years. There has been nothing wrong in the relationship between his wife and him, and the marriage can hitherto[?] be said to have been happy until last summer, when the deponent began the connection with the neighbour Tyge Nielsen’s daughter, with whom he went away from home in the month of December and has since lived together. When his wife discovered this love affair and could in general feel that the prisoner was not towards her as he had been before, she drew his attention to the relationship, without this however bringing any change for the better. Any real rift in the relationship between him and his wife there has not, however, been.

Confronted with the incestuous relationship with his stepdaughter Kristine Oline Enevoldsen of which he is now accused, he admits that he has had intercourse many times with his stepdaughter, whom he has now made pregnant. The relationship began in the summer of 1911, when, as the daughter stated in report A, he had intercourse with her for the first time one evening at harvest time, though he cannot give the time more exactly. It took place in the barn of his property at Aargab. [The record here describes the first occasion and the acts in physical detail, together with his assertion that she went with him willingly and without the slightest threat or violence on his part; that passage is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original After that the prisoner had intercourse with her a few more times before 1 Nov. that year, when the daughter went into service, at any rate in her room, but he cannot at all remember having had intercourse with her in the barn again; after the daughter came home from service on 1/4 1912 the prisoner often had intercourse with her, always in her room. [A further physical detail is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original He states that his stepdaughter always gave herself to him willingly and without any trace of compulsion on his part, which the prisoner of course was clear was in the highest degree wrong. The prisoner must admit that his stepdaughter drew his attention to the danger in their relationship, but that he always brushed it aside and reassured his stepdaughter that it did not matter, as long as the relationship did not get out among strangers.

It may well be right, as stated by the stepdaughter, that the last intercourse between them took place in the month of August last year. With the girl with whom he went away, Nielsine Nielsen, the prisoner has also had intercourse several times, in particular also during the time when they lived as neighbours on the dunes, which always took place in Nielsine’s room at her parents’. Asked, the prisoner says he has not had physical relations with other women. Read out and confirmed. The prisoner was led away.

Blodskamsforhold, incestuous relationship, is the register’s word. Corrections in the clerk’s own hand have been smoothed out in the transcription, and words written above the line have been included; see caveat 28. On the untranslated detail about the occasions in 1912 the register has “kun en enkelt Gang” (only a single time) — “en” is written above the line — as does the criminal file’s certified transcript; in the examination of 22 March, on the other hand, he confirmed his stepdaughter’s statement that it was every time. The contradiction stands in the sources themselves. [S119, S174]

Kristiane’s statement · the police court, 7 March 1913
Police register pp. 153—155 · case 26/13

There appeared before the court the prisoner’s wife, Christiane, née Enevoldsen, who confirmed her statement previously given in report A and was made acquainted with the prisoner’s statements in the examinations of the 24th and 28th of last month and with her daughter Christine Oline Enevoldsen’s statement in report A, to which she found nothing to object. The deponent had no idea of the punishable relationship that existed between her husband and her daughter until the daughter one day about the middle of last month, without any prompting from the deponent, revealed it to her. The deponent had noticed that the daughter had grown a little stouter lately, without it occurring to her that the daughter might be with child, and she had not herself asked the daughter or in any other way given her occasion to speak about the pregnancy. The disclosure came about in this way: the daughter, who without the deponent’s knowledge had written to Pastor Hornbeck of Randers, who as itinerant preacher for the Inner Mission has visited the dunes several times in recent years and so has sometimes had occasion to talk with the deponent’s daughter, and had confided in him about her pregnancy and her relationship with the deponent’s husband, handed the deponent a letter from the said pastor to the daughter, in which he charged her to confide in the deponent. After giving the deponent the letter the daughter went away, but after the deponent had read the letter, she went in to the daughter, who thereupon, with strong emotion and in tears, confirmed to the deponent what she had told the pastor, and on the deponent’s express question firmly declared that she had had nothing to do with other men and that the prisoner was therefore the father of the expected child. The daughter has not been examined by either midwife or doctor, but her pregnancy is now unmistakable, and in the deponent’s opinion — [the grounds she gives for it are not translated] Read this passage in the Danish original — the birth is expected in May. The deponent promises, however, to have the daughter examined by the midwife and to send the police a certificate from her.

Inasmuch as the daughter and the prisoner have stated in agreement that she gave herself to him at once without any resistance at his first request, the deponent finds no reason to doubt that this is correct, although she does not understand how it can have come about. She explains in this respect that the daughter, who was born of the deponent’s first marriage to fisherman Chresten Enevoldsen, who drowned on 1/4 1896, about 1½ months before the daughter came into the world, and who is therefore not yet 17 years old, [a description of the girl’s physical development follows; it is not translated] Read this passage in the Danish original. Mentally the daughter is normally developed and of ordinary intelligence ⟨corrected from “good understanding”⟩. She has always been a good girl in her home, has never, as far as the deponent knows, shown any inclination to excess in any direction [a further remark of the same kind is not translated] Read this passage in the Danish original. She went through school with those of her own age and has both there and at home received the usual upbringing, so that she was presumably no more ignorant of such matters than other young girls in the country of her age, and certainly had also taken in the common moral and religious convictions, so that she knew that loose relations between the sexes went against the commandments of religion and morality, and that in particular entering into such a relationship within the forbidden degrees of kinship is especially punishable.

Asked whether the prisoner then has something in his nature that affects women particularly strongly, and whether it must be assumed that it is this that has caused the daughter to fall at once for his first attack, the deponent answers that she cannot express an opinion on that; just as little as she had been aware at all that the relationship in question existed between her husband and her daughter, is she now, thinking back, able to remember anything that could suggest that the first intercourse between them had been preceded by any erotic influence or anything that could in any way be described as courting on her husband’s part towards the daughter.

The deponent’s marriage to the prisoner was entered into in May 1906 after she had at that time lived as a widow for c. 10 years with her 3 children. The deponent was entirely without means and as a widow received support from the Harboøre Fund. Just as the marriage on the part of her husband, who is 9 years younger than herself, was not based on considerations of property, so the union was not entered into on her side for the sake of support either, but was grounded in a strong and deep love, which has also made their marriage happy right up to the sudden collapse in the autumn just past. Her husband is not only in her judgement but also in the general opinion among those who know him a very likeable person and besides capable, diligent and hard-working. Her life with him has in every respect given her happiness and contentment, and she noticed in no way any cooling or reserve on his part before his sudden disappearance on 14 December last year.

The deponent had indeed during the late summer noticed that he often called at Tyge Nielsen Vem’s, with whose daughter he went away, and she had, also because there was talk in the district about it, asked him whether there was anything between him and Tyge Nielsen’s daughter, but as he firmly denied it, the deponent did not believe it either and thought no more about it. As the deponent has thus never seen him try to win any other woman, she is unable to say whether he must be said to possess any particularly erotically influential personality. Nor has the deponent, after the marriage was broken on his side, heard it suggested that he should have had to do with other women than Tyge Nielsen’s said daughter Nielsine and the deponent’s daughter referred to in this case. Read out and confirmed. On being asked, the deponent finally adds that she does not wish charges to be brought against the prisoner on account of his having been guilty of H. (adultery) towards her. Finally the deponent adds that her daughter, who has likewise been summoned to appear in court today, on account of her condition is not able to appear in court in Ringkjøbing until after the birth has taken place. The examination adjourned.

The same court day the maintenance case (36/13) was heard: he acknowledged the marriage and his going away and had nothing to object to his wife’s claim for 300 kr. a year to her and 90 kr. a year to each of the three children of the marriage until they turned 18, and she accepted his offer. It is also in that case that the expulsion from Kiel and his finances are explained. The register has “midt i forr. Maaned” (in the middle of last month) — that is, February — as does the criminal file’s certified transcript; report A dates the evening precisely to Thursday 13 February. [S119, S174]

The maintenance case · police court, 7 March 1913
Police register pp. 155—156 · case 36/13 · the same court day

36/13. Examination of Thomas Nielsen Silkjær in connection with a request from his deserted wife that he be ordered to pay maintenance to her and her children.

There were filed under A. a petition to Ringkjøbing County of February this year, under B. an examination, under C. a marriage certificate and under D, E, F, G. 4 baptismal certificates.

From the gaol there was[?] brought forward fisherman and smallholder Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, who is at present held in custody on remand, charged with breach of Penal Code § 162 etc.

The prisoner was made acquainted with petition A and examination B, to which he found nothing to object. It is correct that on 5[?] May 1906 he was married to his wife Christiane Silkjær, née Enevoldsen, with whom he has the 3 children named in the petition, and that on 14 December last he secretly left his wife, ⟨he⟩ leaving home together with an unmarried girl from Aargab, Nielsine Nielsen, and going away from the dunes. They went first to Kiel, where the deponent looked for work, but was expelled from there before he had obtained any[?] such. He and the said girl then travelled together to Copenhagen, where they have since lived together as man and wife, until the prisoner on the 21st of last month was arrested, charged with having made his stepdaughter pregnant, and transported here to the gaol. He admits that it was his intention not to return to his wife or his home, and he has nothing to object to his wife’s request that he be ordered to pay ⟨to her⟩ maintenance of 300 kr. a year and in addition maintenance of 90 kr. a year to each of their 3 children of the marriage until they have reached the age of 18.

Finally he observes that he was born on 10/1 1882 in Husby and that he considers himself entitled to poor relief in the municipality of his birth, since he, who after reaching the age of 18 first stayed c. 3 years in Vedersø, then ½ year on Holmslands Klit, c. 2 years in Esbjerg, did his military service in Copenhagen from the autumn of 1905[?] to the spring of 1906, then again lived in Esbjerg for c. 2 years and finally had fixed residence at Aargab on Holmslands Klit from 1/11 1908 to 14/12 1912, has thus not had uninterrupted fixed residence ⟨for 5 years⟩ in any municipality other than that of his birth.

As regards his financial circumstances he explains that he owns a holding for 4 cows and 2 small horses at Aargab, which he bought for 5000 kr. and against taking over a larger retirement maintenance (aftægt) resting on it. The holding is, however, mortgaged for 5000 kr. and would presumably yield no surplus if realised. Further the deponent is part-owner of a motor boat, which is used for fishing and freight sailing between Aargab and Ringkøbing, but which was bought with the help of a state loan against a guarantee. Finally the deponent is part-owner of 5[?] pound nets and various other fishing gear, but they are now almost worn out and therefore of no further value. He therefore considers that he must be said to be without means. His income in recent years he estimates, as stated in the petition, at 10[?] to 1200 kr. a year, but as a consequence of the punishment that now awaits him he will presumably not be able to earn anything in the next few years. Read out and confirmed.

The prisoner was taken out.

In accordance with the request there appeared before the court the petitioner Christiane Silkjær, née Enevoldsen, who was made acquainted with the prisoner’s foregoing statement and offer, to which she found nothing to object.

The examination closed.

In the register the case follows immediately after Kristiane’s statement the same day. Words and figures marked [?] are uncertain readings; ⟨…⟩ is written above the line or in the margin. [S119]

Kristine Oline’s statement · the court session at Årgab, 17 March 1913
Travelling police register pp. 72—74 · the court convened on the property at Årgab, the regular judge · Kptd./Kptden: the deponent (female), the person examined

1913, 17 March, 3½ in the afternoon, the Police Court of Ulfborg-Hind Hundreds was convened on Thomas Silkjær’s property at Aargab, Holmslands Klit, and administered by the regular judge with the witnesses named below, where No 26/1913 was then taken up — the examination continued. The judge observed that the court was convened here because the girl Christine Oline Enevoldsen cannot appear in court in Ringkøbing in her advanced state of pregnancy, and that the weather in the past week has made it impossible for the judge to travel to Aargab before today.

There appeared before the court the girl Christine Oline Enevoldsen, who confirmed her statement in report A, read out to her. She repeats that she was born on 17 May 1896 at Aargab of the parents fisherman Christen Olsen Enevoldsen, who had drowned shortly before the deponent’s birth, and his wife Christiane née Enevoldsen, who later married the prisoner. She further repeats her admission that since the harvest of 1911 she has on several occasions had physical relations with her said stepfather, the prisoner Thomas Silkjær, and that she is now with child by him and expects her confinement in the month of May. Finally she repeats that she never offered any resistance to the prisoner’s requests to allow him physical relations.

The deponent was some months over 15 years old when the first intercourse took place. She was confirmed in the spring when she turned 14, and she admits that she knew both that physical relations between man and woman can result in the woman becoming pregnant, and that physical relations outside marriage are as much against the commandment of religion as against human morality, and that it is likewise regarded in both respects as especially reprehensible when such relations take place between persons who stand to each other as parents and children or stepparents and stepchildren — on the other hand she did not know before that such intercourse was punishable ⟨inserted above the line⟩. She says that the prisoner never, before the first intercourse took place, behaved towards her in a way that could arouse any suspicion in her that he was thinking of obtaining physical relations with her; she never noticed that he behaved towards her, in word or deed, otherwise than as the one who stood in a father’s place to her.

When he asked her the first time to go out with him into the barn and lie down with him in the hay — they were both standing in the cowshed at the time, and the deponent’s mother was not at home at that moment — she understood at once what he meant, and she also thought at once that she was doing wrong, particularly towards her mother, in doing his will; she also said to him that it was surely not right of them and that it might lead to her becoming with child, but when he answered that when no one knew it, it did not matter, and that the deponent could be calm, he would see to it that nothing happened, she made no further objections but followed him into the barn. [The record goes on to describe the act in physical detail; that passage is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original

After that she had intercourse with him 2 more times that same autumn, before she went into service on 1 November. Both times it was the prisoner who asked for it — the deponent never herself made any approach — and she believes that both times she first answered that it was wrong, but gave in at once when he answered in the same way as the first time. In the half year she was away in service she never had intercourse with him, although she was in service here at Aargab; but after she had come back home in the spring of 1912, they again had intercourse with each other a few times, though at rather long intervals, and the deponent believes that she then no longer made any attempt to object to his demands. The last time was at the end of August. [The record here gives details of her body and of the signs of pregnancy; they are not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original In October she concluded that she was with child. She confided in an 18-year-old son of Anders Hejde in Bjerregaard, who has always been her confidant, and he asked her whether he might tell her mother; but when she asked him not to, he also promised her to keep quiet.

One day, shortly before the prisoner went away in December, the deponent was not well, and the prisoner then asked her whether anything was wrong with her; she replied that it was he who was to blame for her being poorly, and then nothing more was said about it; whether the prisoner understood that she was with child, she does not know. — In January the deponent wrote and confided in Pastor Hornbæk of Randers, who has been here on the dunes and with whom the deponent had then talked, and his answer then led her to confide in her mother. [A final physical detail in the deponent’s statement is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original The deponent finally observes that she has not previously been charged or punished. The deponent stood down. The examination adjourned. […] Witnesses: Enev. J. Enevoldsen · Chr. Silkær.

The sentence about punishability is inserted above the line in the original with an insertion mark. “The harvest of 1911” and the witness signature “Chr. Silkær” are readings — see caveat 29; “Hejde” is confirmed by the parish register. [S163, S170]

The police report · report A, 17 February 1913
The police report of 17 February 1913, exhibit A of the case · taken at Årgab by Constable Jensen · Kpt. = the deponent, the person examined

Ulfborg-Hind Hundreds Police, Ulfborg, at present Aargab, 17 February 1913. Report.

As it has come to the knowledge of the police that smallholder and fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkjær of Aargab has made himself guilty of a breach of §162 of the General Civil Penal Code of 10/2 66, in that he is said to have made pregnant his stepchild, not yet 17 years old, and the proper persons concerned have moreover wished the matter to be made the subject of public investigation, I have on the chief constable’s orders carried out an investigation in this matter.

The grandfather · former fisheries inspector Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen

There appeared for the report the pregnant girl’s grandfather, former fisheries inspector Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen, at present of Aargab, who in connection with the case stated the following: The pregnant girl’s mother Christiane was married to the deponent’s son Christen Olsen Enevoldsen, who drowned at sea on 1 April 1896. In this marriage there were 3 children, 2 sons and 1 daughter, namely the pregnant girl, whose name is Christine Oline Enevoldsen, and who was born only after her father’s death, namely on 17 May 1896. The deponent’s daughter-in-law then remained a widow about 7 or 8 years, after which time she entered into marriage with the then bachelor Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, who was then, as far as the deponent knows, only about twenty years old, while the deponent’s daughter-in-law was around 30. In this marriage there are 3 children aged from about 9 years to 2 or 3 years. The marriage appeared in the deponent’s view to be happy, and the husband was diligent and hard-working. He had, however, lately come to stand in a love relationship with the neighbour Thyger Nielsen’s daughter Nielsine, who is a little over 25 years old, with whom he went away last autumn, leaving his wife and children. On a search for them they were found between Christmas and New Year in Kiel, where they were living together in one room. It was the girl’s father who found them, and he got them to come with him to Vamdrup, but here they left him and are said to have gone to Copenhagen, where they are said to have been seen in the street by a soldier from the district, and presumably they are still in Copenhagen, but where they live is not known. —

As to the deserting husband having made his stepdaughter pregnant, the deponent states that last Thursday evening he received this information from Anders Hejde of Bjerregaard, who had been in Randers, where he had met a Pastor Hornbæk, who lives in Randers but is an itinerant preacher for the Danish Missionary Society; he had then told Anders Hejde that he had received a letter from the pregnant girl about the matter; the reason she had confided in him was that he had been on the dunes and held a service, and that she had not felt she could confide in anyone here at home. The next morning the deponent, who was then staying at Bjerregaard, travelled to Aargab to have the matter looked into more closely, but Christine had by then already confided in her mother, to whom she had said that she was with child by her deserting stepfather. The deponent has heard that she expects her confinement in the month of May this year. The deponent never personally noticed that any immoral relationship existed between the deserter and his stepdaughter, and it is something he could never have imagined.

The mother · Christiane née Enevoldsen

Next there appeared for the report Silkjær’s deserted wife Christiane née Enevoldsen, 40 years old, who stated that, as far as she remembers, she married Silkjær in 1906, and the marriage has been happy. On 14 December last year, however, he left her, as explained more fully by her father-in-law, and took the neighbour’s daughter with him; since then she has not seen him, but she assumes that he is staying in Copenhagen together with the girl he took with him. She concludes this from the fact that a son of the Bjerregaard postman, Jens Ottosen, who is at present in Copenhagen as a marine, and whose name is Otto Hejde, one evening around New Year, when he was standing guard at the “Yellow Palace”, saw them pass by together walking along the street, but otherwise she knows nothing of Silkjær’s whereabouts. She was quite unaware that any love relationship existed between Silkjær and Thyger Nielsen’s daughter. She was likewise quite unaware that any immoral relationship existed between her daughter Christine and Silkjær, and she had not before now noticed that her daughter Christine is with child. Christine, however, last Thursday evening confided this to the deponent, and that she was with child by Silkjær. The deponent could then also see that Christine was with child, and she does not doubt that it is by Silkjær. When the relationship between the daughter and Silkjær began, she does not know. She expects her confinement in the month of May this year. She has not been examined by any midwife or doctor, but the deponent believes that the time fits.

Kristine Oline

Then there appeared the girl Christine Oline Enevoldsen, who stated that her full name is as given, that she was born at Aargab on Holmslands Klit on 17 May 1896 of the parents fisherman Christen Olsen Enevoldsen and his wife Christiane née Enevoldsen, and that she later acquired a stepfather, whose name is Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, by whom she is with child, and that she expects her confinement at the end of May this year. She lives at home with her mother at Aargab.

She explains further that her stepfather and no one else is the father of the child she is expecting, as she has not had physical relations with any other man. The first time was one evening in the summer of 1911, as far as she remembers at harvest time. It took place out in the barn, in some hay, where Silkjær asked the deponent to go with him, and where he asked her to lie down, which she then, after several requests, did of her own will. [The report goes on to describe the act in physical detail; that passage is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original After that, until 1 November 1911, it happened 2 more times, once in the hay in the barn and the other time in the deponent’s bed, which stood in an out-of-the-way room. From 1 November 1911 to 1 April 1912 the deponent was away in service, and in that time she never had intercourse with her stepfather or with any other man. On 1 April 1912 the deponent came home and took up residence here. A short time after her return it happened again, in her room, and here it happened several times until the month of August. At the end of October the deponent realised that she was with child, but she did not mention this to her stepfather or to anyone else. The report records that it always took place of the deponent’s free will, and that the stepfather never obtained it from her by threats.

She, who knew very well that what they were doing was wrong, said so several times to her stepfather, but he then always said that when no one knew it, there was nothing wrong in it, and with that the deponent let herself be reassured.

Nielsine’s father · smallholder and fisherman Thyge Nielsen

Finally there appeared smallholder and fisherman Thyge Nielsen of Aargab, who stated that it is his daughter Silkjær has gone away with. Her name is Nielsine Nielsen and she is 25 years old, she speaks West Jutland dialect, is tall, thin, slight and pale. The deponent firmly believes that she is living with Silkjær somewhere or other in Copenhagen, but where he knows nothing whatever. After they went away the deponent searched for them and then found them in Kiel, where he had taken lodgings as fisherman Thomas Nielsen and wife from Esbjerg. When it was cleared up that this was not correct, he was expelled by the police, and both he and the daughter then went with the deponent to Vamdrup, from where they bought tickets, apparently to Fredericia. While with them the deponent could understand from them that they intended to go to Copenhagen. The deponent does not think they had very much money with them on the journey.

The description

Silkjær is a little under middle height, and he has a very fair moustache; he is ruddy and speaks West Jutland dialect; he has been a marine in Copenhagen; he is a fisherman and labourer.

Respectfully
J. […]. Jensen
Constable

The report is the birth certificate of the case: four statements taken at Årgab in a single day, four days after Kristine Oline had confided in her mother, and four days before her stepfather was arrested in Copenhagen. The exhibit lies in the criminal file, marked “A” in blue, with filing stamps from both courts — see image 61. [S174]

The admission and the waiver of § 174 · 22 and 26 March 1913
Police register p. 174 · the examination of 22 March, the regular judge

The prisoner was brought before the court. The judge went through with him the statements given by his wife in the examination of the 7th inst. and by Christine Oline on the 17th of the same month, the correctness of which the prisoner confirmed on every point. As regards Christine Oline’s statement in particular, he confirms that before the first intercourse took place she answered his request by saying that it was wrong of them to act so, and that she might of course become pregnant, and that the prisoner answered to this as she stated. [A physical detail of his statement is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original The prisoner admits that he knew very well that the girl was only 15 years old when he first had intercourse with her, and he admits that in view of her young age and his particular position towards her as her stepfather he must be said to have seduced her into the lewdness that took place between them, even though her resistance to it was only weak and brief. Read out and confirmed.

There were filed under E. and F. 2 baptismal certificates, under G. a marriage certificate, under H. a midwife’s certificate, under I and K. 2 criminal record certificates. The prisoner was shown baptismal certificate E., marriage certificate G. and criminal record certificate I., and he acknowledges them all as concerning him and correct. The examination adjourned.

Police register p. 177 · the final court session, 26 March

There appeared before the court the prisoner’s wife, Christiane, née Enevoldsen, and former fisheries inspector Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen. The judge observed that he has summoned the deponent Enevoldsen to appear as Christine Oline’s paternal grandfather, the judge in the present circumstances having found occasion, in addition to the deponent Christiane Silkjær, to require also of the deponent Enevoldsen, as Oline Christine’s natural guardian, a declaration as to whether a prosecution is desired against the prisoner for breach of Penal Code § 174. Both those present declared in agreement that they do not request prosecution of the prisoner for breach of the said penal provision. Read out and confirmed. The deponents were made acquainted with the statement given by the prisoner in the examination of the 22nd inst., to which they found nothing to object. The prisoner was brought in and was made acquainted with the statements given by the deponents today, to which he found nothing to object. On request, the deponent Enevoldsen and the deponent Silkjær were awarded for travel of respectively 12 and 8 running miles 6 and 4 kr., and in compensation for loss of earnings 2 kr. each. The examination closed for transcription.

Two criminal record certificates (I and K) — one for each of the two accused; the exhibits themselves, which lie in the criminal file, are marked “I” and “K” in blue; the register’s clerk forms I and J alike. § 174 — the seduction of a girl between twelve and sixteen — could only be prosecuted at the request of parents or guardian; when the family waived it, the case was left resting on § 162 alone — the provision that punishes both parties. [S119]

The defence counsel’s pleading · attorney Kamp, 3 April 1913
Handwritten on attorney M. P. Kamp’s notepaper · filed in the extraordinary court on 11 April 1913 by attorney Hammersø · the case’s only speech for the defence

To the Extraordinary Court of Ulfborg Hind Hundreds in the criminal case: High Court attorney P. Grove, prosecutor, v. the prisoner Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and the accused Christine Oline Enevoldsen.

As appointed defence counsel for the accused, while accepting the prosecutor’s account of the case, I beg leave to state the following:

The prisoner Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, who is about 9 years younger than his wife Christiane Enevoldsen, married her at the age of about 24; his marriage is or has been — from what has emerged — good, and he is not seen to have been in conflict with the law before. When this has nonetheless now happened, to his misfortune, the age difference between the spouses cannot be left entirely out of consideration in judging this case. It is not seldom seen that such an age difference, particularly when it is the woman who is the elder, has its fateful influence on the more intimate life together, even if the life together otherwise seems good and happy to outsiders. The prisoner has 3 children with his wife, and it has been established that besides the other accused in the case he has had physical relations with a Thyge Nielsen’s daughter, with whom he was living at the time of the arrest. — One is compelled to the assumption that the prisoner’s sexual drive is more than normally developed, and that his counter-motives are not or have not been so strong that they could provide the necessary counterweight to the strong primal drive.

It is true that our Penal Code does not take the right and rational account of the kind of thing one must call mental abnormalities, but it does not exclude their being taken into consideration in fixing the penalty.

Besides what has been stated, I ask that it be taken into consideration as a mitigating circumstance that the prisoner is otherwise a capable and honourable man, of whom nothing unfavourable is otherwise to be said in any respect. He is no sexual criminal of the sinister kind, and has been willing to admit his punishable conduct.

I can only recommend him for the law’s mildest penalty.

As regards the accused Christine, the offence that has taken place has already been in the highest degree ruinous for her and has carried its punishment in itself, when one considers the disgrace that falls most heavily on the woman in relationships of this kind.

[The defence counsel opens this passage with remarks on the girl’s physical development; they are not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original Her mental maturity has presumably not matched it; she lives in her home together with the prisoner, and probably does not feel particularly “related” to him — she was already about 10 years old when her mother married for the second time. [A further remark of the same kind is not translated.] Read this passage in the Danish original When he then makes his approaches to her, she is not repelled for any refined reasons; even so she does not give herself up at once without a will; she feels the “wrongness” of it, but he persuades her, and his persuasions — that when no one knew it, it did no harm — together with his purely moral ascendancy as stepfather, make her give in time after time, and her moral scruples are fought down. As he also reassured her with regard to the possible consequences, it is understandable that she fell for the temptations. The accused may well have known that it was a morally wrong relationship she had come into, but she has declared that the punishable nature of the relationship was not known to her. Had she been clear about it, there is every reason to assume that such knowledge would have torn her out of her dormant moral scruples, and she would have resisted the prisoner’s approach. She seems to have stood rather isolated in her relationship with her mother — the one in whom she might otherwise most naturally be thought to seek guidance and support; even when the relationship with the prisoner has consequences, she cannot confide in her mother — but only in a pastor who happened to visit her district.

Her offence was committed before she was 18. It was, as mentioned, the prisoner who asked her to have intercourse; she herself made no approaches to him, who is thus the one who has seduced her. She has — by her own statement — not had physical relations with any other man, and in the half year she was away from home and thus from the prisoner’s influence, she had no such relations with him; her conduct has thus, apart from the case here, been clean.

According to what has been stated, there is in the accused’s case legal ground for a suspended sentence. That such a sentence will in this case be in the highest degree appropriate will, besides following from what has been set out, be supported by the fact that the moral effect of the offence on her and the offence’s open consequence must be punishment enough for her, so that by that alone she will be brought back.

Forced labour or imprisonment will here do more harm than good.

Nor should considerations of deterrence motivate an unconditional penalty, for these considerations have, in relation to the world around, been satisfied by the disgrace alone that has befallen the accused.

In accordance with what has been stated I therefore claim, as regards the prisoner Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, that the law’s mildest penalty be applied, while for the accused Christine Oline Enevoldsen I recommend and claim a suspended sentence with the mildest penalty, alternatively the law’s mildest penalty — all under mitigating circumstances.

Further I claim a fee for my defence of both the accused.

Ringkjøbing, 3 April 1913
respectfully, Kamp
Hammersø

So the same appointed defence counsel represented both the adult stepfather and the sixteen-year-old stepdaughter he was charged with. Corrections in Kamp’s own hand have been smoothed out — among them, Kamp himself corrected “retsstridigt” (unlawful) to “urigtigt” (wrong). The pleading is dated 3 April and was filed at the extraordinary court on 11 April. Below the signature Hammersø has co-signed — it was also he who appeared in court. The pleading lies in the criminal file; the last page of the prosecutor’s counterpart is shown as image 64. [S174]
