The judgment · the register of judgments, 14 April 1913
Register of judgments fol. 101—102 · case no. 6/1913

In the year 1913, on 14 April, in the criminal case of High Court attorney Grove, prosecutor, v. Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen for breach of § 162 of the Penal Code (defence counsel Kamp), the following judgment was given:

In this case the prisoner Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen are charged with breach of § 162 of the Penal Code. The prisoner was born on 10 January 1882, the accused on 17 May 1896. Neither of them is found to have been previously charged. According to the prisoner’s and the accused’s concurring confessions, which agree with what has otherwise been established, the circumstances of the case are as follows: after the accused’s mother, Christiane, née Enevoldsen, had in April 1896 been widowed by her first husband, fisherman Christen Enevoldsen, of which marriage the accused was born about 1½ months after her father’s death, she entered on 5 May 1906 into a new marriage with the prisoner, in which marriage, which still subsists, 3 children have been born. At the same time as the prisoner has lived together with his wife in this marriage, until in December 1912 he secretly left home and went away together with an unmarried daughter of one of his neighbours, he has since the summer of 1911, at which time the accused was only some months over 15 years old, had intercourse several times with the accused [a remark on her physical development is not translated] Read this passage in the Danish original; which relationship has resulted in the accused having become pregnant and, according to a midwife’s certificate, being expected to give birth in the month of May this year.

The prisoner never used violence or threats to get his will with the accused; the first time the prisoner asked her for intercourse, the accused made some weak objections to it, but gave in immediately afterwards when the prisoner reassured her that he would see to it that the relationship had no consequences, and that it did not matter when no one knew it; according to the accused’s statement it must be assumed that before the occasions immediately following she repeated her objections, but likewise quickly gave in, and gradually she gave up entirely every objection to the prisoner’s demands for intercourse.

The prisoner has admitted that he, who knew very well that the accused was only 15 years old when he first had intercourse with her, in view of her young age and his particular position as her stepfather must be said to have seduced her into the immoral relationship that took place between them; [a physical detail of his statement is not translated] Read this passage in the Danish original. In accordance with what has been stated the prisoner and the accused are to be judged under § 162 of the Penal Code, in the accused’s case taken together with §§ 21 and 37, and the penalty is found in the circumstances to be fixed for the prisoner at hard labour in the house of correction for 18 months, and for the accused at simple imprisonment for one month. In view of the accused’s young age the serving of the sentence is further found, pursuant to § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911, to be suspended, so that the penalty, provided the conditions laid down in the said provisions are fulfilled, lapses after the expiry of 5 years from the pronouncement of this judgment. The costs of the prosecution, including the fees to prosecutor and defence counsel given below, are to be laid on the prisoner and the accused in solidum. The appointed conduct of the case has been lawful.

It is therefore adjudged: Thomas Nielsen Silkjær shall be punished with hard labour in the house of correction for Eighteen Months. Christine Oline Enevoldsen shall be punished with simple imprisonment for one month, but the execution of the sentence is suspended and the sentence lapses after the expiry of 5 years from the pronouncement of this judgment, provided the conditions laid down in § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911 are fulfilled. The costs of the prosecution, including a fee to the prosecutor, High Court attorney Grove, of 30 kr. and to the defence counsel, attorney Kamp, of 25 kr., are to be paid by the prisoner and the accused one for both and both for one. To be complied with under penalty of law.

The register of the extraordinary court records the two sessions: the trial on 11 April at half past ten at the court house — where “The accused Christine Oline Enevoldsen did not appear when called” — and the pronouncement of judgment on 14 April at 4 p.m. at the district office, with the reference “(see register of judgments fol. 101)”. The judge’s signature, which could not be deciphered in the register, is written out in the criminal file’s transcript of the judgment: John Finsen. [S121, S122, S174]

Tap anywhere in the transcription and the place lights up on the original — or tap the original to find the text.

And the registers must be read for what they are. They were written by men — judges, deputies, clerks of the court, a prison official — in a time when both the offender and the wronged were sentenced, and when a sixteen-year-old girl’s own voice had no column. Her words exist only as reported, confirmed by him, filtered through the court’s language. But they exist: she said it was wrong. She said she could become pregnant. And when everything else closed around her, she wrote a letter.

The chronicle carries it with it, because it is there. Not because it explains anything — but because a family history that holds only cutters and crosses of honour is not the family’s history.

13
Chapter 13 · 1913—1998

Kristine Oline and Arne

The child was born at Årgab on 26 May 1913 and carried to baptism in Haurvig Church three weeks later. Seventeen years later he stood in the census as a foster child in his own father’s household.

He was the child who came out of the case, but not an epilogue to it. This chapter follows him and his mother — two lives of their own, which the papers have only partly preserved.

26 May and 15 June 1913
The birth and the baptism

The child was born at Aargab on 26 May 1913. Kristine Oline had turned seventeen nine days before. She gave birth at home at Årgab — no going away, no lying-in hospital in another town.

The father was already in custody. He had been sentenced for the relationship that had led to the pregnancy, and he was not there when the child was born.

And when he was entered in the record, the pastor hid nothing. The parish register of Ny parish, births, male, 1913, no. 5:

1913, the 26th (twenty-sixth) of May. — Aargab, Holmslands Klit, Ny parish, Hind Hundred. — Arne Enevoldsen — Unmarried mother Christine Oline Enevoldsen, Aargab. 17 years. Named father: stepfather Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, 31 years.
Ny parish, Hind Hundred · births, male, 1913, no. 5 [S47]

One word makes all the difference: stepfather. The pastor could have made do with name and age, as the form required. He wrote out the relationship. The child was given his mother’s surname: Arne Enevoldsen.

The baptism stands in the last three columns of the same opening:

1913, the 15th (fifteenth) of June. — Pastor S. R. Madsen in Haurvig Church. — The girl Johanne Andersen, smallholder Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen, smallholder Søren Andersen Jensen, smallholder Thyge Nielsen. All of Aargab.

Three weeks after the birth. No hasty home baptism, no postponement, no quiet dispatch to another church. The child was carried into the parish church and held over the font by four named neighbours — while the father sat in Ringkjøbing jail.

Notice, then, who is not there. No Silkjær. Thomas’ family in Husby is not represented by a single name, and Kristiane does not stand as godparent either. It is the mother’s side and the neighbourhood that carry the child forward — not the father’s side. So it was too at Kristen’s baptism in 1904: godparents were taken from the parish’s own circle, and Husby lay a day’s journey away.

And read the last of the godparents’ names once more: smallholder Thyge Nielsen. It is Nielsine’s father — the father of the woman the child’s father had fled with half a year before, and who was at that very moment carrying his next child. He stood at the font for Kristine Oline’s boy all the same. Two families that the same man had brought to grief, each in its own way, held on to each other across it. On the dunes neighbourliness was older than scandal. [S47, S119]

Two of the names come from chapter 10

Read the list of godparents together with the crew list of “Forsøget”, 1 April 1896. Two of the four names are already there.

Smallholder Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen

The drowned skipper’s father — and so Kristine Oline’s grandfather. It is he whom the prison register calls Kristiane’s father-in-law, whose property at Aargab they got. And it was the fourth time in nine years that he turned out around the family: godfather at Kristen’s baptism in 1904, witness at Kristiane’s new marriage in 1906, summoned to court as Kristine Oline’s natural guardian in March 1913 — and now, three months later, godfather again. It was also an Enevold Enevoldsen who pulled the survivor ashore on a line in 1896.

Smallholder Søren Andersen Jensen

The only one who survived the wreck. The man from her father’s boat who came ashore alive — driven south in the surf, unconscious, given up and revived. He was not hired crew by chance: he owned the boat and the boat partnership together with Christen Olesen Enevoldsen. Born at Årgab on 17 November 1869, married in Haurvig Church on 7 February 1893, died at Årgab on 29 December 1937 — he stayed all his life where the accident happened.

What the two of them felt about what had happened in that home, we do not know. But they turned out, and they carried the child.

Søren Andersen Jensen is the more certain of the two: name, place and title are the same in 1896 and 1913, and he is registered at Årgab from his birth in 1869 to his death in 1937. The grandfather relationship is in the Enevoldsen family book — Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen and Ane Iversen as parents of the drowned boat skipper — and his three appearances around Kristiane, 1904, 1906 and 1913, are in the parish registers. The name Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen is also borne by Kristine Oline’s elder brother, b. 13.10.1892 — the title smallholder points to the elder man. [S31, S32, S40, S47, S48, S55, S56, S70, S71]

And the church is the same. Christen Olesen Enevoldsen was buried from Haurvig Church on 6 April 1896. Seventeen years later his daughter’s son was baptised in the same room. Arne was carried in; his grandfather lies outside.

The revival had had its breakthrough when the sea took four men. The baptismal entry of 1913 shows two of the names from 1896 gathered around a child again — carried forward by the mother’s family and the neighbourhood. How the rest of the awakened community received him, the sources do not say.

1913—1940
Kristine Oline

The first document in which she stands as the one making a claim is older than you might think — it came three days after the baptism. On 18 June 1913 the district bailiff’s office opened a new case in the list of cases: “Pat. S. Christine Oline Enevoldsen v. Thomas Nielsen Silkjær” — a paternity case, number 82/1913. She stood as first party. Seventeen years old, a month after the birth, with the child’s father in Ringkjøbing jail, she stood as a party in a maintenance case against her stepfather — the same road her mother had taken in February. The case was closed as early as 20 June; the maintenance order itself lay with the county and has not been found. But the single line in the list of cases is enough to show that the boy’s support was put on a formal footing while his father was inside — and that the case stood in her name. [S120]

That the payments also had to be enforced is shown by a find a year and a half later. Politiets Efterretninger — the same gazette that in February 1913 had carried the arrest — lists him in no. 12 of 28 January 1915 under the heading “Wanted maintenance debtors”: debtors the authorities were looking for because an ordered payment stood unpaid. Which payment was in arrears, the notice does not say — it may have been Arne’s or Else Margrethe’s, but also the older maintenance case of March 1913 concerning Kristiane and the three children of the marriage. But he had not vanished: he was living with his family in Esbjerg, where the census finds them together the year after, and the day after the notice, on 29 January 1915, Kristiane gave birth to his son Ejlerth Marius at Hjertinggade 13. While his name stood in print in the police gazette as a wanted maintenance debtor, his wife lay in childbed with the next child. The notice must therefore be read for what it proves — arrears and a gazette that did not know where the man was — not as a sign that he had left home again. [S76, S176]

The prison register had already put an address on the move in the summer of 1913: the property at Aargab was sold, and Kristiane moved “again with the children” to Esbjerg, to Gl. Færgevej 7. Arne was six weeks old. But one did not move with them. The census of 1921 records Kristine Oline as having moved to Esbjerg in 1916, from Holmsland. She stayed on the dunes, while the child at a time still unknown came into the family’s household in Esbjerg. [S44, S78]

The sources show the arrangement by February 1916 at the latest: the boy was then in Esbjerg, while his mother had only just come from Holmsland. When Arne was separated from her and came into his grandmother’s household, no known source says — nor who decided it, whether it was meant as a temporary arrangement, or what any of them thought about it. An unmarried mother of seventeen in 1913 seldom had that kind of choice on her own. Where on Holmsland she was in the years between remains open — and no census can answer: the only one between 1911 and 1921 is precisely the census of February 1916, and by then she was already in Esbjerg. [S133]

The family in Esbjerg meanwhile moved again: on 1 February 1916 no Silkjær household stood on Gl. Færgevej. The census records the fisherman Thomas Silkjær with Kristiane and five children at Hjertinggade 13 — Ejlert had been born there in January 1915. And in the column Children, without distinction from the others: Arne Silkjær. Two years old, recorded with the family’s name, as one of the children of the house. [S76]

And on the same census day she herself stands in the returns — for the first time in Esbjerg. At Nørregade 44 in Vor Frelser parish the census records Kristine Oline Enevoldsen, born 17 May 1896, unmarried servant, occupation domestic help — in the house of Anders Hansen Larsen and Anne Marie Larsen, their children and a lodger. Nineteen, in service with strangers. On 1 February 1916, then, mother and son were in the same town: he as one of the children of the house in Hjertinggade, she as the maid in the house in Nørregade — a few streets apart, and two different households. At Helgolandsgade 14, the address at her wedding seven months later, she was not yet living; the census does not record her in any of the property’s households. And the year of arrival, 1916, in the census five years later only just fits: she must have come to the town in the very first weeks of the year — or else the year has been rounded. [S76, S78, S133]

That same autumn, on 19 September 1916, she was married in Esbjerg, twenty years old:

The girl Christine Oline Enevoldsen, Helgolandsgade 14, Esbjerg, born Holmslands Klit, Ny parish, on 17 May 1896, daughter of the late fisherman Christen Olesen Enevoldsen and his wife Kristiane Enevoldsen, Esbjerg.
Esbjerg, marriages, 19 September 1916 [S75]

The groom was the fisherman Niels Peder Edvard Nielsen, twenty-one, born in Esbjerg — son of the fisherman Jens Højberg Nielsen, whose family lived in the same property at Helgolandsgade 14 that the bride gave as her address. Notice her mother’s name: the pastor recorded her as “wife Kristiane Enevoldsen” — the first marriage’s name, ten years into the second. And the stepfather appears nowhere in the entry. The witnesses were the groom’s father and “fisherman Enevold J. Enevoldsen, Esbjerg” — the grandfather or the elder brother; the entry does not distinguish.The witness “fisherman Enevold J. Enevoldsen, Esbjerg” may be the grandfather (b. 1848) or the elder brother (b. 13.10.1892) — the title fits both. The residence points to the elder brother: the grandfather was in Ny parish at the census seven months before the wedding and does not appear in Esbjerg in 1921 either. The entry does not settle it. See caveat 11. [S75, S77, S78] All caveats → [S75]

Their daughter Gerda Jensine was born on 23 February 1917, five months after the wedding — Kristine Oline was with child when she married. In the generation before, too, the child had come before the marriage: Kristiane gave birth to Kristen in 1904 and married Thomas in 1906. The child’s name has an H. between the first names in the 1921 return, and the census of 1925 writes it out: Gerda Jensine Højbjerg — her father’s byname, written into the middle of the child’s name, thirteen years before the family received it as a surname by royal licence. That the enumerator wrote Højbjerg for Højberg is, by the way, the same wavering as Silkær for Silkjær. [S75, S78, S81]

The census of 1921 shows the new household: Helgolandsgade 14, first floor, flat 2 — her husband, Kristine Oline and Gerda. Three people. Arne is not there; he lived with his grandmother and his father both as a two-year-old in 1916 and as a seventeen-year-old in 1930. [S78]

The trail can be followed two steps further. The census of 1925 finds the three still together at Helgolandsgade 14, and in November 1930 Kristine Oline stands in the household at Cort Adelersgade 15b — thirty-four years old. [S81, S82]

She died on 18 May 1940, at three o’clock in the night, at Esbjerg Municipal Hospital. The day before she had turned forty-four. Four days later she was buried in Gormsgade Cemetery, from Zion’s parish, by Pastor Birke. [S84]

The parish register records her as Christine Oline Højberg née Enevoldsen and writes out her parentage: born at Aargab, Holmsland Klit parish, on 17 May 1896 as the daughter of fisherman Christen Olesen Enevoldsen and his wife Kristiane. The book that recorded her birth six weeks after the wreck names her father again at her death — forty-four years later, in another town, by another pastor. [S84]

The death certificate was filled in by the doctor Jakob Bak in the surgical department that same morning. The principal disease is given as c. uteri — cancer of the womb — with kakeksia, wasting, as a complication; the weakening of the heart in the next column is only the way it ended. The wasting points to a long illness, but the certificate does not say how long she had been ill.Box 7 of the certificate gives the principal disease, box 8 the immediate cause of death. The register of deaths’ copy reproduces only box 8 — “weakening of the heart, paresis cordis” — and leaves out the cancer diagnosis above it. The chronicle follows the certificate. [S83] All caveats →

Box 3 of the certificate is meant to hold the deceased’s position and occupation. It holds three words: married to fisherman. That is how the papers kept her — but between a parish register entry six weeks after a wreck and a death certificate issued the day after a birthday lies a whole life that none of the boxes had room for. [S83]

1930
Foster child

In 1930 the family was back at Gl. Færgevej 7 — the address from the prison register, left along the way for Hjertinggade. The census of 5 November 1930 records the household with Thomas Nielsen Silkjær as head, Kristiane as wife and six children — and in the middle of the children, on the sixth line of the household, Arne Enevoldsen, 17, with his position in the family given as foster child.

It is his father’s household, the family his mother herself had grown up in, and on paper he is neither son nor brother. He is in care.

Lay the three documents side by side. On the dunes in 1913 everything stood in the parish register — the mother’s name, her age, the father’s name, his age and the relationship between them. The parish knew it, the godparents turned out, and the pastor wrote it down. In 1916 he is Arne Silkjær, one child among five in the column Children. In 1930 he is Arne Enevoldsen, foster child.

The two returns can be read either way. “Arne Silkjær, child” may be everyday language about a two-year-old in the house; “Arne Enevoldsen, foster child” is legally correct, for his name was Enevoldsen. The change may be a movement from the informal to the precise — or from closeness to distance. The returns show the difference; they do not explain it.

The column followed him on. When he was confirmed in Zion’s Church on 24 April 1927, thirteen years old, the pastor had sent for the baptismal certificate from Ny parish and copied the entry — word for word. The father’s three columns stand empty. The mother’s position is given as “unmarried girl of 17”, and in the remarks it says “Named father: Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, 31 years”. She was thirty in 1927 and lived in the town; he was forty-five and lived in the same house as the boy. It is not a description of anyone — it is 1913 copied fourteen years forward and four parishes further east. [S88]

The residence in the entry is Færgevej 7. The pastor was Pastor Bentzen, who thirteen years later would marry him.

1940—1998
Arne

But Arne does not stay in the column. Ten years later he appears in the papers again, this time on his own account. On 11 May 1940, fifteen days before he turned twenty-seven, he was married in Zion’s Church by Pastor Bentzen: bachelor, accountant Arne Enevoldsen, Havnegade 179, and the girl, dental technician Annagrethe Thomsen, born at Jerne on 4 April 1916, daughter of the customs officer Emil Peter Thomsen. The census of 5 November the same year records them on Rolfsgade in Esbjerg. [S85]

Two things in that entry should be read slowly. The address: Havnegade 179 is the fishing skipper’s house. Arne was twenty-six and still living with his father when he married. And the witnesses: the bride’s father stood for her, and for him stood “fishing skipper Silkjær, Havnegade 179”.

At the baptism in 1913 not one Silkjær stood among the godparents. Twenty-seven years later the man signs as witness — while the entry above records the groom as son of Christine Oline Enevoldsen, Frodesgade 149. Only the mother. The father is unnamed in the column and present on the same page, exactly as in 1913, when the pastor wrote “Named father: stepfather”. The difference is that now it is his own hand.

And the date carries more than it seems to. The mother’s address in the entry is Frodesgade 149 — she was still alive. Seven days after the wedding she died in hospital. Arne married in the last week of his mother’s life, in the parish she was buried from eleven days later. [S83, S84, S85]

And then there are pictures. In Esbjerg Byhistoriske Arkiv there are three negatives that the photographer Paul Bølling took for the Enevoldsen family, Rolfsgade 127, in the middle of the Occupation years. The archive records them as accountant Arne Enevoldsen, born 1913, and his wife Annegrethe, born 1916. One is a party in the living room, where some of the guests wear little paper hats. The other two were taken when their daughter came into the world in May 1944: the mother in childbed with the baby beside her, and the baby alone in a cradle with a bonnet on.The identification rests on three coincidences: the year of birth 1913, the address Rolfsgade, where the census of 1940 also records him, and the wife’s name and year of birth. The archive itself is guarded about who is seen in the two birth pictures — “It must be Annagrethe Enevoldsen. Perhaps with the daughter Annette” — while the family and the address stand firm. The marriage of 11.5.1940 has been read in the Zion’s parish register; the census of 5.11.1940 is in the family file. [S40, S57, S85] All caveats →

Kristine Oline’s mother, Kristiane, stayed with Thomas. She stood as his wife in 1930, as his widow at Thomas’ funeral in 1950, and she died in 1963 with his name. What they said to each other in the years after 1913 lies outside any source.

Read it together with the parish register of 1913. The boy who was born to a seventeen-year-old girl in a fisherman’s house at Årgab and entered in the parish’s book with his mother’s stepfather as named father was, thirty-one years later, an accountant in Esbjerg, married, in a home of his own — and had the means and the heart to book a photographer when his daughter was born.

The road there can be followed year by year, for Esbjerg printed its tax books. In 1932 he appears as an office trainee on Havnegade paying twenty-one kroner in tax — and just above him on the page, the number before in the book, T. N. Silkjær, fishing skipper, paying seventy-three. Nineteen years old, in his father’s house, with his first employment of his own. In 1935 he is a clerk, still at Havnegade 179. In 1939 it says accountant. [S89]

Two years later Regnskabs-Kontoret (the Accounts Office) appears in Krak’s directory: bookkeeping and auditing, Ny Havn, telephone 2143. The office lay on the harbour, a few hundred metres from the quay where his father’s E.94 lay, and where his half-brothers Niels and Ejlert had their cutters. At Christmas 1944 he advertised in the workers’ first-aid association’s Christmas magazine: “Regnskabskontoret · Accountant Arne Enevoldsen, M. L. R.” [S90]

And then came the position that put the two names on the same page of Statstidende, the official gazette. The fishermen’s own liability insurance in Esbjerg had for many years had the bank official E. Enevoldsen as treasurer and bookkeeper; after his death the work was handed over to the accountant Arne Enevoldsen. [S140] On 5 January 1945 the society was entered in the Insurance Register as no. 468, and the notice lists the persons:

Registreringstidende · 5 January 1945 · no. 468

“Board: fishing skipper Christian Enevold Sørensen (chairman), fishing skipper Søren Andreas Jensen, fishing skipper Anton Kristensen, fishing skipper Thomas Silkjær, fishing skipper Peder Heide, all of Esbjerg. Manager: Arne Enevoldsen, Esbjerg.”

“The association is bound by the signature of the chairman of the board together with a member of the board or with the manager.”

Four lines between them. The father on the board, the son as manager — and a signing rule that made it possible to commit the association with the chairman’s signature and Arne’s. In the parish register of 1913 Thomas stood as named father, but the child bore his mother’s name. In Statstidende in 1945 Enevoldsen and Silkjær stood side by side, each with his own title, in the same small association on the harbour.The notice gives no dates of birth. That “fishing skipper Thomas Silkjær, Esbjerg” is Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, and that “Arne Enevoldsen, Esbjerg” is the accountant from Regnskabs-Kontoret, rests on occupation, town and year: both names are rare in Esbjerg’s fishing world, Thomas owned E.94 until 1948, and Arne was advertising as an accountant in the town a few weeks before the registration. How closely the two worked together, the source does not say — only that they sat in the same association with separate functions. The predecessor, the bank official E. Enevoldsen, has not been identified; whether he was related to Arne’s mother’s family is not known. [S140, S141]

And he became a man others asked to sign for them. On 21 December 1943 “accountant Arne Enevoldsen, Rolfsgade 127” stood as witness at a wedding in Esbjerg — for the business manager Thomas Kaj Nielsen, married by the same Pastor Bentzen. [S91]

The tax books draw the arc drily: 21 kroner as an office trainee in 1932, 16 as a clerk in 1935, 247 as a newly qualified accountant in 1939, 719 in 1943, 1,174 in 1946. And they follow him address by address through twenty-four years — Havnegade 179, Rolfsgade 127, Gl. Vardevej 5, Strandbygade 39, Strandbygade 90a. From his father’s house to a home of his own, and from there on through three addresses, within the same town. As far as the books reach, he stayed in Esbjerg. [S89]

The marriage did not last, and the tax books show the break as a household that becomes two. Rolfsgade 127 is Arne’s address up to and including 1946. In 1949 he is at Gl. Vardevej 5 — and at Rolfsgade 127 stands A. Enevoldsen, Mrs, assessed separately at 1,045 kroner. She stayed in the flat, he moved out, and for tax purposes they became two people somewhere between 1946 and 1949.

The man she later married appears in the same books. Ronald Søren Hyllested — born in Aarhus in 1916, a coachman’s son — was a police constable in Esbjerg from 1941 and had himself been married before: on 19 July 1942 he was married in Vor Frelser Church to the machine manufacturer’s daughter Ane Marie Villemoes of Teglværksgade. In 1951 he still appears as a police constable, now at Kirkegade 101. And in 1954 the occupation has changed: sales representative. That is, word for word, the description the royal licence of 22 March the same year uses of him — “sales representative Ronald Søren Hyllested, Esbjerg” — when the daughter was adopted and thereafter bore the name Annette Hyllested. The tax books have Arne in Esbjerg both before and after: Strandbygade in 1951 and again in 1956. He was alive and in the town when the licence was granted. The endorsement stands in the margin by her baptism in 1944: Enevoldsen struck out, Hyllested written instead. And the name was used: when Annette was confirmed in 1959, she appears in the parish register as Annette Hyllested, daughter of “sales representative Ronald Søren Hyllested and his wife Annagrethe Thomsen”, with the home at Spangsbjerg Kirkevej 42 — and with birth and baptism traced back to Zion’s parish, 16 May and 2 July 1944. [S113] Annagrethe and Ronald both died in 2004, five months apart; at their deaths they lived at the same address on Kongensgade in Esbjerg.Annagrethe was divorced from Arne by licence on 3 June 1949. Ronald Søren Hyllested was divorced from his first wife by licence on 27 July 1949. Annagrethe and Ronald were married by the Copenhagen Magistracy on 11 February 1950; all three facts stand in Esbjerg’s register of civil marriages. [S139] The endorsement of the adoption documents the licence of 22 March 1954, but not Arne’s declaration or the considerations behind the adoption; that requires the adoption file itself. See caveat 25. [S86, S89, S93, S99, S113] All caveats →

Annette trained as a nurse and in connection with her training moved to Copenhagen, where she came to live for the rest of her life. She had two children. The family does not believe that she later had contact with her biological father, but it cannot be established with certainty. She died in 2024, shortly after her 80th birthday — a day she lived to celebrate with the family in her daughter’s garden, in bright sunshine and with music playing. [S173]

The marriage to Annagrethe was dissolved by licence on 3 June 1949. The year after, he began again. On 2 December 1950 at 12.10 Arne was married in a civil ceremony at Esbjerg town hall to the telephonist Edna Alice Söderwall, née Gram. Both were divorced, both were born in 1913 — he at Årgab in May, she in Esbjerg in September — and they were already living at the same address, Strandbygade 39, the address the tax book gives for him the year after. The witnesses were two women from the offices, a municipal assistant and an office assistant. No family members stood as witnesses.

No sign of a further divorce has been found. Edna bore the name Enevoldsen until her death in Vejle in 2002. Arne died on 27 December 1998 in Vejle, eighty-five years old — the man who was born at Årgab while his father sat in Ringkjøbing jail, and who bore his mother’s name because his father’s did not become his. [S40, S139, S147]

But the name followed him all the way: office trainee, clerk, accountant, Enevoldsen. The name he was given, when his father’s did not become his, became the one he put on his own office.

Part IV

Out from the dunes

Chapters 14—20 · 1883—today
14
Chapter 14 · 1883—1956

Ane Johanne

Here the story leaves the harbour in Esbjerg and winds back to 1883. For while Thomas’ trail ran through tax books and registers, another part of the family of brothers and sisters had long since set off the opposite way — inland.

Ane Johanne was Niels Thomsen Silkjær’s eldest daughter with Ane Jensen. She stands in the middle of the line this chronicle follows — and she is the one the sources say least about.

Born at Økjær on 22 October 1883, baptised in Husby Church on 18 November — daughter of Niels and his second wife, Ane Jensen. We know her dates, her marriage, her children. We do not know her voice: no letters, no memories. But in one place in the sources her imprint can be glimpsed, and we will come back to it.

On 22 March 1906 she was married in Husby Church, 22 years old. The groom did not come from the coast: Mads Erik Madsen, born on 28 July 1879 in Hanning parish and baptised in Hanning Church on 17 August, son of Knud Madsen and Ane Eriksen. He was a bricklayer — later a master mason at Rækker Mølle. At the census of 1901 he was living on Sofievej in Copenhagen: he had been out in the world before he came back and fetched a wife from Husby.

“Husby Kᵉ” — the church where she was baptised and married — and the parish around it: the dunes, the marshes and the lake.
Image 1c · Survey sheets 1:20,000, sheets AA15, AA16, Ø15 and Ø16, surveyed 1872 · free map material · credit historiskekort.dk
All the women before her in this story had married within the same landscape: from Tarpgaard to Økjær, from Økjær to Husby Klit. Ane Johanne married a trade — and a trade did not live in any particular place.

A bricklayer followed the work, and in those years the building was happening inland: in the railway towns, along the new lines, in the growing country parishes on the reclaimed heath. She became the first in the direct line to leave the coast altogether.

15
Chapter 15 · 1906—1930

From Husby to
Rækker Mølle

Husby1883—1906Rækker Mølle1908—1917Vorgod1930

The road can be followed in the children’s parishes of birth — and in the censuses, which show Ane Johanne in Husby in 1890 and the family in Sædding in 1911, 1916, 1921 and 1925, and in Vorgod in 1930.

1883—1906
Husby
Dune, marsh and surf. Ane Johanne is born and marries.
1908—1917
Rækker Mølle
Forty kilometres to the south-east, Sædding parish. Mill and dairy instead of a landing beach. Bricks instead of nets.
1930
Vorgod
Another stretch inland, into the parishes of the heath reclamation. The census of 1930 finds the family here — and here both husband and wife died.

The direction is clear: away from the sea, into the Denmark that was building. And now to the place where the sources come closest to Ane Johanne.

Sædding parish, 2 April 1909
Niels Silkjær Madsen

The children took the surname Madsen — that was the rule. But someone chose to set the mother’s family name in the middle of the boy’s name, for a child born forty kilometres from the farm, in a parish where the name meant nothing to anyone else.

That choice of name is the closest we come to an imprint from her side of the family: someone wrote her family’s place into her son’s name — perhaps she herself, perhaps the parents together. She had left Økjær, and the place travelled with her.

And then she had fourteen children.

The eldest, Anne, came in 1907, the year after the wedding. The youngest, Elisabeth, in 1925. Eighteen years, fourteen births, three parishes — eleven of the children came into the world between 1907 and 1918.

The family scattered, as large families did: Niels Silkjær to Ikast, Dagmar and Laura stayed in the Vorgod district, Christian ended up in Videbæk — and Knud, the second eldest, died in 1973 in Calgary in Canada. The son of the mason from Rækker Mølle lies buried on the far side of the Atlantic.

Mads Erik died on 2 August 1951. Ane Johanne outlived him by five years and died on 19 November 1956. The Ikast district, with which the family is later associated, did not come through her but through her son Niels Silkjær Madsen: he married in Isenvad Church in 1933 and died in Ikast in 1972.

Read more about the traces in the parish registers

The son Niels Silkjær Madsen was born on 2 April 1909 in Sædding parish, Bølling Hundred — according to the parish register index. The daughter Laura is confirmed in the original baptismal entry in the Sædding parish register: born on 25 March 1917 at Rækker Mølle as the daughter of Mads Erik Madsen and Ane Johanne. The traces towards the Ikast district still rest on indexes, not on original entries.

Sources: 1uz.dk, Mads Erik Madsen / Ane Johanne Jensen Silkjær [S5] · Hugo Dynesen, index to the Sædding parish register [S6] · Sædding parish register, Laura’s baptism 1917 [S159] · Den Christen Møller Schmidtske Stamtavle [S7].

16
Chapter 16 · 1917—1997

Laura

Among the fourteen children of the master mason Mads Erik and Ane Johanne was a daughter, Laura — the tenth in the row. She was born on 25 March 1917 at Rækker Mølle in Sædding parish; the baptismal entry names her parents as Mads Erik Madsen and Ane Johanne. [S159]

She was a domestic help. On 29 December 1938 she was married in Vorgod Church to Laurids Mikkelsen, born on 11 September 1911 at Fjelstervang in the same parish, owner of the farm Nygaard. She had followed her parents inland and found her husband where they had come to rest.

They had five children: Knud, born on 19 November 1943 in Sædding, Birte in 1945, Ernst in 1947, Edith in 1949 and Leif in 1956. Notice who was given the name. Only the eldest and the youngest have Silkjær in their own names — Knud Silkjær Mikkelsen and Leif Silkjær Mikkelsen. The three in the middle were not given it. The name did not pass on evenly; it was set on two of five, thirteen years apart.

Knud Silkjær Mikkelsen · 1943—2019 Birte Mikkelsen · b. 1945 Ernst Mikkelsen · b. 1947 Edith Mikkelsen · b. 1949 Leif Silkjær Mikkelsen · b. 1956 The family file records all five
Laura did not herself carry Silkjær in her official name; it was her mother’s, not hers. Nothing required her to carry it on. Two of her five children had it written into their own all the same.

Laurids died on 22 September 1996. Laura followed the year after, on 30 September 1997, in Vorgod — ninety-one years after her mother left the coast, and forty kilometres from the marsh the name came from. They lie together in the churchyard at Fjelstervang under four lines and three words.

17
Chapter 17 · 1945

Anne Kirstine
and the war in the North Sea

The story now leaves the heath and returns to the harbour in Esbjerg — to the sons of fishing skipper Thomas Nielsen Silkjær from Havnegade 179, whom we left as boys in chapter 11. This chapter is about the family’s cutter.

The first ANNE KIRSTINE had been built in Assens in 1897 of oak and pine, measured 34 gross register tons and came to Esbjerg in 1917. By 1945 she was an ageing workboat in a watched harbour: the Atlantic Wall ran like a line of concrete through the dunes, and the fishermen sailed with German eyes on them. The war cost 127 Danish fishermen their lives in the North Sea and the Skagerrak.

It was in this situation that the arms runs across the North Sea were to be started up again. The head of all airdrops and arms receptions in Jutland was known by the cover name Toldstrup; behind it stood the customs assistant Anton Jensen. He handed the work over to Lonsdale — cover name “Oscar Dahl” — and to the parish priest of Sdr. Onsild near Randers, Hans Kvist-Jensen, who went underground as “Jørgen Jensen” and many years later became Bishop of Roskilde. In December 1944 their group in Randers was broken up, and the two were sent to Esbjerg to re-establish the sea operations.

The priest had one thing no other envoy had: he was married to the daughter of Esbjerg’s former chairman of the fishermen’s association. And it was through his mother-in-law, Eline Christiansen, that he made contact with a fishing skipper who had the cutter ANNE KIRSTINE at his disposal. The skipper’s name was Niels Silkjær. He said yes — and found the next man himself: skipper Jens Frich of the cutter VEGA.

So the contact with the Esbjerg fishermen was not made through an organisation but through a woman who knew whom one could trust in the harbour. Once again in this story, the decisive connection runs through a kitchen and not an office.
The kinship

Niels and Ejlert were the sons of Thomas Nielsen Silkjær. Niels Silkær was born on 26 September 1910 at Aargab and baptised in Haurvig Church on 16 October; Ejlerth Marius Silkær was born on 29 January 1915 at Hjertinggade 13 in Esbjerg and baptised in Zion’s Church on 7 March.

With that the line is complete: the man who ran arms through Esbjerg harbour in March 1945 was the grandson of the smallholder from Økjær — and the great-grandson of the fisherman who drowned in 1878. Three generations, the same coast, the same sea.

The tax books say where the two men stood when it happened. Niels had a home of his own: Gormsgade 122, where the census of November 1940 lists four Silkjærs — Niels, Ane Kirstine, Jørgen Georg and Elisabeth. A father of two. His wife was Ane Kirstine, née Hansen, born on 10 September 1910 — sixteen days before him. They were married in Vor Frelsers Church on 21 December 1930, both twenty years old, six weeks after the census had found him living with his parents on Gl. Færgevej. She was an Esbjerg girl: born in Vor Frelsers parish, daughter of the brickworks labourer Jørgen Georg Hansen and his wife Ane Margrethe Kristensen Holm of Bag Teglværket 8, and herself a domestic help when they married. In August 1931 she gave birth to the son Jørgen Georg at Knudsgade 18 — the address the tax book gives for Niels the following year. He was given his maternal grandfather’s name, and at the baptism in Vor Frelsers Church the child’s paternal grandparents, fishing skipper Thomas Silkjær and Mrs Kristiane, stood as godparents. [S154] The daughter Elisabeth (1940—1997) arrived on 6 July 1940 at the Municipal Hospital; at her presentation in Zion’s Church in September both sets of grandparents stood as witnesses — Thomas and Kristiane from Havnegade 179 and the labourer Georg Hansen and his wife. She married a Jensen and died in Esbjerg in November 1997. [S155, S156] Ane Kirstine died in 1969; Niels was laid beside her seventeen years later. Ejlert still lived at Havnegade 179, but no longer as a son at home: he had married Dagmar Lodberg on 24 September 1939, and the census lists the couple as a household of their own in the house, with a single lodger. In the books he appeared as a share fisherman — a man on shares, not a skipper. He only became one in 1954, nine years later. So it was a fisherman on other men’s boats who travelled with the priest to Hvide Sande and Thyborøn.The tax books give only an initial, but the sequence is closed at both ends. The census of 1930 has him at home with his parents at Gl. Færgevej 7; he was married on 21 December the same year; his son’s baptismal entry gives the birthplace Knudsgade 18 in August 1931, where the tax book lists N. Silkjær in 1932; and the census of 1940 gives Gormsgade 122, where the tax book has him from 1939 to 1943. The census columns for position in the household are not reproduced in the page consulted, so that the other two are children is inferred from the order, not read. That Ane Kirstine is the wife, on the other hand, is supported by the burial register: Ane Kirstine Silkjær, née Hansen, b. 10.9.1910, died 30 March 1969 with last residence in Guldager, buried on 3 April in Fourfeldt Cemetery, section D 2, row 9, no. 1 — the same cemetery where Ejlert and Niels came to lie in 1985 and 1986. E. M. Silkjær is Ejlerth Marius, whose initials and address follow Havnegade 179 without a break from 1932 — first in his father’s household, and from the marriage in 1939 as his own. The wedding date of 24 September 1939 stands in the census form. [S94, S95, S102, S109] All caveats →

  1. 6 JANUARY 1945
    The two boats were ready to sail. The meeting point had been agreed: a position on Outer Silver Pit, a fishing bank in the middle of the North Sea. Then the weather set in — truly foul winter weather with almost constant gales — and the boats stayed at home for ten weeks.
  2. 8 MARCH · THE WAIT PUT TO USE
    Kvist travelled with Ejlert Silkjær to Hvide Sande and got an immediate yes from the fishing skipper Jens Aae. But once Kvist had looked at the conditions, he gave up on the harbour: it could be watched from a German observation bunker, and the checks were unusually thorough. The two went on to Thyborøn, where the former Esbjerg fisherman Harald Iversen said yes and quickly found more skippers. Then they travelled back to Esbjerg.
  3. 16 MARCH 1945
    The weather was finally good enough. ANNE KIRSTINE and VEGA sailed.
    They reached the meeting point without trouble, and for the last stretch they were escorted by English aircraft that came in low over the cutters and waggled their wings.
  4. THE CARGO
    The goods were packed in watertight tin containers, placed in canvas bags. On VEGA the bags went down into the hold. ANNE KIRSTINE had a well — the water-filled compartment where the catch was normally kept alive — so her share had to be lowered into it. That went well enough, except for some containers of detonators: they would not sink and ended up hidden in a cupboard in the cabin. Besides the goods, the cutters were given paraffin, coffee, tea, whisky and cigars.
  5. EASTER SATURDAY · 31 MARCH
    Both cutters got safely through the harbour checks in Esbjerg and landed their fish.
  6. THE NIGHT AFTER
    The goods for the resistance were brought ashore a hundred metres from the German guards at the Halle restaurant. Nine mission fishermen carried the heavy load, while Kvist and the leader of the harbour company, Holger Nielsen, covered the operation with sub-machine guns. It went well. Everyone came home.
Esbjerg — Outer Silver Pit · 1945

The story should be made neither larger nor smaller than it is. Niels Silkjær said yes to running arms through a watched harbour in the last months of the war, brought Jens Frich in on VEGA, and his brother Ejlert helped the priest find more skippers — with the death penalty as the obvious consequence had they been discovered.

Preparations began at once for the next run, and in all six Esbjerg cutters had said yes. It never set out. So late in the war there was strong opposition to fishing for Germany, and the local resistance — which knew nothing of the arms transports — forbade the cutters to fish for anything but the home market. A few days later the Danish Freedom Council called on the Esbjerg cutters to sail to England. Esbjerg was thereby finished as a receiving port, and the work moved to Thyborøn. ANNE KIRSTINE’s run was the one that succeeded.

And then the proportions: eight cargoes in all reached Denmark by sea — an estimated 16 to 32 tons. Measured against what was dropped from the air, it is vanishingly little. The transports should therefore not be weighed by their military importance but by what they demanded: had a cargo been found, the fishermen would not even have had weapons to defend themselves. The skippers in Thyborøn were offered 10,000 kroner per cargo, and all three said no — they wanted only the normal price for the fish. Recognition from official Denmark never came.The course of events, the names and the figures in this chapter follow Knud Jakobsen, “Nordsøfiskernes krig” (The North Sea fishermen’s war), parts 2—3, in Under Dannebrog nos. 4 and 5/2023 — a recent account based on Hans Kvist’s post-war report and interviews with participating fishermen. The date of Easter Saturday is 31 March 1945. [S10] All caveats →

Esbjerg’s own fleet register mentions it drily in the entry for E.94, between the tonnage and the list of owners: “Sailed arms to Esbjerg during the Second World War from English cutters.” A handful of words in a vessel register — the closest thing to official recognition the fishermen received.

From a marsh in Husby to the North Sea at war. The name had travelled far.

18
Chapter 18 · 1897—1990

The cutter

The cutter was the family’s livelihood. She had a name, a number and a life story that runs through three generations.

The vessel
E.94 ANNE KIRSTINE
Built1897 in Assens, of oak and pine Tonnage33.61 gross register tons RegistrationE.94, Esbjerg · call sign NQLk / OZCF Before EsbjergFN.64 “Anne Kirstine” of Frederikshavn, bought here in 1917 OwnersFiskeriselskabet Nordsøen A/S 1917—1923 · T. N. Silkjær 1923—1948

Niels and Ejlert’s father, Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, trained at the Fishing Skippers’ School in Esbjerg in 1916—17. From 1923 he was master and owner, and with ANNE KIRSTINE he fished out of Esbjerg into the North Sea through the inter-war years.

Like many Danish west-coast fishermen, he also sailed his fish to England. From early spring until the autumn gales set in, the cutters fished the North Sea and landed their catch in the English ports — it gave them a market and foreign currency.

It was that route which in March 1945 made an arms run credible. And it was that route which three years later put her aground.

The grounding at Hartlepool · according to the maritime inquiry
14 MARCH 1948 · ABOUT 20.45
Heading into Hartlepool with fish. A steady south-easterly breeze, a north-going current. She lay about 200 metres south of the end of the old harbour pier and was signalling for a pilot when she was set towards the shore.
MINUTES LATER
Engine full ahead, helm to port — and then she grounded by the stern about 225 metres from the end of the pier and stuck fast.
15 MARCH · ABOUT 4.45
Refloated with outside help. The false keel was lost, and the rudder broke.

The maritime inquiry in Esbjerg on 3 April 1948 established that the grounding was caused by the set of the current. So the cutter came free and was not lost in the grounding itself. The following year, 1949, a new ANNE KIRSTINE was built at Hobro Shipyard — 31.58 gross register tons, call sign OUKN — and took over both the name and the harbour number E.94.

On 20 March 1950 Thomas Nielsen Silkjær died at Havnegade 179; he was buried four days later in the churchyard in Gormsgade, section Ø, row 11, no. 9. The cemetery’s day journal notes one more thing beside the grave: D.D. — double depth. Room had been left for one more. Thirteen years later, on 4 August 1963, Kristiane was laid in the same grave, ninety years old. [S108] In the year of his death the cutter passed by inheritance to his son Niels Silkjær, who was listed as owner until 1976. The son took over the new ANNE KIRSTINE of 1949 — the successor to the vessel in which he had run arms five years earlier — not through a sale between strangers, but because his father had died.

Ejlert stayed in fishing, but by the long road. The tax books list him as a share fisherman — a man on shares on other men’s boats — in every year consulted from 1932 to 1951, in 1939 simply as fisherman, living in his father’s house at Havnegade 179. Only in 1954, thirty-nine years old and twenty-two years into the work, does fishing skipper stand beside his name.

And he was not alone in waiting. The eldest brother, Christian Lauritsen, passed his skipper’s examination as early as 1924 and commanded E.426 BERGIT — yet the books call him fisherman and share fisherman for twenty-nine years, from Gl. Færgevej in 1925 to Havnegade 179 in 1951. In 1954 his title too changes to fishing skipper, the same year as his younger brother’s — and at the same time he moves out of his father’s house for the first time, fifty years old, to Spangsbergsgade 51.

The father died in 1950, and Niels inherited the cutter. Four years later both remaining brothers stand as skippers in the tax book for the first time, and the house on Havnegade has only one of them left. What happened between 1951 and 1954 the books do not say — only that it happened to both of them at once.Two brothers receiving the same new title in the same year could also be a reclassification by the tax authorities rather than two changes of career. Against that, the titles otherwise change at scattered times: the father became a fishing skipper in the book in 1932, the brother-in-law Christen Torbensen in 1943. The book records how a man was assessed, not what he was qualified to do. Christian Lauritsen also appears alternately as C. L. (1928, 1930, 1932) and as K. L. after his baptismal name Kristen Lauridsen (1925 and 1935—1956); the two forms never occur in the same year, and the address is the same — so they are read as one man. [S8, S94] All caveats →

By then both brothers had long had families of their own in the town. Niels and Ane Kirstine had two children, Jørgen Georg in 1931 and Elisabeth. Ejlert married Dagmar, née Lodberg, on 24 September 1939 — the census the following year lists the couple as a household of their own in his father’s house at Havnegade 179 — and they had three children: Frans, Torben and Anne-Mette. Dagmar died as early as 1966, and Ejlert was a widower for his last nineteen years. [S40, S95]

Later E.714 LACERTA was built for Ejlert, and he was still sailing her out of Esbjerg in 1984. [S94] Then the brothers went within less than a year. Ejlert died on 28 May 1985, the eldest, Christian Lauritsen, just over nine weeks later on 31 July, and Niels on 16 April 1986 — three brothers within eleven months. They were not laid in the same place. Christian Lauritsen went to Gormsgade Cemetery, where his parents lay; Ejlert and Niels to Fovrfeld, but apart — Ejlert in section B, Niels in D 2, beside his wife Ane Kirstine, who had gone before him in 1969.The family remembered Niels’ and Ejlert’s deaths as falling in the same year, six weeks apart. Esbjerg’s burial register shows something else: Ejlert died on 28 May 1985 and was buried on 1 June, Niels died on 16 April 1986 and was buried on 19 April. The short interval the family remembered does, on the other hand, fit Ejlert and Christian Lauritsen, who died just over nine weeks apart in the summer of 1985. The graves lie in separate sections — Ejlert section B, row 2, no. 23; Niels section D 2, row 9, no. 2, with his wife in no. 1 in the same row. The neighbouring grave is also what secures her identification. Christian Lauritsen’s death and burial are in the family file, not in the register consulted. [S40, S108] All caveats →

A ship that was inherited, and a name that went with it.

LINDA VIGL.651
JOHNNY MARIANNEL.651
CHARLOTTE FRANKL.651

The rest of her life · Esbjerg’s fleet register

In 1976 the family let go of the cutter — and then she lost her name. She was sold to Lemvig, given the harbour number L.651 and was afterwards called three other things: Linda Vig (1976—80, part-owners c/o P. E. Enemark), Johnny Marianne (1980—81, E. Høj) and Charlotte Frank (from 1981, part-owners c/o Theodor S. M. Madsen, Struer).

In the end she was no longer a fishing vessel. From 1983 Finn Hansen sailed her from Handbjerg and Gudum near Lemvig as M.s. “Charlotte Frank” of Lemvig — sailing ship with auxiliary engine, cargo ship.

“Deleted on 29 May 1990 by DAS as broken up.”

The Hobro hull lasted forty-one years. Niels owned it for twenty-six of them. When the family let go, the name went with it — the exact reverse of what happens everywhere else in this chronicle. The people took the name with them when they moved. The ship lost it when it changed hands.

“Two cutters coming into harbour at Esbjerg. On the left E.94 ANNE KIRSTINE — built 1897 of oak and pine, 34 tons. The family’s livelihood from 1923, and the vessel that in March 1945 carried arms in through the harbour checks with the cargo lowered into the well.”
Photo: William Revald · Esbjerg City Archives B473 · arkiv.dk
“Esbjerg fishing harbour seen from the air in 1956 — the cutters lie side by side along the jetties, hundreds of them. From here ANNE KIRSTINE sailed to the North Sea and to England with fish; here she lay, Niels Silkjær having taken her over six years before the picture was taken.”
Sylvest Jensen Luftfoto, 1956 · Det Kgl. Bibliotek, B00344_002 · kb.dk
19
Chapter 19 · 1886—1969

When the name
went east

Once more the story goes back to the family of children from Økjær. Where Ane Johanne went to Rækker Mølle and Thomas to Esbjerg, the younger brother Jens Klaus went furthest — right across to the other side of Jutland.

ØkjærØster Alling

He was born into the fisherman’s home at Økjær on 6 May 1886, son of Niels Thomsen Silkjær and Ane Jensen. But Jens Klaus Nielsen Silkjær left the west coast.The year of birth is 1886: both censuses (1925 and 1930) give 06.05.1886, and the year 1880 given in one archive is an error. The censuses, on the other hand, give the birthplace as “Ringkøbing”, where the family’s records say Husby — both in Ringkøbing County, so the discrepancy is probably because the county has been used as the birthplace. [S34] All caveats →

How far east he had come is written on a postcard. On 18 April 1911 he wrote home from Øster Alling Præstegaard — the rectory farm at Øster Alling on Djursland — to “Frk. Kirstine Silkjær, Husby Præstegaard”: two of the fisherman’s children were that spring at a rectory each — she at home in the parish, he on the other side of Jutland.The card is dated “d 18/4 11” and postmarked in Auning; the eight in the day can also be read as a 3. By age, the recipient “Frk. Kirstine Silkjær” is probably Ane Kirstine, b. 3.9.1892 — eighteen that spring; the younger sister Jensine Kristine, b. 17.12.1896, was only fourteen. The card itself does not decide it. Nor does it say what Jens Klaus did at Øster Alling Præstegaard: that he belonged to the farm’s people is inferred from the place of sending and the weekend trip, not from a source about his employment. A few words in the transcription are read from the context, among them “da saa hele”. [S130] All caveats → The front of the card shows the farm’s household, and the back reads:

Dear Sister! Here you see the whole tenant family and the servants at Øster Alling Præstegaard, and they look well, don’t they. I want to tell you that my sweetheart and I are coming home for a visit on Saturday evening and leaving again on Monday morning; we hope to see you. Kind regards from your brother Jens
Postcard, Øster Alling Præstegaard, 18 April 1911 [S130]
ØkjærØster AllingAuningVejlby

The sweetheart was in all likelihood Bodil Marie Bossow, born on 8 April 1887 in Auning, the parish next to Øster Alling. Half a year after the card, on 28 October 1911, they were married in Fausing. So the road east did not run through the wedding; it ran through the rectory farm — and the girl from Auning made Djursland his part of the country for the rest of his life.

The family settled on Djursland. Judging by the children’s birthplaces, they lived first in Øster Alling, where the eldest came into the world, then in Nimtofte by 1921 at the latest, and by 1925 at Vejlbyvej 2 in Vejlby near Allingåbro.

Here Jens Klaus was verger and gravedigger at Vejlby Church — a Romanesque church from the twelfth century, raised on the highest point of the village, with a tower and porch of red monastery brick from around 1500 and a granite portal carved by the stonemason Horder, who worked on Djursland in the thirteenth century. In 1922—23 the church was heavily rebuilt and extended with a new nave chancel and apse in red brick.

The gravedigger’s work followed the church year and the weather: digging the graves and filling them in, ringing the bells, heating the church and keeping the churchyard.

The man who had grown up on a coast where the drowned were now and then cast up on another man’s stretch of beach now laid the dead in the earth inland, far from the sea.

With Jens Klaus, Silkjær became a settled surname in a quite different part of Jutland — and not only there: one of the sons carried it to Esbjerg, where his uncle’s branch already had it standing on the harbour. The sons carried it on; one of them, Henry Silkjær, is later described precisely as the “son of gravedigger and verger Jens Silkjær in Allingåbro”. Jens Klaus stayed in the parish to the last: he died on 25 July 1959 in Allingåbro, seventy-three years old. Bodil Marie outlived him by almost ten years and died on 13 July 1969. [S40]

Read more: the name in the censuses’ spellings

The wife is entered in the census of 1925 as “Bodil Alycia Silkjær” and in 1930 as “Bodil Marie Silkær” — both with the birth date 8 April 1887 in Auning. It is the same woman; “Alycia” is a variant or mistaken spelling. The correct form, cf. the marriage in Fausing in 1911, is Bodil Marie Bossow.

The children too change spelling between Silkjær and Silkær from form to form — sometimes within the same household. That is not carelessness but the naming culture of the time: the sound was fixed, the letters were not.

Whether Vejlbyvej 2 was the official gravedigger’s house is not documented in the sources consulted. Sources: censuses, Vejlby parish 1925 and 1930 [S34] · Henry Silkjær, Rougsø Local History Society [S35] · Trap Danmark and lex.dk on Vejlby Church [S36].

Back to the west · 1940—1969

The soft-drinks manufacturer

One of the sons went the opposite way. Tage Ewald Silkjær, born at Oustrup on 8 October 1917, appears in the census of November 1940 at Finsensgade 9 in Esbjerg — lodging with a wholesaler in bicycles and radio, and himself listed as chief clerk in the same trade, twenty-three years old. The tax books follow him from there: Finsensgade 9 in 1941, Strandbygade 70 from 1943 and every year consulted until the books end in 1956.The tax books give only the initials T. E. The census of 1940 gives the full name, the birth date 8 October 1917 and the birthplace Ø. Alling — Oustrup lies in Øster Alling parish — and so ties the chief clerk in the tax books to the gravedigger’s son. The company history of Tropil records him as born in October 1917 in the Randers area and trained as a salesman with, among others, Esbjerg Cykellager — the same three features the census gives him in 1940. [S94, S97, S98] All caveats →

He stayed in the town, and he became his own master. After years as a salesman — with Esbjerg Cykellager and with Nellemann in Aarhus — on 1 October 1961 he bought the mineral-water factory Tropil from its founder, Villy Bratborg. Production had by then fallen to around 300,000 bottles a year. Silkjær began by having the soft drinks analysed in a laboratory and made a new recipe; some of the old customers did not care for it, but sales rose. On 1 October 1964 he moved the factory to a new building at Randersvej 8, and in the years 1965—67 he was up to around a million bottles a year with ten to twelve employees.

Then the times turned. The customers were still mostly private households, but women had gone out to work, and a factory that sold to homes could only reach them in the evenings and on Saturday afternoons. Carrying on would have demanded fully automatic machines and an entirely different operation. Together with serious illness in the family, it took the heart out of him. On 24 February 1969 he closed Tropil. His wife, Karen Marie, née Schmidt, born on 9 September 1917 — a month before him — died four years later, on 12 January 1973, and was buried in Fourfeldt Cemetery.The company history mentions “a serious case of illness in Silkjær’s family” as contributing to the factory’s closure in February 1969, but does not say who was ill. That it was his wife, who died in January 1973, is a natural thought, but it is not stated in any source — and the four years between make it an assumption and nothing more. [S98, S108] All caveats → The machines went to Ceres in Aarhus, the stock to Saltum Brewery, the building to a furnishing company — and Tage Ewald Silkjær went back to his old trade as a commission salesman. He died on 2 January 1995, seventy-seven years old. [S40, S98]

What remains of the factory is the names. Tropil’s labels were collected by bottle collectors and still exist, and they sketch a whole little language: Citronvand and Appelsinvand (lemon and orange water), Blodappelsin (blood orange), Banan Brus (banana fizz), Grape-Squash and Lemon-Squash, Orangeade and Franceade, Sportsvand with pineapple, Ginger-Water, Apollinaris, an alcohol-free Cocktail Drik and Æblemost (apple juice). Two of them carry a pair of pixies each drinking from a cup, and all the oldest have the same telephone number printed under the name: 2445.Which soft drink Tage Ewald Silkjær himself came up with, the sources do not say. Both accounts mention that he had the old recipes analysed in a laboratory and then introduced a new drink, but neither gives it a name, and the labels are not dated. The list above therefore cannot be divided into Bratborg’s and Silkjær’s. [S98, S100] All caveats →

The soft drinks stand out in this story, and they are welcome to. Two generations earlier the livelihood was whatever the sea would give; now a factory with ten to twelve employees was sending out around a million bottles a year. Banan Brus and Grape-Squash are not a curiosity in the chronicle — they are the new age, poured into bottles.

There is a story of a name hidden in it, and it is not his. Bratborg had gained his experience with an ice company in the American town of Liport and called his factory Tropil — the town’s name spelt backwards. For eight years a gravedigger’s son from Djursland was the owner of a name turned back to front — in the town where his grandfather had died.

20
Chapter 20 · 1880—today

The branches

Ten children grew up in and around Økjær. The story has followed three of them closely — Thomas in Esbjerg, Ane Johanne at Rækker Mølle, Jens Klaus on Djursland. The others did what everyone else did: grew up, married, moved away — and took the name with them. They need not be remembered one by one; what matters is to see how the name travelled.

That is why Silkjær is not one family in Husby but a net of families. Within a single generation the family was settled in Gudum, on Djursland, in the harbour streets of Esbjerg, in Fjand and in Vallensbæk west of Copenhagen. Some of the branches have lived far from one another for around a hundred years. They are equally related to the marsh.

Gudum
The millwright’s branch

Esper Nielsen Silkjær (1888—1960) became a farmer and millwright. On 17 March 1913 — his twenty-fifth birthday — he married Jensine Mortensen in Gudum, and the couple set up home on the farm where she was born, the small holding of Nørre Tangshus — twenty-five kilometres from the sea, but still in Ringkøbing County.

There Jensine bore eight children over nineteen years. The eldest, Knud Vognsgaard (1913—1959), became a smelter at the steelworks in Frederiksværk and was killed in the great explosion there — his story stands by itself below. Niels (1914—1999) became a farmer in Gudum and had eight children. Jens (1916—2000) became a farmer and millstone dresser — the craftsman who cuts the millstones sharp again — and later chairman of the parish council; he married Gertrud Marie, known as Misse, in Andst in 1952, had nine children and died in Skive hospital in 2000. Anne Kristiane (1917—2009) had twelve children on a farm in Hjerm and died in Holstebro. Krista (1920—2006) ended her days in a care home on Amager, Alma (1923—2013) on Ærø, Helga (1925—2004) in Arnborg near Herning. And the youngest, Otto (b. 1932), emigrated as a young man — in his generation the marsh had reached all the way to Australia.

In their old age Esper and Jensine left the farm and moved to a house at Fredensgade 11 in Struer. Esper died there a year and a half after his eldest son; his widow Jensine lived to ninety-three and died in Struer in 1982. The millwright’s son sharpened millstones. The trade went on, while the sea became something one heard about.

The information on Esper and Jensine’s children follows a record of descendants kept by the family and has only partly been checked against original sources. [S40, S148]

Esbjerg · Havnegade
Neighbours in the harbour town

Ane Kirstine (1892—1977) was married on New Year’s Day 1920 in Nysogn Church to the fisherman Christen Tarbensen. She was then a servant girl in Haurvig, he a fisherman in the same place, and the witnesses were the two fathers. The groom’s father was called Christen Fjord Tarbensen, a farmer in Haurvig — and that name went two ways: the son called his cutter “Chr. Fjord”, E.477, and his first child Christian Fjord. Their four children were born in Esbjerg, and all had their mother’s farm name written into their own: Christen Fjord Silkjær Torbensen (1921—1985), Kamma (1926—1997), Anna Kirstine (1929—2018) and Gerda (1938—1986).

Anna Kirstine came into the world on 15 April 1929 at Havnegade 132. Forty-seven numbers further up the same street her uncle Thomas, the fishing skipper, lived at number 179. Two households from Økjær, the same street in the new town.

She was married in Zion’s Church on 25 November 1950 to Jens Sand Christensen from Sønder Lyngvig on Holmsland Klit — one more tie back to the dunes — and died in the care home at Hjerting at eighty-nine, the last of the Esbjerg-born brothers and sisters. Their daughter Kirsten Sand Christensen (1951—2025) was born and died in Esbjerg.

Sjælborg · Esbjerg · Vallensbæk
The Bøndergaard branch

Karen Marie (1890—1933) became a smallholder’s wife in Sjælborg with Kristian Kornelius Bøndergaard and had thirteen children in fourteen years: Kristen Magnus (1913), Niels Silkjær (1915), Anna (1916), Theodor Salomon (1917), Henry (1918—2016), Ida Marentha (1919), Kaj (1920), Anker (1921—2005), Ninna Dagny (1922), Edith (1923—1962), Josva (1925—2015), Inga (1926) and Bent Karl (1927). Six years after the youngest she was dead, forty-three years old.

One of the thirteen had the farm name written into his own. Niels Silkjær Bøndergaard (1915—1996) became a fisherman and later master of a tanker boat in Esbjerg — the coastal trade in a new form, with engine and oil instead of sail and herring; his wife Mary Margrethe came from Holbæk County, was an office assistant and lived until 2013. His sister Anna Bøndergaard (1916—1979) ended her days in Vallensbæk near Copenhagen.

With her the family reached Zealand.

Fjand · Damhus · Husby
Those who stayed

Jensine Kristine (1896—1964) married Martin Jeppesen Nørfjand from the neighbouring parish of Sønder Nissum, lost him in 1936 and stayed on in Fjand as a widow for twenty-eight years.

Ellen (1902—1980) — probably the girl in the school photograph of 1915 — married Peder Christian Burkarl and died in Esbjerg. They had nine children; seven are named in the family tree available: Niels Kristian, Evald, Knud Peder, Karoline Kjærstine, Anne, Anna and Oda. All seven carried Silkjær on in their names as Silkjær Burkarl. [S160]

Sidsel Kathrine (1894—1938) also followed her brothers and sisters to Esbjerg. In the tax list of 1927 she was entered as head nurse at Gl. Færgevej 7, the same address as her brother Thomas — and the same list notes that on 1 December that year she moved from the town to Læborg, lodging with a haulier. At the census of November 1930 she is still living there, but no longer as a lodger: by then she has her own household. An unmarried woman with a profession and now a household of her own.

When she came back to Esbjerg the sources do not say. But at her death in 1938 she was living at Havnegade 152 — the same street as Thomas at number 179 and her brother-in-law Christen Torbensen at number 132 — and the death certificate then lists her as a former nurse. She never married, and she died at her home address and not in a hospital, on 18 May 1938, forty-three years old, of pulmonary tuberculosis. Eight days later she was buried in the churchyard in Gormsgade — twelve years before her brother Thomas was laid there. [S108, S142, S145, S146]

And Ane Marie (1880—1960), the eldest, never left Husby. She was born in the parish, married in the parish, sat as a widow on the farm for almost forty-four years and died in the parish. They had eight children: Margrethe Dorthea (1908), Ane Johanne (1909), Agnethe (1910—1998), Niels Silkjær Lauridsen (1911—1986), Kristine and Valdemar (both 1913), Maren (1915—1998) and Ole (1916). Only one of them was given the farm name: the son called Niels Silkjær Lauridsen.

Gudum · Skævinge · Frederiksværk
The smelter from Nørre Tangshus

The millwright’s eldest son went a third way — neither the farm nor the mills, but the new heavy industry of the post-war years. From 1953 Knud Vognsgaard (1913—1959) was a smelter at Det Danske Staalvalseværk in Frederiksværk — a large steelworks with almost a thousand employees and a hundred thousand tons of steel a year. He lived with his wife Ebba and their three children in a house with a garden in Skævinge and drove to the works every day. [S148, S150]

On the morning of Wednesday 27 May 1959 he drove there as on every other day. A few hours later he was dead — one of the five workers who lost their lives in the great explosion at the works that day; many more were marked for life. He was buried in Skævinge on 31 May. The children were nineteen, sixteen and eight. [S148, S149, S150]

We could not grasp that it could be true; we fell so strangely silent. Knud was here no more; he went briskly to his work in the morning, and a few hours later the thread of his life was cut. … We saw him for the last time at Easter, when he was at home in Struer with the family. … What matters is to be ready; we know neither the day nor the hour, but what matters for us is to come to live in safety with God.
His sister Ane Pedersen, née Silkjær · Nr. Nissum Folk High School alumni magazine, June 1959 [S149]

Notice the language. “We know neither the day nor the hour” belongs to the same biblical register the chronicle met earlier in the revival on the dunes (chapter 10). Here the words came from another Inner Mission milieu: Nørre Nissum Folk High School — the Inner Mission’s first in the country, founded in 1887 a few kilometres from Gudum — where both Knud and his sister had been students. [S149]

“At home in Struer” meant with his parents at Fredensgade 11 — the Easter visit was the family’s last meeting with him.

The East Jutland branch is not repeated here, because it has already been told in chapter 19: Jens Klaus’ six children at Oustrup and Vejlby, where Silkjær for the first time became a quite ordinary surname.

10
children from Økjær

5

7

One pattern recurs across the branches: the name travelled on in two ways. In several of the sons’ branches Silkjær became a true surname; through several of the daughters it was written into the next generation as a name element before the family’s surname.

Part V

The inheritance

Chapters 21—22 · today
21
Chapter 21

The name as inheritance

You cannot tell the story of this family properly by following the surnames. Do that, and you get a string of changing names — Jensen, Thomsen, Madsen, Mikkelsen — and lose the thread at the first bend.

The thread is Silkjær, and it runs through both sexes and every branch.

Niels Thomsen
made the farm name the family’s — the children bore it in the census of 1890, and in 1905 he received a name certificate for it.
Thomas
carried it to Esbjerg harbour, where it became a skipper’s name for several generations.
Jens Klaus
took it to Vejlby as a settled surname.
Ane Marie
passed it on in the middle of her son’s name, Niels Silkjær Lauridsen.
Karen Marie
carried it into the Bøndergaard family and on to Esbjerg.
Ane Kirstine
gave it to all four children in the Tarbensen family in Esbjerg.
Ane Johanne
did the same in the Madsen family — and through her daughter Laura it continued in the Mikkelsen children.
Three cousins, six years, the same choice
