The family archive

Three sisters from Økjær. Three different husbands, three different surnames, three different parishes. And within six years all three call their son Niels Silkjær — named after their father, with the farm’s name fixed in the middle. No document tells us they had agreed on it. Yet the pattern is so clear that the choices of name were hardly a coincidence.

The men carried the name on because they kept it. Through the women it was carried on even though they lost it as a surname at their wedding: at the baptisms, Silkjær was written into the next generation.

Of Niels Thomsen’s daughters, five passed the name on to their children: Ane Marie, Ane Johanne, Karen Marie, Ane Kirstine and Ellen. In the next generation Laura and Elna Elisabeth, among others, did the same.

The family lived in a time of transition, when place name, byname, middle name and surname overlapped. The same person can appear in the sources as Thomsen, as Nielsen Silkjær or simply as Silkjær — and that is not muddle. It is the naming culture itself. Nor was the custom the family’s own: the fishing family in Esbjerg that Kristine Oline married into in 1916 likewise used a byname as a middle name before it became a fixed surname — Højberg carried in the middle of the name, unevenly shared among the sons, and in 1930 made a surname by royal licence, twenty-five years after Niels Thomsen’s name certificate. [S75, S76] What is remarkable is not that the name changed place. It is that it stayed there.

22
Chapter 22 · today

The name now

Today Silkjær is once again borne as a surname in the Mikkelsen line — by the children and grandchildren of Laura’s youngest son, Leif, born in 1956. And they are not alone: the name lives on in other branches of the family, where it never had time to disappear.

And the name did not travel only across the map. The story began among copyhold farmers and smallholders who launched open boats from the beach — and within a few generations the family included fishing skippers with cutters of their own, a chairman of a parish council, an accountant with his own office on the harbour and a chief clerk who ended up owning a mineral-water factory. None of them did anything out of the ordinary; they did what the century made possible. It was not one straight climb, and the branches went different ways. But laid end to end, the lives show how much the society around the name had changed.

And the name stayed where it came from. In a school photograph from Husby in 1960 a boy is noted as “Kurt Pedersen (Silkjær)”. His name was Pedersen, and his family had taken over the farm long after the Silkjærs had moved away; the parish still knew him by the name of the place. So Silkjær existed as a place name before there was a family of that name — and went on existing in the place after the family had taken it with them out into the country. [S114]

The circle is not quite closed; circles of this kind never close entirely. None of the living has lived on the farm, and most have never worked at sea. But the name stands where it stood with Niels Thomsen a good hundred and forty years ago: as the family’s.

It began as a description of a wet piece of land in Husby parish.
It became a man.
It became a family.
And it became what a family chose to remember — every single time they had the chance not to.

The descendants can still stand on the land the name came from. But they stand there as guests.

Silkjær today
The range with its fieldstone plinth. A mossy roof, low ceilings — built to lie still in the west wind.
The outbuilding with the conical roof and the three diamond-shaped windows — the white house in the 1948 photograph.
Seen from the meadow in early spring. The low, wet strip in front of the house is still there — it is what the name is about.
The brick bread oven with its iron doors. Every farm had one in the days when bread was baked at home.
Appendices

Sources, names and open questions

A—E
A
Appendix A · cadastral numbers, ownership and use of the name

Silkjær, Økjær and Øe

Chapter 1 tells the story of the place, and chapter 6 how the name became the family’s. Here is the documentation: the cadastral numbers, the deeds and the place designations that do not fit together without further thought. The property can be followed document by document in the land registers and the deed and mortgage books; the use of names around it demands more patience. First the two kinds of source that seem to pull in different directions:

The parish-register entries consistently say Økjær when they give a place of residence. Thomas Jensen was a smallholder and fisherman in Økjær. Niels Thomsen was a smallholder and fisherman in Økjær. The children were born in Økjær. The censuses say something else: they list the household in Øe — and from 1890 with a cadastral number, 13b, the number on which Silkjær lies today.

The otherwise obvious conclusion — that the family lived at Øhusevej 3 and merely borrowed the name from the neighbouring farm — does not hold up against the sources. Three censuses, 1890, 1901 and 1911, place the household directly on cad. no. 13b in Øe — a span of twenty-one years. The census of 1880 lists Niels Thomsen in Øe, but without a cadastral number; the land register shows, however, that he had already obtained title to 13b in January 1879. Further back the lists are silent on the cadastral number: 1855, 1860 and 1870 have Thomas Jensen in Øe, but the older censuses do not give cadastral numbers. [S60, S61]

So much for the censuses. The court books put dates on the chain from chapter 1: the Ministry of the Interior’s resolution of 24 May 1851 on the division of parcel no. 2 from cad. no. 13; a deed of 19 June 1851 from Jens Thomsen — written in the deed as “af Øe Bye” (of Øe village), with the parcel located “beliggende i Øe i Husbye Sogn” (lying in Øe in Husby parish) — to Niels Jensen; and the deed to Thomas Jensen, signed on 18 December 1854 and registered on 4 April 1855. The farm the land came from can still be located in the landscape: in all likelihood it lay at what is now Bækbyvej 121 — registered in 1960 under the building name Øby — where the cadastral numbers still begin with the 13 of the main holding, and where the Building and Dwelling Register dates the present building to 1857, six years after the division. [S61, S62, S63]

The deed to Thomas Jensen describes what was sold as “et fritliggende Huus, der er beliggende i Silkjær og er Parcellen No. 2, Matr. No. 13b” — a detached house lying in Silkjær, being parcel no. 2, cad. no. 13b. The price was 240 rigsbankdaler, and with the purchase came the duty to bear his share of the aftægt — the retirement maintenance — owed to the old couple from the farm. Thomas Miltersen and Maren Madsdatter lived until 1864 and 1865, so for his first ten years on the place Thomas Jensen was obliged to help provide for the people from whose land it had been divided. The deed further stipulates that the property “maa ingenlunde mere anvendes til Brændeviinsbrænding eller til Drift af Brænderi” — may in no way any longer be used for distilling spirits or running a distillery. A corresponding clause stands in the next, unrelated deed in the same book, so the wording cannot be used as evidence that a distillery was ever run at Silkjær. [S63]

The seller stayed on as a pensioner in the house he had just sold; the household at the census of 1 February 1855 is described in chapter 3. The family’s records put years to it: the seller was Niels Jensen Poulsgaard, born in Øe in 1802 and a widower since February 1851, when his wife Maren Jacobsdatter died; the stepdaughter Sidsel Cathrine Nielsdatter was her daughter from before the marriage, born in Møborg in 1820 — her father was Niels Christensen Roigård, hence the patronymic. The family were already people of the place: the census of 1850 lists the three together in a house in Øe — the rest of the entry is difficult to decipher. [S40, S60, S63]

He had bought the parcel four months after he became a widower — and when he sold it again, both he and his stepdaughter stayed on. Against that background the transaction can be read as a provision for his old age: the house exchanged for maintenance and a roof over his wife’s daughter’s head. The prices — 200 rigsbankdaler in 1851 and 240 three years later, when the deed expressly mentions a house — can be read the same way: the modest rise may be connected with the seller’s continued residence and maintenance forming part of the bargain. But the deeds give reasons neither for the sale nor for the difference in price — the reading is an interpretation. [S40, S63]

The dates fit into the family’s years: the deed was read on 4 April 1855, and on 9 July the same year Anne Marie Jansdatter gave birth to her son Niels. The deeds suggest the house may have been built during Niels Jensen’s short ownership. The deed of 1851 refers to the parcel with its appurtenances, crops and harvest, but mentions no buildings; the deed of 1854, by contrast, expressly mentions a detached house. That makes the years 1851—54 a likely possibility, but it does not prove the house was built precisely then. The parcel’s hartkorn land-tax assessment — 1 skæppe ¾ album, a little over an eighth of a tønde — shows a very small holding that could hardly feed a family on its own. Fishing was therefore not a sideline but a necessary part of the living; the census’s “han lever mest ved Fiskerie” — he lives mostly by fishing — says the same.

Twenty-one years later the name had moved from the land to the man. When Thomas bought parcel 44b in Vedersø in 1876 and added it to the holding, the deed wrote him as “Thomas Jensen Silkjær” — the earliest known record of the name borne by a person, two years before the newspapers used it in the notice of his death. [S64]

After the wreck, an endorsement of allotment in January 1879 gave the son Niels Thomsen title to the property — the father’s estate, settled two months after the disaster. So 1878 was not a change of place but a change of generation. And on 21 November 1905 Niels received a name certificate entitling him to bear the name Niels Silkjær: the name of the place had become the family’s legal surname — endorsed in the margin beside his baptismal entry of 1855. [S61, S64, S65]

The property grew and later passed on. Around 1917 land from cad. no. 78d was added, and on 24 May 1924 the whole was sold out of the family to J. F. Nielsen Lillevang. The land register carries the title on to Johannes Madsen in 1937 and Aksel Pedersen in 1952. [S61]

The parish registers’ “Økjær” covered more than one house. The registers place Thomas Jensen in Økjær, and in 1911 a woman from outside the family dies in the same place. The seller’s own family points the same way — and even shows the same double pattern: the census of 1850 lists Niels Jensen Poulsgaard, his wife and his stepdaughter in a house in Øe, but when his wife died in February 1851 — before the parcel in the marsh had been sold off — she was entered in Økjær, and the family file records both his death in 1862 and his stepdaughter’s in 1908 in the same place. The census says Øe, the parish register Økjær: the same pattern the family was later caught in. [S40, S60] The newspapers of 1878 put the byname “Ø.” after two other Husby men in the same boat — Thomas Jensen’s brother-in-law Anders Knudsen and his brother Esper Jensen (chapter 5) — while Iver Kristian Olesen, whom the family books place in Økjær, is there called Kløve. So Økjær held several households. For Esper Jensen the designations can be laid directly on top of one another: the newspapers call him Ø., the children in his household are born in Øe — and when he drowned in 1883, the parish register entered him as “2den Gang gift Huusmand, i Økjær og Fisker, født paa Husby Klit” — twice-married smallholder, in Økjær, and fisherman, born on Husby Klit. The same household, three designations. [S66] So Økjær was the name of an area and not of one building — which is why a family could sit on cad. no. 13b and still have “Økjær” written in the parish register.

The geography fits. Økjær did not lie in the middle of a village but in the open country between Øby and Øhuse, where cad. no. 15 lay side by side with Silkjær’s no. 13 along the road that later became Øhusevej. The designation covered a farm, its smallholdings and the land around the low marsh — and the censuses’ “Øe” likewise covers both. The present property at Øhusevej 3 carries on the name Økjær and the cadastral number, but it is not the house the parish registers wrote about when they placed the family in Økjær.

Two cadastral numbers through two hundred years

The trail runs backwards: from today’s 15f and 13b back through the historical cadastral maps to the two main holdings they were divided from.

The maps, the censuses and the deeds meet in 13b: the maps take the number back to main holding 13, the deeds show the division in 1851, and the censuses place the family on it from 1890 — the land register from the allotment in 1879. The maps also settle that the two places were separate cadastral units all the way through, so the Silkjær property and the property associated today with Økjær lay on different numbers. What the maps do not show is the use of names: a main holding is not one house, and the area name Økjær lay across both.The sequence in the table is based on the cadastral maps; ownership is recorded in the land register and the deeds: Thomas Jensen received the deed to 13b in 1854/55, and the title can be followed in the family until the sale in 1924.

The use of names followed two layers. Økjær was the name of the area in the parish’s own language — the marsh and the houses around it, cad. no. 13b among them — and so the residence the priest wrote down. Silkjær was the property and later the man. On the lifeboat crew’s note of 1915, Silkjær is precisely the fixed point from which the neighbour gets his address. The name also appears in several spellings — Silkjær and Silkær — sometimes in the same document. And one entry shows the two names in the same line: at Thomas Nielsen Silkjær’s confirmation in Husby in 1896, the parish register lists the confirmand “af Økjær” (of Økjær) and his father as “Husmd. og Fisker Niels Thomsen (kaldt Silkjær)” — smallholder and fisherman Niels Thomsen (called Silkjær). The priest himself recorded that the man was officially called Thomsen but went by the name of the place, a decade before the name certificate. So the two designations appeared as two layers: Økjær was the address; Silkjær was the father’s byname. There is therefore no contradiction between the parish registers’ Økjær and the ownership of 13b. Where the boundary of the Økjær area ran is not known — but that does not change where the family lived. [S73]

What we know
  • Where it lies: Øhusevej 1B, cad. no. 13b — separated from the farm in Øe in 1851
  • That Thomas Jensen received the deed to the house in 1854/55, that Niels obtained title by allotment in 1879, and that the property was sold out of the family in 1924
  • That the deed of 1854/55 is the oldest dated record of the name — as the name of the place
  • That Thomas Jensen appears as “Thomas Jensen Silkjær” in the deed of 1876, and that Niels received a name certificate in 1905
  • That the censuses of 1890, 1901 and 1911 place the household on cad. no. 13b
  • That Niels’ baptismal entry of 1855 in the original parish register gives his father as “Hmd. Øekjær Thomas Jensen”, while later family transcripts likewise use Økjær for the family’s home
  • That the confirmation entry of 1896 lists the son Thomas “af Økjær” and the father as “Niels Thomsen (kaldt Silkjær)” — the address and the byname in the same line
  • That the census of 1901 lists the nineteen-year-old Thomas as “Tomas Nielsen Silkær”, farmhand at Klit By in Vedersø parish — the name borne outside the parish, four years before the name certificate
  • That the Silkjær property and the property associated today with Økjær lay on different main holdings, 13 and 15
  • That Johannes Madsen bought the farm in 1936 — with title registered in 1937
  • What it looked like in 1948 and 2025
What we do not know
  • How old the place name Silkjær is — the deed of 1854/55 is the oldest record found
  • The year the house was built and who built it — the deeds make 1851—54 a likely possibility, but the silence of the 1851 deed about buildings does not prove the house was not yet standing
  • Where the boundary of the Økjær area ran
The parish book, c. 1950

The Husby parish book has a biography for the farm — spelt Silkær. Johannes Madsen, born in Husby on 15 June 1891, married to Marie Jensen from Madum, seven children born between 1916 and 1933. And then the sentence that dates the change of ownership:

“Madsen bought the farm in 1936 with 17 tønder of land, cultivated and uncultivated, and planted.”

So from 1936 the Madsen family were on the farm — the deed was registered the following year — twenty-four years before the school photograph in which the farm name still clung to the parish’s way of speaking. Whom Johannes Madsen bought it from, the parish book does not say — the land register does: J. F. Nielsen Lillevang, who had taken over the property from the family in 1924. That the family who bore the name had owned the place for almost seventy years the book does not mention by a single word. Two cows, three head of cattle, fattening pigs, two horses, and thirty years of milk carting: that was what life on the place looked like, long after the name had travelled on without it.

The sequence before 1936 is in the court books: the family itself from 1855 to 1924, then Lillevang. When Niels Thomsen took the farm’s name for himself, he was living on his father’s property.

A school photograph from Husby School in 1960 shows the farm name’s later life: a boy is noted as “Kurt Pedersen (Silkjær)”. His name was Pedersen; the parish identified him by the place, while another family owned the property. So the farm name was still in use as a place designation in 1960. The local history archive confirms that the custom was common in the district: people were called by the name of their farm, and with the Names Act of 1905 many officially took a surname after their farm — exactly the road Silkjær took in this family. [S114]

The parish registers’ Økjær

Vort Sogns Historie (Our Parish’s History) for Husby parish contains 48 residents’ biographies, and Silkjær appears in two of them: Johannes Madsen’s entry on the farm itself (bought 1936) and Ole Lauridsen’s entry, in which his wife Ane Marie Nielsen Silkjær has her parents and grandparents listed. The sequence before 1936 is not in the book. The work was paid for by subscribers and includes only the places that bought space — and only the owner living on the place around 1950.

The parish registers use Økjær consistently for the family’s home over forty years — as the name of an area, not as a cadastral address. The property that bears the name today lies on cad. no. 15, now 15f, and is linked to Thomas Jensen or Niels Thomsen neither in deeds nor in the land register; the family’s title concerns 13b. The picture of a consistent Økjær rests on six original entries. At Niels Thomsen’s baptism in 1855 the register gives his father as “Hmd. Øekjær Thomas Jensen”. In the register of deaths for 1863 the wife appears as “Huusm. i Øekjær Thomas Jensens Hustru” and the daughter Kjerstine as “Datter af ovennævnte huusmand i Øekjær Thomas Jensen … født i Øekjær”. In 1869 the daughter Karen Marie is “Datter af Hmd. i Økjær Thomas Jensen”. At Jesper Jensen’s death in 1883 he appears as a smallholder “i Økjær”, and at Thomas Nielsen Silkjær’s confirmation in 1896 the confirmand stands “af Økjær”, while his father is entered as “Niels Thomsen (kaldt Silkjær)”. So the designation stands in the originals throughout the period — in 1896 explicitly as an address beside the byname — and the register itself alternates between Øekjær and Økjær. [S38, S65, S66, S73]

Sources: ulfborgarkiv.dk (the PDFs HUSBY-SOGN and SOeNDER-NISSUM-SOGN) · arkiv.dk/vis/6507768 [S20]

The sources thus document the course of ownership and naming for cad. no. 13b: Økjær was the area, Silkjær was the place and later the man. The confirmation entry of 1896 shows the two layers in the same line — the confirmand “af Økjær”, the father “kaldt Silkjær”. Still unresolved are the year the house was built, the age of the place name and the precise historical boundary of the Økjær area.

The same farm from the air with seventy-seven years between — 1948 and 31 March 2025. The thatched range stands where it stood. The windbreaks have grown into woodland, the strip fields have become grass, and a white house has been added to the north.

B
Appendix B · Key to names

Eight Nielses
and three Ane Johannes

In a family where children were named after their grandparents in every generation — and where a new wife could give her daughter the name of the dead first wife — the same four or five names come round again and again. Here the namesakes are set side by side, so they can be told apart.

A rule of thumb: -sen and -datter tell you who the father was — Jansdatter is Jan’s daughter, Ibsdatter is Ib’s daughter. Klit and Silkjær, on the other hand, tell you where people lived. The first dies with the generation; the second can be inherited.

Niels
eight men, one name
1855—1928Niels Thomsen Silkjær — the one who made Silkjær a fixed, heritable family name. Smallholder, fisherman and boatman in Økjær.
1910—1986Niels Silkær — the fishing skipper’s son, born at Årgab. Ran arms across the North Sea in 1945 and owned E.94 until 1976.
1909—1972Niels Silkjær Madsen — Ane Johanne’s son. Bore his mother’s family name as a middle name; married in Isenvad in 1933 and died in Ikast in 1972.
1911—1986Niels Silkjær Lauridsen — Ane Marie’s son. Smallholder at Damhus, Sønder Nissum. The boy in the school photograph of 1919.
1914—Niels Silkjær — Jens Klaus’ son at Oustrup on Djursland, born on 28 February. Here Silkjær is purely a surname.
1914—1999Niels Silkjær — Esper’s son in Gudum, born the same year as his cousin on Djursland, on 17 November — exactly the same name, two sides of Jutland. A farmer in Gudum with eight children; died in Struer.
1915—1996Niels Silkjær Bøndergaard — Karen Marie’s son. Fisherman and tanker-boat master in Esbjerg.
Niels Kristian Silkjær Burkarl — Ellen Nielsen Silkjær’s son; one of seven named children in the Burkarl branch, where all seven carried Silkjær on as part of their names.
Ane Johanne
a wife, a daughter, a grandchild
1843—1880Ane Johanne Kristensen — Niels Thomsen’s first wife, twelve years older than he. Died in Økjær half a year after her only childbirth.
1883—1956Ane Johanne Nielsen Silkjær — his daughter by his second wife, named after the first. Married to the master mason Mads Erik Madsen; the pivot of the chronicle, chapter 14.
1909—Ane Johanne Lauridsen — the granddaughter, named after her aunt. Daughter of Ane Marie in Husby.
Anne Marie, Ane Marie / Ane Kirstine
and a cutter with almost the same name
1827—1863Anne Marie Jansdatter Tarpgaard — a farmer’s daughter from Vedersø, married to Thomas Jensen. Died in Økjær at 35.
b. 1837Anne Marie Jensdatter — Thomas Jensen’s sister from Husby Klit, married to Anders Knudsen Øe — in all likelihood the beach bailiff who drowned together with her brother in 1878, while her brother Esper survived. It is she who makes the boat one of two brothers and a brother-in-law (chapter 5).
1880—1960Ane Marie Nielsen Silkjær — her son’s daughter and namesake. The eldest of the brothers and sisters, married name Lauridsen, stayed in Husby all her life.
1892—1977Ane Kirstine Nielsen Silkjær — the sister, married on New Year’s Day 1920 in Nysogn Church to the fisherman Christen Tarbensen; their four children had Silkjær in their names. Not to be confused with Ane Kirstine Silkjær, née Hansen (1910—1969), the wife of her nephew Niels.
1897—1990ANNE KIRSTINE, E.94 — the cutter, in two hulls: the 1897 build and the new Hobro build of 1949, which took over name and number. A vessel, not a person; she is the one chapters 17 and 18 are about.
Thomas
three generations, the same first name
1754—1824Thomas Nielsen Langager — smallholder and enrolled seaman in Stadil. Maternal grandfather of the next.
1825—1878Thomas Jensen — smallholder and fisherman in Økjær. Lost at sea on 9 November 1878. The first of the family to be recorded with the name Silkjær — in the deed of 1876.
1882—1950Thomas Nielsen Silkjær — his grandson. Fishing skipper in Esbjerg, in the registers “T. N. Silkjær”.
Laura and Laurids
two names, one married couple
1917—1997Laura, née Madsen — Ane Johanne’s daughter, domestic help, number ten of fourteen.
1911—1996Laurids Mikkelsen — her husband, owner of Nygaard in Fjelstervang. The names look alike; they are not related.
Jens Claus and Jens Klaus
the grandfather and the grandson
c. 1830Jens Claus — Ane Jensen’s father, known from the parish book’s list of maternal grandparents.
1886—1959Jens Klaus Nielsen Silkjær — his daughter’s son, named after him. Gravedigger at Vejlby Church; founder of the Djursland branch.
Klit · Silkjær · Silkær
the same family, three spellings
1710—1861Klit — the family’s byname while it lived at Sønder Klit and Husby Klit.
1876—1905Silkjær — the farm name that became the family name in three steps: written on Thomas Jensen in the deed of 1876, used for the children in the census of 1890 and as a byname for Niels Thomsen in the parish register of 1896, and made the lawful family name by Niels’ name certificate of 21 November 1905. The form the family itself writes.
The 1900sSilkær — a spelling found in parts of the Esbjerg branch’s parish registers and vessel registers. The same name, just without the j.

Nine generations

From the copyhold farms on Sønder Klit in 1710 to the present day. All ten of Niels Thomsen Silkjær’s known children have a column each. Together the next generation numbers 73 grandchildren. Under Laura’s name her five children — Niels Thomsen Silkjær’s great-grandchildren — are also shown, to carry the main line down to today. Appendix C · Person cards

The person cards

The brown names in the text open these cards. Here all twenty are gathered together.

Generation 1

Thomas Jensen

12.12.1825, Husby — 9.11.1878, at sea

The oldest man we know for certain in the family. Smallholder, fisherman and beach bailiff in Økjær — a holding on land, nets in the sea and an office on the beach. Bought the house in Silkjær in 1854/55; in the deed to the Vedersø land of 1876 he appears as “Thomas Jensen Silkjær” — the earliest known record of the family name, which the newspapers’ death notice later repeated.

Occupation
Smallholder and fisherman in Økjær, Husby parish — and beach bailiff, the parish office for wrecks and stranded goods
Father
Jens Olesen Klit, b. 17 May 1785
Paternal grandfather
Ole Jensen Klit, b. 1753 on Sønder Klit — the family’s roots go back to the middle of the eighteenth century, and the byname then was Klit, not Silkjær
Married
20 November 1853 in Vedersø Church to Anne Marie Jansdatter — the witnesses were the two fathers, and before the wedding he lived with his brother Ole Jensen on Husby Klit [S68]
Brothers and sisters
Among them his brother Ole Jensen, b. 1818; his brother Esper Jensen Klit, 1829—1883, the survivor of the wreck of 1878; and his sister Anne Marie, b. 1837, married to Anders Knudsen Øe, who drowned in the same boat [S69]
Baptised
1 January 1826, Husby Church
Mother
Maren Thomasdatter, b. 4 February 1790 in Stadil
Five children
Niels 1855 · Maren 1857 · Marie 1859 · Kirstine 1860 · Karen Marie 1862
Widower
For fifteen years — from Anne Marie’s death in 1863 to his own in 1878
Died
Lost at sea on 9 November 1878, aged 52, when the boat capsized on the innermost bar off the Stage lifeboat station. Five of six men drowned. Buried in Husby on 17 November
Caveat
He is named among the five dead in Dannevirke 13.11.1878 and Korsør Avis 14.11.1878. The newspapers, written on the day of the disaster, reported that no bodies had drifted ashore; the parish register’s collective note at the burials singles out only Iver Chr. Olesen Kløve’s body as not having come ashore — the other four, Thomas Jensen among them, did.

Chapters 1—6 · mentioned again in chapter 9

Sources: S1, S2, S25, S42, S67

Generation 1 · the Tarpgaard family

Anne Marie Jansdatter

25.9.1827, Tarp in Vedersø — 15.8.1863, Økjær

A farmer’s daughter from the neighbouring parish, who married down in land and up in risk. She had barely nine years in Økjær and died at 35, leaving small children. Without her there would have been no Niels — and none of the chapters that follow.

Family
The Tarpgaard family, Tarp in Vedersø parish. Daughter of the farmer Jan Andersen, Tarpgaard
Born
25 September 1827; baptised at home the same day and presented in Vedersø Church on 4 November [S92]
Married
20 November 1853, Vedersø Church
Moved
First to Husby Klit, where the couple lived with Thomas’ brother Ole Jensen; from 1854/55 in their own house in the marsh [S68]
Died
15 August 1863 in Økjær, 35 years old — six weeks before her birthday; the register of deaths writes 36. Buried on 23 August. The column for cause of death is blank, as in several of the parish’s entries that year.
Chapters
Chapters 3—4

Sources: S1, S2, S38, S92

Generation 2 · the man who took the name

Niels Thomsen Silkjær

9.7.1855, Husby — 17.6.1928, Esbjerg Hospital

Smallholder and fisherman in Økjær like his father. In the oldest papers he is simply Niels Thomsen; in the later ones Niels Thomsen Silkjær; the name certificate of 1905 made the name legal, and the parish register of 1920 writes “smallholder Niels Silkjær”. With the farm name the family had, for the first time, a name that could be inherited.

Baptised
22 July 1855, Husby Church
Conscription board
Entered in the levy roll in 1873 (levy district 28, Husby, letter Y, serial no. 5) as Niels Thomsen, son of the smallholder Thomas Jensen — 62¾ inches tall, about 164 cm. The board’s note in 1878: chest measurement 29½ inches, found exempt from military service and struck off the roll. The following year he stood at the lifeboat. [S112]
Married 1)
14 November 1878 — five days after his father’s death and three days before his funeral — to Ane Johanne Kristensen, b. 1843, twelve years older than he. His father stood as witness — the declaration had been made while he was alive. She bore the daughter Ane Marie on 2.3.1880 and died the same year.
Married 2)
10 November 1881 in Husby to Ane Jensen, b. 29.4.1858 in Ejsing near Vinderup
Honoured
The Dannebrogsmænd’s Badge of Honour, awarded on 10 November 1915 as serving boatman — in his thirty-seventh year at the station. He signed the oath of loyalty in Vedersø on 30 November 1915, and his own account of his life lies in the archive of the Chapter of the Royal Orders; after his death the cross was returned on 9 July 1928. The title Dannebrogsmand recurs in Dansk Fiskeristat 1935—36, and the badge is worn visibly in the portrait. [S8, S58, S110, S111]
Occupation 2
Boatman at the Vedersø lifeboat station, appointed on 1 January 1879, retired on grounds of age on 1 October 1916 — 37 years and 9 months. He stands second from the left in the crew photograph, which the archive dates to 1915. [S58]
At the rescues
Took part 7 times with the lifeboat and 8 times with the rocket apparatus in the rescue of 195 shipwrecked people. In his years of service exactly fifteen successful rescue operations are recorded at Vedersø. [S58]
The date
He was appointed 53 days after his father drowned, and 45 days after the burial date in the parish register — at the station whose boat could not put out on 9 November 1878.
Died
17 June 1928 in Esbjerg, buried in Gormsgade Cemetery — in the sources of the time, Esbjerg New Cemetery
Chapters
Chapters 5—8 · mentioned as father and grandfather through to chapter 22

Sources: S1, S2, S8, S15, S58, S110, S111, S112

Generation 2 · first wife

Ane Johanne Kristensen

25.9.1843, Rindom parish — 13.9.1880, Økjær

She married Niels on 14 November 1878 — five days after his father drowned and three days before his father’s funeral. She was about twelve years older than he, and the marriage lasted less than two years.

Married
14 November 1878, Vedersø Church
Age
She was born in 1843, he in 1855 — she was about twelve years older. Whether the difference in age or the circumstances on the place mattered for the marriage, the sources do not say.
Daughter
Ane Marie, born on 2 March 1880
Died
13 September 1880 in Økjær, 36 years old, just over six months after the birth. Buried in Husby churchyard on 19 September.
Caveat
The marriage entry gives the groom’s father as witness — the declaration was made when the banns were read, so the wedding was being prepared before his death. [S28]

Generation 2 · second wife

Ane Jensen

29.4.1858, Ejsing near Vinderup — 28.6.1936, Esbjerg

She came into a home with a baby after a dead wife and herself bore a large family by dune and marsh. Her last years were spent in a fishing skipper’s home on the harbour in Esbjerg.

Married
10 November 1881, Husby
Nine children
Thomas 1882 · Ane Johanne 1883 · Jens Klaus 1886 · Esper 1888 · Karen Marie 1890 · Ane Kirstine 1892 · Sidsel Kathrine 1894 · Jensine Kristine 1896 · Ellen 1902
Her roots
The parish book points to her parents as Jens Claus and Stine. The family file identifies them as Jens Claus Matzen, b. c. 1831 in Schleswig, and Ane Kirstine Hansdatter of Landtingmark; the full names have not been checked in the Ejsing parish register. The local history account records a schoolboy Jens Claus Mattzen in Husby — examined in arithmetic and discharged from school by the parish board on 15 April 1846, with the booklet’s remark that the foreign-looking spelling was probably owing to his birth and baptism in Angeln in South Schleswig. If the schoolboy is her father — name, parish and age fit — the family’s thread towards the duchies gains both a place and a figure; see caveat 07 [S169]
Died
28 June 1936 at 3 o’clock at Havnegade 179 in Esbjerg — her son Thomas’ address — 78 years old. Buried on 3 July in Gormsgade Cemetery, section Ø, row 11, no. 10, next to her son’s grave. Cause of death: heart failure. The family file has 23 June; the death certificate takes precedence. [S143, S144]
The arc
From Ejsing in 1858 to Esbjerg harbour in 1936: from open boats hauled up on the sand to decked boats with engines

Chapters 6 and 8 · mentioned in chapters 11, 14, 19 and 21

Generation 3 · of the 1st marriage

Ane Marie

2.3.1880 — 26.3.1960, Husby

The eldest of the children, daughter of Niels and his first wife. She passed the name on in the way that came to mark the women of the family: in the middle of her child’s name.

Married
1908 in Husby to the smallholder Ole Lauridsen, b. 29.5.1861 in Husby, of the family the district called “Klem”
Son
Niels Silkjær Lauridsen, b. 9 August 1911 on Husby Klit — his father’s surname last, his mother’s family name in the middle
The son’s life
Smallholder at Damhus, Sønder Nissum, married in 1938 to Elin Kamma Lillelund. Seen at the age of eight in the school photograph from Husby School, 1919.
Eight children
Vort Sogns Historie gives eight [S27]; Margrethe Dorthea 2.9.1908 [S161] · Ane Johanne 1909 · Agnethe 1910 · Niels Silkjær 1911 · Kristine 1913 · Valdemar 1913 · Maren 1915 · Ole 14.5.1916 [S162]
Died
26 March 1960 in Husby, buried there on 31 March — she lived in the parish all her life

Generation 3 · fishing skipper

Thomas Nielsen Silkjær

10.1.1882, Husby — 20.3.1950, Havnegade 179, Esbjerg

Where his sister Ane Johanne went inland, he went out towards the sea — to Esbjerg, the town that grew in one generation from open field to Denmark’s foremost fishing town. He has a full biography in Dansk Fiskeristat 1935—36.

Baptised
5 February 1882
Young
Confirmed in Husby in 1896 — the parish register lists him “af Økjær” and his father as “Niels Thomsen (kaldt Silkjær)”. Seaman’s book 28 September 1903; called up to the Navy, service 21.9.1905—23.4.1906. The levy roll moves him from the Husby district directly to Esbjerg with a removal certificate of 12 May 1906, and in 1910 on to the Holmsland Klit district — with a short recall to the Navy in October the same year
Married
5 May 1906 on Holmsland Klit to Kristiane Enevoldsen, b. 27.3.1873, daughter of the farmer Simon Enevoldsen of Haurvig. The witnesses were her father and her former father-in-law, the fishery warden Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen; marriage licence 30 April, probate court certificate 3 May 1906. She died on 31.7.1963 at the old people’s home in Esbjerg, buried in Gormsgade Cemetery.
Trained
The Fishing Skippers’ School in Esbjerg, 1916—17
Vessel
Master and owner of the cutter E.94 ANNE KIRSTINE, 1923—1948. Registered as “T. N. Silkjær”.
Home
Havnegade 179, Esbjerg — the bridge between the family’s two worlds
Seven children
Five with Kristiane, and the two of 1913, each with a different woman — the son Arne with his stepdaughter Kristine Oline and the daughter Else Margrethe with Nielsine Nielsen; see the sections below. The five: Kristen Lauridsen (4.5.1904 at Aargab — 31.7.1985 in Esbjerg, buried on 3 August in Gormsgade Cemetery; baptised in Haurvig Church two years before his parents’ wedding, where the parish register names Thomas as the declared father. Skipper’s examination 1924, master of E.426 BERGIT; in the tax books alternately C. L. and K. L. from 1925 to 1956) · Anna (17.2.1907 in Esbjerg — 10.10.1952 in the same place; the birthplace confirmed by the census of 1921, the dates by the Register of Deaths [S86]) · Niels (b. 26.9.1910 at Aargab, baptised in Haurvig Church) · Ejlerth Marius (b. 29.1.1915, Hjertinggade 13, baptised in Zion’s Church) · Elna Elisabeth (b. 20.1.1919) — she also appears in the census of 1930 at Gl. Færgevej 7. The family file also lists a twin sister Kirsten; the parish register has only one birth on 4 May 1904, and Kirsten is therefore treated as a duplicate.
The sons
Niels ran arms in through Esbjerg harbour with ANNE KIRSTINE in March 1945 and brought in skipper Jens Frich on VEGA; Ejlert helped Hans Kvist find more skippers. Ejlert died on 28 May 1985 and Niels on 16 April 1986; both lie in Fovrfeld Cemetery, but in separate sections. [S10, S108]
The flight, 1912
On 14 December 1912 he secretly left the home at Årgab together with the neighbours’ daughter, Nielsine Nielsen, b. 23.11.1887 — first to Kiel, where her father found them between Christmas and New Year, lodging as a married couple “from Esbjerg”; the police expelled him, and from Vamdrup they disappeared again. Then Copenhagen, where they lived together “as man and wife” — he in work at the Copenhagen Floating Dock — until he was arrested on 21 February 1913 at a quarter to seven in the morning on the corner of Strandgade and Torvegade. He declared in court that it had been his intention not to return. [S119, S129, S174, S175]
Sentenced, 1913
On 14 April 1913 the Extraordinary Court of Ulfborg-Hind Hundred sentenced him to “Eighteen Months” of hard labour in the house of correction for breach of § 162 of the Penal Code — incest with his stepdaughter Kristine Oline Enevoldsen since the summer of 1911, when she was fifteen. At the examination on 22 March he himself admitted that he “must be said to have seduced her”. The prosecutor asked for the severest penalty the law allowed, the defence for the mildest; the sentence was read to him outside the gaol on 15 April — he declared himself “satisfied” and waived his right of appeal. He began serving his sentence in Ringkjøbing Gaol on 27 April; admitted to Vridsløselille on 3 July 1913 as prisoner no. 240. His counsel, the solicitor Kamp, applied for a pardon in July with the judge’s recommendation — the Ministry of Justice refused; at the King’s jubilee on 15 November 1913 he was pardoned by royal resolution of the same day, as one of seven prisoners recommended, and released at 4 p.m. [S119, S121, S166, S167, S168]
Two children, 1913
In 1913 he appears in two parish registers as the declared father: Arne, born on 26 May at Årgab to his stepdaughter, and Else Margrethe, born on 15 November in Aarhus to Nielsine Nielsen. Arne was born while he was held in Ringkjøbing Gaol; Else Margrethe on the day he was released from Vridsløselille. [S47, S124]
Arne
The child was born on 26 May 1913 at Aargab, while he was held in Ringkjøbing Gaol, and baptised in Haurvig Church: Arne Enevoldsen. The parish register names him as “Udlagt Barnefader: Stiffader Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, 31 Aar” — declared father: stepfather Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, 31 years. In 1930 he still lives in the household at Gl. Færgevej 7 — entered as a foster child. His later life is followed in chapter 13.
Died
20 March 1950 at Havnegade 179, 68 years old; buried on 24 March in the churchyard in Gormsgade, section Ø, row 11, no. 9, with the note “D.D. (double depth)”. Kristiane was laid in the same grave on 4 August 1963. In the year of his death E.94 ANNE KIRSTINE passed to his son Niels. [S108]

Chapters 9—13 · the sons and the cutter in chapters 17—18

Sources: S8, S9, S10, S44, S45, S46, S70, S71, S72, S73, S119, S121, S124, S166, S167, S168, S174, S175, S176

Generation 3 · the stepdaughter

Kristine Oline Enevoldsen

17.5.1896, Nysogn — 18.5.1940, Esbjerg

She was born six weeks after her father, the boat skipper Christen Olesen Enevoldsen, drowned off Årgab. She never saw him. When her mother remarried in 1906, Thomas Nielsen Silkjær became her stepfather; she was nine.

Parents
Christen Olesen Enevoldsen, b. 17.10.1871 at Aargab — skipper of the boat “Forsøget”, lost in the wreck of 1.4.1896, buried from Haurvig Church on 6.4.1896 — and Christiane Enevoldsen, b. 27.3.1873
Posthumous child
She was born six weeks after the wreck and never saw her father. His name stands at the top of the memorial stone at Renderne. [S48]
Brothers and sisters
Enevold Jepsen, b. 1892, and Simon, b. 1894 — both later fishing skippers in Esbjerg
The letter
It was she herself who brought the case to light: pregnant, and without her mother’s knowledge, she wrote to Pastor Hornbech in Randers, the mission’s travelling preacher, whom she knew from his visits to the dunes — in all probability Carl Marius Hornbech, travelling preacher 1909—15, living in Randers; see caveat 31. In his reply he urged her to confide in her mother — and she did so on the Thursday evening of 13 February 1913, by handing her the letter; four days later the police constable wrote his report. [S119, S172, S174]
The case, 1911—13
The records preserve her words in reported form: before the first time, she said that it was wrong and that she might become pregnant — he brushed it aside. He admitted in court that he had seduced her. Even so, she herself was sentenced under § 162: one month’s simple imprisonment, reduced under the youth provisions §§ 21 and 37 and suspended under § 20 of the provisional Penal Code of 1 April 1911 — the court expressly gave her young age as the reason. The prosecutor had asked for the severest penalty the law allowed for her as well; the defence for a suspended sentence, and the court followed the defence. She was heavily pregnant and did not appear in court; the sentence was read to her and her guardian in person at the home at Årgab on 19 April by the parish summons officers — both declared themselves “satisfied with the Judgment”. [S119, S121, S122, S123, S174]
17 March 1913
Her own statement was taken in the home at Årgab: the court travelled out to her, because she could not come to Ringkøbing. She explained, among other things, that she knew it was wrong — but not that it was punishable; that her confidant was Anders Hejde’s eighteen-year-old son in Bjerregaard — Søren Mathiasen Heide, born on 17 November 1893; and that in December she had told her stepfather that he was to blame for her being unwell. [S163, S170]
The maintenance case
Three days after the baptism, on 18 June 1913, a paternity case was brought in her name against her stepfather — case 82/1913, “Christine Oline Enevoldsen v. Thomas Nielsen Silkjær”, concluded on 20 June. Seventeen years old, with the child’s father in gaol. [S120]
Son
Arne Enevoldsen, b. 26.5.1913 at Aargab — nine days after her seventeenth birthday. She gave birth at home at Årgab; the parish register lists her by name and age as “Ugift Moder” — unmarried mother. [S47]
After 1913
She stayed on the dunes when her mother moved to Esbjerg with the children in 1913, but by 1 February 1916 at the latest she was in the town herself: the census lists her as an unmarried domestic help at Nørregade 44 — on the same census day that Arne was listed as one of the household’s children in Hjertinggade. Married on 19.9.1916 to the fisherman Niels Peder Edvard Nielsen, from 1930 Højberg. The daughter Gerda Jensine born 23.2.1917. A household of her own at Helgolandsgade 14, first floor, in 1921 and still in 1925 — without Arne; in November 1930 at Cort Adelersgade 15b. [S75, S78, S81, S82, S133]
Died 1940
She died on 18 May 1940, at three o’clock in the night, at Esbjerg Municipal Hospital — the day after her forty-fourth birthday. The death certificate gives cancer of the uterus as the principal illness, with wasting as a complication; her home was Frodesgade 149. Buried on 22 May 1940 in Esbjerg New Cemetery — now Gormsgade Cemetery — from Zion’s parish by Pastor Birke, entered as Christine Oline Højberg née Enevoldsen. See caveat 22. [S83, S84]

Generation 4 · the foster child

Arne Enevoldsen

26.5.1913, Aargab — 27.12.1998, Vejle

Born six weeks after the sentence and five weeks before his father was delivered to Vridsløselille. He was given his mother’s surname and grew up in his father’s house — on paper as a foster child.

Baptised
15 June 1913 in Haurvig Church by Pastor S. R. Madsen. Godparents: the girl Johanne Andersen, smallholder Enevold Jepsen Enevoldsen, smallholder Søren Andersen Jensen and smallholder Thyge Nielsen — all of Årgab
The parish register
The Nysogn parish register names them both and writes the relationship out: “Ugift Moder Christine Oline Enevoldsen, Aargab. 17 Aar. Udlagt Barnefader: Stiffader Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, 31 Aar.” — unmarried mother Christine Oline Enevoldsen, Aargab, 17 years; declared father: stepfather Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, 31 years. [S47]
The father
He was held in Ringkjøbing Gaol when Arne was born — sentenced on 14 April, admitted to Vridsløselille on 3 July. He was present neither at the birth nor at the baptism.
The maintenance
Three days after the baptism a paternity case was brought in the mother’s name against the child’s father — case 82/1913 in the district bailiff’s case list, 18—20 June 1913. The boy’s maintenance was put on a formal footing before he was a month old. [S120]
1916
The census of 1 February lists him as a two-year-old in the household at Hjertinggade 13, Esbjerg — as “Arne Silkjær”, under Children, with no distinction from Thomas and Kristiane’s own children. See caveat 21. [S76]
1930
The census of 5 November lists him as a seventeen-year-old in the household at Gl. Færgevej 7, Esbjerg, with his position in the family given as foster child — the only one in the house not called Silkjær
Married 1940
Married on 11 May 1940 in Zion’s Church by Pastor Bentzen, entered as “Ungkarl Revisor Arne Enevoldsen, Havnegade 179” — bachelor, accountant, at his father’s address — to Annagrethe Thomsen, dental technician, b. 4.4.1916 in Jerne. Witnesses: the bride’s father and “Fiskeskipper Silkjær, Havnegade 179”. The entry names only his mother. Seven days later Arne’s mother, Kristine Oline, died. [S85]
After 1940
The census of 5 November 1940 lists him on Rolfsgade in Esbjerg, and the tax books then follow him address by address in the town until 1956, when the series ends. In 1943—45 he is an accountant at Rolfsgade 127, where the family orders three photographs from Paul Bølling — a gathering in the living room and two pictures from the birth of their daughter in May 1944. By royal licence of 22 March 1954 the daughter was adopted by Annagrethe’s new husband, Ronald Søren Hyllested, and thereafter bore the name Hyllested — at her confirmation in 1959 she appears as Annette Hyllested with her mother and adoptive father at Spangsbjerg Kirkevej 42. The daughter became a nurse and moved to Copenhagen, where she lived for the rest of her life and had two children; the family does not believe she later had contact with Arne, but that cannot be established with certainty. She died in 2024, shortly after her eightieth birthday. The tax books have Arne in Esbjerg on both sides of the licence — he was alive when the adoption was granted. He died in Vejle on 27 December 1998, eighty-five years old; the death notice was placed by Edna on the family’s behalf, after the funeral had taken place. See caveats 12 and 25. [S40, S57, S86, S89, S93, S113, S147, S173]
The insurance society
The fishermen’s liability insurance society in Esbjerg had had the bank clerk E. Enevoldsen as treasurer and bookkeeper; after his death Arne took over the work. When the society was entered in the Insurance Register as no. 468 on 5 January 1945, he appears as its manager — and on the board sat, among others, the fishing skipper Thomas Silkjær. The society could be bound by the chairman together with the manager. [S140, S141]
The divorce, 1949
The marriage to Annagrethe was dissolved by licence on 3 June 1949. She was married to Ronald Søren Hyllested by the Copenhagen Magistrates on 11 February 1950. [S139]
Married 1950
Married in a civil ceremony in Esbjerg on 2 December 1950 at 12.10 to the telephonist Edna Alice Söderwall, née Gram, b. 21.9.1913 in Esbjerg. Both divorced; both residing at Strandbygade 39. The witnesses were two office workers; no family members stood as witnesses. At her death in Vejle in 2002 Edna still bore the name Enevoldsen. [S40, S139]

Generation 3 · the Vejlby branch

Bodil Marie Bossow

8.4.1887, Auning — 13.7.1969

Generation 3 · the widow from Årgab

Kristiane Enevoldsen

27.3.1873, Haurvig — 31.7.1963, Esbjerg

Married at 19, widowed at 23, married again at 33 to a man almost nine years younger than she was. She lived to 90 and died in Esbjerg, a hundred kilometres from the dunes where she was born.

Parents
Farmer Simon Enevoldsen and Ane Marie Christensen, Haurvig
Married 1)
1 April 1892 in Haurvig Church to Christen Olesen Enevoldsen, b. 17.10.1871 at Årgab, smallholder, fisherman and boat skipper — the same surname, but two different Enevoldsen families on the dunes
Widow
He drowned off Årgab beach on 1 April 1896 — exactly four years after the wedding. The body was found the next day on Peder Christian Nielsen’s (Dahl) stretch of beach at Bjerregaard and buried from Haurvig Church on 6 April, Easter Monday.
Sons
Enevold Jepsen, b. 13 October 1892, named after his paternal grandfather — and Simon, b. 2 May 1894, named after his maternal grandfather.
Married 2)
5 May 1906 in Haurvig Church to the fisherman Thomas Nielsen Silkjær, b. 1882 — the witnesses were her father and her former father-in-law. The son Kristen had been born two years before the wedding, in 1904; the parish register named Thomas as the declared father.
The widow’s years
She lived as a widow for ten years with three children, “entirely without Means”, and received support from the Harboøre Fund — the fund from the disaster of 1893. Of her second marriage she said in court that it had not been entered into for the sake of support but was founded on “a strong and deep Love”. [S119]
In court, 1913
Her statement of 7 March 1913 is the longest in the case: how her daughter handed her Hornbech’s letter, the marriage, the suspicion about Nielsine, which he denied. She did not wish charges to be brought against him for adultery — and the same day reached a settlement in the maintenance case: 300 kroner a year for her and 90 kroner for each of the three children of the marriage. When the court sat in the home at Årgab on 17 March to examine her daughter, she was in all probability herself one of the two court witnesses — the signature “Chr. Silkær”; see caveat 29. At the final hearing on 26 March she and the guardian withdrew charges under § 174. [S119, S163]
Died
31 July 1963 in Esbjerg, 90 years old
Caveat
The sons’ birth entries have not been read in the original in Nysogn (Haurvig church district), births 1892—1894. The number of three children is confirmed by the prison register’s “3 Stedbørn” — three stepchildren. [S31, S32, S44, S45]

Generation 3 · the Gudum branch

Esper

17.3.1888, Økjær — 1.12.1960

The brother who took the name inland. Esper became a farmer and millwright, married into Gudum and had eight children on the farm Nørre Tangshus — one of them carried the trade on as a millstone dresser, and the youngest took the name all the way to Australia.

Born
17 March 1888 in Økjær, Husby parish — baptised on 29 March in Husby Church
Occupation
Farmer and millwright, later farm owner
Married
17 March 1913 — his twenty-fifth birthday — in Gudum to Jensine Mortensen, b. 9 July 1889 at Nørre Tangshus in Gudum parish, daughter of Jens Mortensen and Kristiane Knudsen — d. 10 December 1982 in Struer, 93 years old
The farm
The couple set up home on the farm where she was born, Nørre Tangshus in Gudum; in their old age they moved to a house at Fredensgade 11 in Struer
Children
Eight children, all born at Nørre Tangshus: Knud Vognsgaard (1913—1959, smelter, killed in the explosion at the steelworks in Frederiksværk — see chapter 20), Niels (1914—1999, farmer in Gudum, eight children), Jens (1916—2000, farmer, millstone dresser and parish council chairman, nine children), Anne Kristiane (1917—2009, twelve children on a farm in Hjerm — it was she who, as “Ane Pedersen, née Silkjær”, wrote the obituary of her brother), Krista (1920—2006), Alma (1923—2013, lived and died on Ærø), Helga (1925—2004) and Otto (b. 1932, emigrated to Australia)
Grief, 1959
A year and a half before his own death, Esper lost his eldest son: Knud was killed on 27 May 1959 in the great explosion at the steelworks in Frederiksværk, one of five workers who lost their lives that day. The family from Skævinge had visited Fredensgade at Easter [S148, S149, S150]
Died
1 December 1960 in Struer

Jensine Kristine

Born

The boy was baptised on Whit Sunday, 27 May, in Husby Church, carried by her sister Ane Kirstine and with her father Niels Silkjær among the godparents.
